## Record 106 — Ministry National Curriculum Assessment and Reporting Policy: historical assessment safeguards, not curriculum indicators

- **Official source:** Fiji Ministry of Education, *Policy in National Curriculum Assessment and Reporting*, Ministry-hosted PDF: https://www.education.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/POLICY-IN-NATIONAL-CURRICULUM-ASSESSMENT-AND-REPORTING.pdf. The PDF title page uses the Ministry name “Ministry of Education, National Heritage, Culture & Arts and Youth & Sports.”
- **Approval and date caution:** The document records Ministerial approval and an effective date of 5 September 2011 (printed p.13; PDF lines 733–770). Its stated review date is 5 September 2012 (printed p.13). The PDF is still hosted on the Ministry domain, but its presence online does not establish that it remains the current operative policy in 2026. No replacement or current-status confirmation has been established in this research. Treat it as an authenticated historical Ministry policy with current status PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW.
- **Assessment principles recorded in the policy:** It calls for valid and reliable assessment; a range of formative and summative evidence over time; fair, developmentally appropriate assessment; explicit criteria; moderation; accurate achievement records; and use of assessment evidence to improve teaching and learning (printed pp.2, 5–10; PDF lines 34–69, 269–333, 411–562, 654–696). It describes multiple forms of evidence including observation, oral and written work, models, performances, interviews, portfolios and self/peer assessment (printed pp.8–9; PDF lines 464–513).
- **Early-childhood/early-primary safeguard:** The policy says assessment from preschool to Class 2 is to support learning and development, not selection or ranking; it describes assessment as descriptive and informal, including observation, anecdotal evidence and developmental journals (printed p.12; PDF lines 703–725). This supports a non-ranking, developmentally appropriate design safeguard, but the policy's current status must be checked before treating it as binding in 2026.
- **Outcome integrity:** The policy cautions that checking isolated facts or component skills may help diagnose learning, but should not replace assessment of the actual learning outcome in its fullest sense (printed p.8; PDF lines 423–444). It also says inclusive assessment can vary the way learners demonstrate the same outcome without diluting the outcome or lowering the achievement standard (printed p.9; PDF lines 515–542).
- **PacEdu application if confirmed current:** Design daily learning evidence around the verified syllabus outcome; show clear success criteria; use varied and accessible ways for learners to demonstrate the same outcome; collect evidence over time; distinguish diagnostic practice from a full outcome judgment; and retain teacher review/moderation. Do not turn this policy into subject-specific indicators, ability labels, a new grading scale or a requirement that every worksheet use a particular assessment format.
- **Curriculum lineage:** This policy is assessment governance, not a subject syllabus. It supplies no English, Mathematics, Science or other subject CLOs/achievement indicators and cannot fill gaps in the prescription register. No older subject indicator is promoted from this policy.
- **CAS contact timing:** All questions about whether this policy has been replaced, its current 2026 status, and any successor policy are recorded for verification during the PacEdu pilot only. No CAS contact or request is to be made now.
- **Classification:** SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY as historical Ministry assessment-policy evidence; current operative status/supersession PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW; CAS verification DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT. No indicator promoted to PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED; no worksheet created from this policy.
- **Source evidence:** Ministry-hosted policy, printed pp.2, 5–10, 12–13 (PDF lines 34–69, 269–333, 411–562, 654–725, 733–770); Education Policy Bank metadata also identifies the Ministry as publisher and the policy's 2011 modified date: https://pacificdata.org/data/dataset/national-curriculum-assessment-and-reporting.

## Record 107 — USP-linked 2021 Year 5 English syllabus research: document retrieval and strand-integration lead

- **Research source:** Evangeline Christina Narayan, *In Search of Principles of Second Language Acquisition in the Design and Unpacking of Fiji’s English Syllabus* (October 2021), University of the South Pacific affiliation; thesis record and abstract hosted on ResearchGate: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/360454874_IN_SEARCH_OF_PRINCIPLES_OF_SECOND_LANGUAGE_ACQUISITION_IN_THE_DESIGN_AND_UNPACKING_OF_FIJI%27S_ENGLISH_SYLLABUS.
- **What it establishes:** The study says its Year 5 document set included the Fiji National Curriculum Framework, a Year 5 English Syllabus, Learning and Teaching Programmes collected from eight primary schools in Labasa, and a Year 5 English Language, Literacy and Communication textbook. This is a strong bibliographic retrieval lead that a distinct Year 5 English syllabus and associated LTPs/textbook were in use by the schools studied. It does not itself authenticate a controlled Ministry copy, establish the syllabus edition or approval date, or show that it remains current in 2026.
- **Strand labels recorded in the research:** Listening and speaking; Writing and shaping; Reading and viewing. The author reports that the study found limited integration among these strands in the materials/practices examined. This is the researcher’s analysis, not a Ministry-issued indicator, current teaching directive or proof that the strands remain unchanged in the current curriculum.
- **Limitations:** The thesis is secondary research, not the original Ministry syllabus. The abstract does not provide the exact CLO wording, coded achievement indicators, page references or complete Year 5 sequence. The sample of eight schools is not a national audit. Do not infer a mandatory daily strand rotation or create indicators from the researcher’s critique.
- **PacEdu use:** Use the thesis as a retrieval lead for identifying the exact Year 5 syllabus title, associated LTPs and Year 5 English Language, Literacy and Communication textbook. If those originals are independently located, record their edition, issuer, page/section, controlled status, older-source lineage and reuse terms separately. As a non-prescriptive pedagogical design consideration only, keep all verified strands visible in curriculum mapping and avoid allowing one strand to displace the others.
- **Rights safeguard:** The thesis record says a full-text PDF is available and that author-uploaded content may be subject to copyright. Do not copy its thesis text, school LTPs or textbook extracts into PacEdu. Obtain and assess permissions before any reproduction/adaptation.
- **CAS contact timing:** Questions for CAS about the identity/current status of the Year 5 syllabus and its controlled predecessors are recorded for the PacEdu pilot only. No CAS contact or request is to be made now.
- **Classification:** SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY as academic research and a retrieval lead; original syllabus identity/current status and exact CLOs PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW; reproduction/adaptation BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW; CAS verification DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT. No indicator promoted to PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED; no worksheet created.
- **Source evidence:** ResearchGate thesis record, abstract and bibliographic details (lines 0–21 and 31–39): https://www.researchgate.net/publication/360454874_IN_SEARCH_OF_PRINCIPLES_OF_SECOND_LANGUAGE_ACQUISITION_IN_THE_DESIGN_AND_UNPACKING_OF_FIJI%27S_ENGLISH_SYLLABUS. USP Discipline of Linguistics and Languages page lists Evangeline Narayan as a USP staff member and provides current research context: https://www.usp.ac.fj/linguistics-languages/news-and-events/.

## Record 113 — Historical primary Mathematics prescription (1994), curriculum-project withdrawal (2008), and later LTP distinction

- **1994 historical prescription lead:** A 2006 peer-reviewed mathematics education article by S. Sharma cites a “new mathematics prescription for classes 1 to 6” attributed to the Fiji Ministry of Education, Women, Culture, Science and Technology (1994). It reports that the prescription gave greater emphasis to statistics at primary level. The article does not reproduce the controlled prescription or its detailed outcomes/indicators. This is a bibliographic and historical lead only; obtain the original 1994 document before using any wording or inferring Year 5/6 indicators.
- **2008 implementation caution:** A FijiVillage report dated 3 December 2008 states that Cabinet withdrew the planned nationwide curriculum implementation schedule, which had been intended to begin in 2009, citing inadequate preparation on professional issues and concerns raised during review of the Fiji Education Sector Program. This report concerns a broad curriculum implementation plan; it does not prove that the specific unpublished 2008 Draft Year 5–6 Mathematics Syllabus cited in Record 111 was the same document/project, nor does it establish whether that draft was later revised, trialled, approved, or abandoned. Do not infer adoption or non-adoption of the individual draft from this report alone.
- **2015 review / current teacher planning distinction:** Datt and Ishii (2022), in a comparative study of Fiji and Japan, report that Fiji's Mathematics curriculum was last revised in 2015 and describe the Ministry-prepared syllabus as the intended curriculum supplied to schools. They distinguish teacher-developed yearly UOW/SOW/LTP plans from the syllabus and describe textbooks as resources rather than the syllabus itself. This is secondary research, not a Ministry status notice; its statement about 2015 is a lead for locating controlled revised documents, not proof of the current 2026 edition or exact effective date.
- **Historical strands evidence:** The same 2022 study describes Fiji Year 1–2 strands as Number, Measurement, Shape and Space, Patterns, Chance and Data; Years 3–4 and Years 7–8 as Numbers and Numeration, Algebra, Measurement, Geometry, Chance and Data. Its extracted summary does not provide a Year 5 strand list, so do not interpolate Year 5 from adjacent levels.
- **Lineage and concept rule:** Sharma's 1994 citation supports investigating the historical place of statistics/data in primary Mathematics. It does not verify the modern Year 5 M5.3.4 time/temperature LTP codes in Record 112. The 2008 draft, 2015 review report, Year 6 activity textbook and teacher LTP must each be traced to original controlled pages before individual concepts are connected into a progression.
- **PacEdu action:** Search for the original 1994 Classes 1–6 Mathematics prescription, the unpublished 2008 Year 5–6 draft and its decision trail, and controlled 2015 Year 5/6 syllabi and scope-and-sequence. Keep syllabus/CLO, indicator, teacher elaboration, LTP sequence, activity, assessment and textbook resource as separate fields. No indicators promoted and no worksheets created.
- **CAS contact timing:** Any authentication, successor-edition, approval, supersession and rights questions are deferred until the PacEdu pilot. No CAS contact or request is to be made now.

## Record 116 — Fiji FinED Class 5/6 manual (2012): CAS-developed 2010 framework, integrated financial learning outcomes, and rights/status controls

- **Source identity:** FinED Fiji: A Manual for Teachers, Class 5/6, published by Young Enterprise Trust and the Pacific Financial Inclusion Programme (PFIP), 2012; © United Nations Capital Development Fund 2012. The manual identifies the Fiji FinED Project as a partnership involving the Ministry of Education, Young Enterprise Trust and PFIP, supported by the Australian Bilateral Aid Programme. Official NFIT Fiji website currently lists the Class 5/6 manual and dates the web resource listing 21 April 2015. The manual itself is dated 2012; do not confuse website upload/listing date with publication date.
- **Framework provenance:** Manual pp.12–17 says the Financial Education Framework for Classes 1–8 was developed in December 2010 by senior members of the Curriculum Advisory Service (CAS), assisted by technical advisers. It contains competency indicators, concepts, conceptual financial understandings, strands/sub-strands and learning outcomes. This is a valuable Ministry-associated curriculum development source, but it is a FinED framework/manual, not a core Mathematics syllabus.
- **Important qualification:** Manual p.6 states that there was no specific policy on Financial Education at the time. Manual p.9 describes activities as integrated across curriculum areas and says the integrated approach was endorsed by the then-current Fiji curriculum prescriptions and the draft Fiji Islands National Curriculum Framework. NFIT's project page describes FinEd as integrated into compulsory primary Maths, English and Social Studies from April 2013. These historical statements support the existence and intended integration of the FinED project, but they do not by themselves establish the current 2026 legal status, current implementation, current prescribed subject allocations or supersession. Keep status pending current controlled confirmation.
- **Framework competencies (p.12):** informed financial judgments and decisions; apply financial knowledge, skills and values; confidence with financial terms/concepts; recognise financial consequences; recognise financial value of cultural wealth; use financial tools to achieve goals; understand time/commitment; respond to personal/economic circumstances; contribute to community financial well-being/security; set/achieve goals consistent with personal and communal values. These are financial competency indicators in the FinED framework, not Mathematics CLOs.
- **Strands/sub-strands (p.16):** Managing Money (money, spending/budgeting, saving, credit); Income and Wealth (income, wealth creation/assets/liabilities); Planning Ahead (financial planning, financial risk). This is a separate financial education structure; do not reclassify these as core Mathematics strands.
- **Class 5/6 learning outcome examples (pp.17–18):** use Fiji coins/notes for transactions up to $50; relate Fiji currency value to other currencies; interpret more complex receipts; describe regular family financial commitments; prioritise needs and wants; prepare an activity/event budget and keep transaction records; evaluate savings deposit options; explain banks' community role; explain how credit and interest work. These are reproduced here only as source-labelled concept/outcome leads. Preserve their original FinED subject integration and historical Class 5/6 context; do not promote to PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED.
- **Pedagogy/assessment (pp.7–9):** action-learning, linking to prior learning and home contexts, revisiting ideas in different contexts; prescriptive testing is not advocated; suggested evidence includes formative assessment, observation, student self-assessment, peer assessment, records/cash books/budgets, anecdotal notes and portfolios. This is historical FinED guidance, not an automatic current PacEdu assessment rule.
- **Curriculum cross-links:** The framework explicitly identifies Maths and English and Maths/English/Social Studies/Social Sciences cross-links (p.17). For PacEdu, store a concept once with subject cross-links rather than duplicate it as a separate mandatory indicator in every subject.
- **Older lineage:** The framework's own history begins with the 2009 Money Pacific Goals, 2010 development of a Classes 1–8 framework, and project phases in 2010–2012. This is lineage for the FinED framework only; no evidence here establishes that the same outcomes were part of the 1994 Primary Mathematics Prescriptions or any later core Mathematics syllabus. Keep those lines of provenance separate.
- **Rights:** UNCDF copyright ©2012 is explicit. Do not copy lesson text, worksheets, games, stories, tables or images into PacEdu without appropriate written permission/licensing. Factual concept names may be recorded in a source register with citation, but adapted/reproduced teaching material remains BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.

## Record 117 — Fiji pre-1970 Mathematics context; 1969 primary-syllabus search false positive corrected (Tanzania)

- **Fiji historical context:** Hem Chand Dayal's USP paper, *Teachers' perceptions of teaching mathematics at the senior secondary level in Fiji*, describes pre-1970 Fiji Mathematics as arithmetic-dominated, listing numbers and calculations, fractions and decimals, time and linear measure, money, ratio, proportions, averages and percentages. It says changes were recommended by the 1969 Royal Commission and the Curriculum Development Unit (CDU) had been established within the Ministry of Education in 1968. This is a secondary research summary of historical context, not the 1969 Commission's original text or a controlled primary syllabus.
- **Important scope correction:** The same paper says the UNDP curriculum review launched in 1970 was confined to Forms 1–4 (Years 7–10), and that this review was completed by 1984. Do not mistake that secondary curriculum review for the primary Mathematics prescription lineage or infer that it rewrote Classes 1–6 content.
- **1969 syllabus false positive:** An ERIC PDF search extract appeared to say “The Primary School Mathematics Syllabus drafted in 1969.” Inspection of the full report identifies that passage within the Tanzania national report, not Fiji. The same report's bibliography names Tanzania's Ministry of National Education and Dar es Salaam. It is therefore excluded from Fiji evidence. No claim is made that Fiji's 1969 Primary School Mathematics syllabus has been found.
- **CDU primary remit:** Clive Whitehead's 1981 historical study of Fiji education states that the CDU, established in 1968, was charged with revising curricula and producing supporting texts for both primary (Classes 1–6) and junior secondary (Forms 1–4) schools. This is useful institutional chronology, not proof of a particular 1969 primary Mathematics syllabus or its detailed contents.
- **Cross-check against 1981/82 curriculum inventory:** Gil Stamp's historical research reproduces a 1982 inventory of extant Fiji science-based primary curricula (Elementary Science, Art and Craft, Health Education and Gardening Programme), but this list is explicitly limited to science-based curricula. It cannot be used to infer that Mathematics was absent from Fiji's curriculum or that the inventory is a complete list of all prescriptions.
- **Concept/source handling:** The historical arithmetic topics listed by Dayal may be retained as broad predecessor-era context only. Do not assign them to a particular Class, convert them into modern CLOs/indicators, or assume unchanged progression into the 1994 prescription without original Fiji primary documents.

(1981), *Education in Fiji: Policy, Problems, and Progress in Primary and Secondary Education, 1939–1973*, LSE thesis: https://etheses.lse.ac.uk/1199/1/U050087.pdf ; Stamp, G. historical education-sector research, Fiji education prescriptions/materials inventory: https://gilstamp.wordpress.com/education-for-skills-part-iv/ ; ERIC report (1983), *An International Review of Applications in School Mathematics*, pp.137–141, Tanzania section and bibliography (false positive only): https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED230443.pdf.

## Record 118 — 1969 Fiji Education Commission report: primary structure and curriculum-revision mandate; 1971 curriculum false positive excluded

- **Original report bibliographic identity:** Fiji Education Commission, *Education for Modern Fiji: Report of the Fiji Education Commission*, Suva: Government Printer, 1969, 126 pages. The ERIC international bibliography identifies the report and summarises its coverage as curriculum and examinations, language and culture, teacher education, primary/secondary/adult education, education of Fijians, education structure, teaching service, finance and priorities. Digital Pasifik's catalogue independently lists the Fiji report as a Fiji text but says it is not online. The original report itself has not yet been obtained or inspected.
- **Commission process chronology:** Clive Whitehead's ANU historical study says the commission was appointed in 1968, visited Fiji in late 1969 and its report was published early in 1970. This explains why later sources sometimes refer to a 1969 commission/report while the publication date may be recorded as 1970. Preserve both distinctions: commission/report title year 1969; publication reported as early 1970 pending title-page inspection.
- **Curriculum-policy evidence:** Helen Tavola's 1990 LSE thesis summarises the commission as criticising narrow, examination-oriented curricula and making 81 recommendations across teacher quality/quantity, geographic and racial disparities, and curriculum. It says post-independence education planning initially relied on late-1960s directives, especially the commission's recommendations. This is a secondary account of policy, not a list of Mathematics learning outcomes.
- **Primary/junior-secondary structural change:** Tavola's thesis reports the commission recommended changing the school structure from eight years primary/four years secondary to six years primary/four years junior secondary, with later senior-college years. Fiji Times' 2015 historical overview independently reports the recommendation for experimental rural junior-secondary schools for Years 7–10 and corresponding primary schools reduced to Years 1–6. This documents school-structure context, not a Mathematics syllabus or a subject-specific outcome.
- **CDU mandate chronology:** Tavola's thesis quotes the 1969 Education Department annual report as saying that in 1968 Government established the Curriculum Development Unit to revise curricula and produce supporting texts for primary Classes 1–6 and junior-secondary Forms 1–4. This is a historical institutional mandate and does not establish the title/content/status of a specific Mathematics prescription.
- **Critical scope limit:** Neither the ERIC bibliography, Tavola's thesis nor the Fiji Times article provides the original Commission's detailed Mathematics recommendations or a Class-by-Class primary Mathematics syllabus. Do not infer that arithmetic topics from the earlier syllabus were altered, removed or retained by the Commission. No Maths indicators can be extracted from this evidence.
- **False-positive correction — “1971 new primary school curriculum”:** A search result claimed that Fiji's new primary curriculum of 1971 was drafted by inspectors, trialled subject syllabi and approved by the Minister. Inspection of the underlying document shows it is *Towards a Better Future: A Review of the Irish School System* (2017), describing Ireland, not Fiji. Exclude the 1971 statement entirely from Fiji's source lineage. Do not confuse it with Fiji's 1971–75 Development Plan or Fiji's 1971 post-independence education developments.
- **Primary-source retrieval lead:** Obtain the original 126-page Fiji Education Commission report and the Fiji Education Department Annual Report for 1969 (the latter is cited by Tavola for the CDU's mandate). These may identify the primary curriculum transition and original source references. No CAS request now; defer direct verification until the PacEdu pilot.

## Record 119 — 1970–1976 Fiji Mathematics reform evidence is junior-secondary, not primary; Hong Kong annual-report search results excluded

- **Primary/secondary distinction:** Hem Chand Dayal's published study of Fiji Mathematics says the UNDP curriculum review initiated in 1970 was confined to Forms 1–4 (Years 7–10) and completed by 1984. It separately describes the pre-1970 Mathematics curriculum as arithmetic-dominated. This is secondary research and does not identify the detailed primary Classes 1–6 syllabus.
- **1971 workshop / later secondary course:** A separate research source on Fiji Mathematics reports that leading Fiji Mathematics teachers took part in a UNDP/UNESCO-funded workshop in 1971, which produced curriculum-development guidelines; it says the resulting Fiji Forms 1–4 Mathematics curriculum was introduced five years later. This is evidence about junior-secondary curriculum development only. Do not import Forms 1–4 content, teaching sequence or workshop guidelines as primary indicators.
- **UNDP/UNESCO scope cross-check:** Gil Stamp's historical research distinguishes regionally oriented UNDP/UNESCO courses from 1970 for Forms I–IV, including Mathematics, from primary science-based courses designed locally. It reports that the secondary courses experienced readability, cost and teacher in-service difficulties, and that CDU later produced locally oriented courses to address those problems. This does not show that a comparable UNDP Mathematics syllabus existed for primary Classes 1–6.
- **Primary syllabus status remains unresolved:** A 2006 Fiji Islands National Curriculum Framework document states that the 1970 UNDP/UNESCO project developed curricula for Forms 1–4, while the CDU later carried responsibility for school curriculum development. This is framework history, not a primary Mathematics prescription. A 1981–82 inventory of primary science-based curricula lists Elementary Science, Art and Craft, Health Education and Gardening; because the inventory is explicitly limited to science-based curricula, its omission of Mathematics is not evidence that primary Mathematics had no syllabus.
- **Historical date caution:** Sources vary on CDU establishment as 1968 or 1969. Record 118 has the 1968 claim from historical thesis/annual-report quotation; Dayal's paper says 1968 in one passage and a 2006 article's abstract refers to 1969. Do not silently standardise the date; retain the discrepancy pending primary records.
- **False-positive correction — Education Department Annual Reports 1968–69 and 1969–70:** Search results for these exact titles led to Hong Kong annual reports, not Fiji. The pages contain Hong Kong school enrolments, Hong Kong currency and other local references. They are excluded from Fiji evidence. Do not cite or use them as Fiji Education Department records.
- **No primary indicator extraction:** None of these sources supplies a controlled Fiji primary Mathematics syllabus, Class-by-Class outcomes or current status. The 1971 workshop and Forms I–IV course are only junior-secondary lineage. No primary worksheet or indicator is generated from them.
- **Sources:** Dayal, H.C., “Teachers' perceptions of teaching mathematics at the senior secondary level in Fiji,” USP repository PDF: https://repository.usp.ac.fj/id/eprint/7805/1/Teachers_perceptions_of_teaching_mathematics_at_the_senior_secondary_level_in_Fiji.pdf ; Fiji Mathematics curriculum history research, Number sense or no sense (ACU Research Bank), section 2.8: https://acuresearchbank.acu.edu.au/download/a6472bad472e43ca5e5c199bffda69e711e1e6d893055c402bd7f3ea8730fd1b/2215394/64903_downloaded_stream_128.pdf ; Stamp, Education for Skills – Part IIA and Part IV: https://gilstamp.wordpress.com/education-for-skills-part-2a/ and https://gilstamp.wordpress.com/education-for-skills-part-iv/ ; Fiji Islands National Curriculum Framework copy (historical account): https://studylib.net/doc/18782043/the-fiji-islands-national-curriculum ; Hong Kong annual reports (excluded): https://www.histsyn.com/2022/12/EDU1968.html and https://www.histsyn.com/2022/12/EDU1969.html.

## Record 123 — 1994 Primary Mathematics Prescription: secondary research clarifies the statistics/probability distinction; 2017 lesson-study paper confirms a later syllabus-use lead

- **1994 prescription described in peer-reviewed research:** Sashi Sharma's 2006 *Waikato Journal of Education* paper, “How Do Pasifika Students Reason About Probability? Some Findings From Fiji,” explicitly says Fiji produced a new primary Mathematics prescription in 1994 that gave greater emphasis to statistics at primary level. The same paper says probability was introduced at secondary level (Form 4) in the context of random events. This is a secondary author's description of the 1994 prescription, not the original document or an itemised CLO/indicator list.
- **Interpretation boundary:** the 2006 paper supports a historical distinction between primary statistics and secondary probability in the 1994 curriculum context. It does not prove that probability is excluded from all later primary curricula, nor establish the current 2026 placement. Do not import the Form 4 statement into current planning without the applicable current prescription.
- **1996 bibliographic lead clarified:** Ravinesh Prasad's 2017 Fiji National University article, “Trainee Teachers’ Feedback and Reflection on Math Lesson Study,” lists the Ministry of Education in Fiji's 1996 *Mathematics Prescription: Classes 1~6* in its references. The article describes trainee teachers selecting topics after consulting Fijian Mathematics syllabi and textbooks, but does not reproduce or analyse the 1996 prescription's content, approval status or current validity. This remains bibliographic evidence only.
- **Teacher-practice evidence kept separate:** Prasad's 2017 paper describes collaborative lesson study, use of prior knowledge, hands-on/minds-on activities and an observer checklist for problem-solving lessons. These are research/practice examples, not Ministry-mandated teaching indicators or a substitute for the prescription.
- **Retrieval status:** the 1994 and 1996 originals remain uninspected. Obtain controlled copies and verify title pages, edition, class-level progression, exact wording, approval/effective dates and reuse rights before any indicator is promoted. Preserve the 1994 and 1996 records as separate documents until comparison establishes their relationship.
- **Sources:** Sharma, S. (2006), *Waikato Journal of Education* 12, “How Do Pasifika Students Reason About Probability? Some Findings From Fiji,” especially pp. 88–89: https://researchcommons.waikato.ac.nz/server/api/core/bitstreams/ec27b07f-b02a-460a-b317-817cfee98f49/content ; Prasad, R. (2017), “Trainee Teachers’ Feedback and Reflection on Math Lesson Study,” *International Journal of Advanced Research* 5(12), 237–242, especially bibliography p. 242 and lesson-study discussion: https://www.journalijar.com/uploads/934_579_IJAR-20937.pdf .

## Record 124 — Extracted Mathematics concept entries for the teaching bank: number, operations, patterns, measurement, shape, data and statistical reasoning

**Purpose:** Content extraction, not source history. Entries below are usable concept-bank candidates. They are NOT verbatim Ministry achievement indicators. Observable statements are PacEdu working indicators derived from cited concepts and remain supplementary until matched to an approved current prescription.

### A. Number and operation sense — USP Numeracy Resource Repository
**Source concepts:** counting and number systems; number line and types of numbers; relative size and multiple representations; place value; decimal notation; addition and subtraction; meanings of numerical operations; prime, even, odd, square and cube numbers; ratios, proportions and percentages; computation and estimation; relationships between numbers.
**PacEdu working indicator candidates (derived, not verbatim):**
- Represent a number in more than one way and explain how the representations show the same value.
- Locate and compare numbers using a number line or another suitable representation.
- Use place value to explain the value of digits in a numeral.
- Select and carry out an appropriate operation for a stated problem, and explain what the operation means in that context.
- Estimate an answer before calculating and use the estimate to check whether the result is reasonable.
- Identify and describe number relationships, including even/odd, prime, square and cube numbers where appropriate to verified year-level scope.
- Represent and use ratios, proportions and percentages in a context when the verified year-level scope requires them.
**Locator:** USP Numeracy Resource Repository, Content and Blocks, lines 44–57 and 112–140. This is a developing regional resource, not a Fiji primary year-by-year prescription.

### B. Patterns, relationships, functions and algebra — USP Numeracy Resource Repository
**Source concepts:** patterns; relationships; functions; representing mathematical situations and structures with algebraic symbols; mathematical models for quantitative relationships; analysing change; introduction to algebra; algebraic operations; deriving algebraic representations; solving algebraic equations; rates and linearity; graphs and functions; linear versus non-linear relationships; intersections and simultaneous equations.
**PacEdu working indicator candidates (derived, not verbatim):**
- Identify, continue and describe a pattern using words, numbers, diagrams or symbols.
- Explain a relationship between quantities using a table, diagram, graph or symbolic representation.
- Use a symbol to represent an unknown quantity in a mathematical situation.
- Construct or interpret a mathematical model to represent a quantitative relationship.
- Describe how a quantity changes when another quantity changes.
**Locator:** USP Numeracy Resource Repository, lines 52–57 and 142–173. The repository includes advanced algebra; do not assign those topics to primary classes without year-level prescription evidence.

### C. Measurement and shape — USP Numeracy Resource Repository
**Source concepts:** direct measurement with standard units; estimating length using reference points; indirect measurement; proportionality of similar figures; Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric ratios; units and measured quantities; angles and lines; parallel and perpendicular lines; vertical and complementary angles; classifying shapes by sides or angles; perimeter, area and volume and the relationship of their formulae to length, width, height and radius.
**PacEdu working indicator candidates (derived, not verbatim):**
- Choose an appropriate measuring tool and standard unit for a given quantity.
- Estimate a measurement, measure it, and compare the estimate with the measured result.
- Classify shapes by observable properties such as number of sides and angles.
- Identify and describe lines and angle relationships when included in the verified year-level scope.
- Explain what perimeter, area or volume measures and identify the dimensions needed to calculate it.
- Use a scale or proportional relationship to solve a measurement problem when included in the verified year-level scope.
**Locator:** USP Numeracy Resource Repository, lines 59–64 and 175–188. The examples include secondary-level content; do not move it into primary worksheets without year-level evidence.

### D. Data, statistics and probability — USP NRR and 1994 prescription research reference
**Source concepts explicitly listed by USP:** collecting, organising and displaying data; selecting an appropriate chart or graph for the data and intended message; analysing and interpreting data; understanding how changes in a data set affect mean and median; chance and probability from impossible (0) to certain (1).
**Fiji-specific historical evidence:** Sharma (2006) states that Fiji's 1994 primary Mathematics prescription gave greater emphasis to statistics at primary level. The same paper describes probability as introduced at Form 4 in that historical curriculum context. This is not the original prescription's detailed wording and does not establish current placement.
**PacEdu working indicator candidates (derived, not verbatim):**
- Collect and record data relevant to a stated question.
- Organise data in a suitable table or display.
- Select a chart or graph that appropriately represents the data and explain the choice.
- Read a data display and state what it shows using evidence from the data.
- Compare data sets and describe how a change may affect a measure such as mean or median, only at a verified level where those measures are taught.
- Discuss chance using appropriate language and distinguish impossible from certain events only where the current year-level prescription includes probability.
**Locators:** USP Numeracy Resource Repository, lines 65–70; Sharma (2006), Waikato Journal of Education 12, pp. 88–89, lines 29–37. The 1994 prescription itself remains unavailable for direct extraction.

### E. Historical arithmetic concept bank — Dayal, Fiji mathematics education paper
**Source concepts reported for pre-1970 Fiji mathematics:** numbers; calculations with numbers; fractions; decimals; time; linear measure; money; ratio; proportions; averages; percentages.
**PacEdu use:** retain as historical concept-lineage prompts and search terms for locating older prescription pages. These are not class-level indicators and must not be presented as current or mandatory.
**Locator:** Dayal, USP paper, lines 48–56.

### F. Cross-cutting mathematical thinking — USP NRR
The repository names conceptual understanding, adaptive reasoning, strategic competence, procedural fluency and productive disposition. Use these only as supplementary planning/evidence lenses:
- Conceptual understanding: learner explains the meaning and relationship behind an idea, not only a procedure.
- Adaptive reasoning: learner gives a logical reason for choosing or applying a method.
- Strategic competence: learner represents a problem and develops a way to solve it.
- Procedural fluency: learner selects an efficient method, calculates accurately and checks reasonableness, including estimation or mental methods where suitable.
- Productive disposition: learner shows willingness to engage, persist and make sense of mathematical tasks.
These are not subject content indicators and do not replace a prescription's own assessment criteria. Locator: USP NRR, lines 72–89.

### Extraction and status rules
- All PacEdu working indicator candidates above are paraphrases created for the concept bank, not quotations from Fiji prescriptions.
- USP NRR content is SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY; it is a regional, evolving resource whose topics span multiple levels. Its page says open-access numeracy modules use a Creative Commons licence but are not for commercial use; PacEdu commercial reuse/adaptation remains BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW pending licence compatibility and permission review.
- Dayal's pre-1970 arithmetic list is SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY and historical.
- Sharma's description of 1994 primary statistics emphasis is SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY; the original 1994 prescription remains PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW.
- No class/year allocation, mandatory status or daily worksheet is authorised by this extraction. Do not promote any entry to PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED until the current controlled Fiji prescription is inspected and exact wording, page, edition, approval/effective date and older-source lineage are recorded.
- **Sources:** USP Numeracy Resource Repository: https://www.usp.ac.fj/usp-stemp/nrr/ ; Dayal, Teachers' perceptions of teaching mathematics at the senior secondary level in Fiji: https://repository.usp.ac.fj/id/eprint/7805/1/Teachers_perceptions_of_teaching_mathematics_at_the_senior_secondary_level_in_Fiji.pdf ; Sharma (2006), How Do Pasifika Students Reason About Probability? Some Findings From Fiji: https://researchcommons.waikato.ac.nz/server/api/core/bitstreams/ec27b07f-b02a-460a-b317-817cfee98f49/content .

## Record 125 — Mandatory extraction standard for the PacEdu daily-activity concept bank

**Requirement:** Every usable curriculum resource must be examined for its actual educational content. Source-history notes alone do not satisfy this requirement. The purpose of this register is to supply traceable content for daily teaching and learning activities.

### Required extraction fields for every entry
- Subject and curriculum area.
- Class/year/form and learner level exactly as stated by the source; if not stated, mark LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED rather than guessing.
- Strand, sub-strand, topic or unit exactly as the source names it.
- Exact achievement indicator, learning outcome, concept, skill, knowledge item or assessment criterion, preserving the source wording where rights permit.
- Content type: ACHIEVEMENT_INDICATOR; CONCEPT; SKILL; KNOWLEDGE; LEARNING_OUTCOME; ASSESSMENT_CRITERION; or PEDAGOGY.
- Source title, issuing body/author, edition/year, version/status, printed page/section and stable URL or file reference.
- Older source lineage for the same concept/indicator, with exact source and page; if not found, record LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND and continue research.
- PacEdu plain-language interpretation and observable learner evidence, clearly distinguished from source wording.
- Candidate daily-activity link: worked example, guided practice, independent practice, application/context, assessment evidence and prerequisite knowledge. These are planning fields, not new official indicators.
- Status: PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED; SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY; PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW; or BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW. Teacher review remains PENDING_TEACHER_REVIEW where applicable.
- Rights/reuse condition and any restriction on copying, adapting, translating or commercial use.

### Extraction rules
- Read the actual source pages, not only its title, catalogue entry, bibliography, search snippet or a secondary author's summary.
- Extract all relevant concepts/indicators in the source section, not just a short historical description. Keep one concept/indicator per entry so it can be sequenced and used independently.
- Preserve exact official indicator wording and source locator. Do not silently rewrite it. Put PacEdu explanation in a separate field.
- Do not manufacture a year/class allocation from a cross-level resource. Mark it LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED until a Fiji scope-and-sequence or prescription provides the allocation.
- Where two sources disagree, keep both source records and flag the discrepancy; do not merge or choose one without approval/status evidence.
- Map each current indicator to its older lineage before daily worksheets are generated, as requested. A lineage match supports provenance but does not itself establish current mandatory status.
- Supplementary concepts can inform separate supplementary activities after source and rights review; they must never be labelled mandatory Ministry indicators.
- A daily activity may be generated only from an extracted, traceable concept/indicator with an identified class/year and appropriate rights status. Mandatory curriculum activities require PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED source content.

### Current extraction queue
1. Fiji Ministry/CAS controlled prescriptions and scope-and-sequence documents, beginning with Years 1–4 English and Mathematics revised curriculum, then Years 5–8 and secondary subjects. The Ministry's 2022–23 annual report states that 648 final syllabus and Literacy/Numeracy Guide copies for Years 1–4 were supplied to primary schools, while 250 draft copies were supplied to 90 trial schools. This establishes a high-priority document set to retrieve; it does not itself disclose their indicator wording.
2. Older Fiji prescriptions and syllabi for each subject/class to identify the source lineage for every extracted current indicator.
3. Fiji Ministry teacher guides and textbooks: extract concepts, examples, teaching sequence and assessment support as supplementary teaching resources, not as substitutes for the prescription.
4. Regional and international resources such as USP NRR: extract concepts and possible teaching approaches, mark level carefully, and check licence terms before PacEdu adaptation or commercial use.

### Record 124 content use
The Number/Operations, Patterns/Algebra, Measurement/Shape, Data/Statistics/Probability and mathematical-thinking entries in Record 124 are cross-level supplementary concept candidates from USP NRR and Fiji historical research. They are not yet assigned to Fiji classes or marked mandatory. The next work is to inspect source modules/pages and match each candidate to the relevant Fiji controlled prescription and older lineage before preparing class-specific daily activities.

**Sources:** Fiji Ministry of Education and Heritage Arts, Annual Report 2022–2023, section “The Revised Curriculum,” reporting final Years 1–4 syllabi and Literacy/Numeracy Guides supplied to schools and draft trial copies: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Ministry-of-Education-Annual-Report-2022%E2%80%932023.pdf ; USP Numeracy Resource Repository, scope, content, cognitive components, blocks and licence notice: https://www.usp.ac.fj/usp-stemp/nrr/ .

## Record 126 — Extracted Fiji Year 6/8 English, Year 6/8 PE and Year 6 Mathematics content from Ministry teaching resources

**Purpose:** Actual source-content extraction for the teaching bank. This record captures content and indicators visible in the inspected source pages. It is not a declaration that the 2015 teaching guide or the 2020/2021 textbook is the current mandatory prescription in 2026.

### Source A — Fiji Ministry of Education, Teachers Guide for Y6 & Y8, Term 3 (2015)

- **Official source URL:** https://www.education.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Y6_Y8_Guideline_2-Teachers_Guide.pdf
- **Publisher:** Curriculum Development Unit, Fiji Ministry of Education.
- **Edition/date:** First edition 2015.
- **Printed pages inspected:** cover/front matter; pp. 1–8.
- **Source purpose statement:** compiled to assist Year 6 and Year 8 teachers to design lessons after the external examination (printed p.1). It is therefore a Term 3 post-examination guide, not proof of the complete annual syllabus.
- **Rights:** Ministry copyright; classroom reproduction permitted with CDU acknowledgement; other use must be referred to the Permanent Secretary through the Director Curriculum Advisory Services. PacEdu digital adaptation/reuse is BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW pending permission.

#### A1. English — Year 6 Reading Skills

- **Source locator:** printed p.7; section heading “ENGLISH READING SKILLS-Y6”; sub-strand EN 6.1.
- **Content Learning Outcome:** EN 6.1.1 — “Evaluate a range of written texts and make meaning out of it.”
- **Achievement-indicator concepts extracted from the source list:**
  1. Identify different text types.
  2. Discuss the main ideas in a passage.
  3. Use skimming and scanning to identify main points.
  4. Summarise a story.
  5. Read fluently with understanding.
  6. Use new vocabulary correctly in a sentence.
  7. Form new words from a root word.
  8. Answer comprehension questions correctly.
  9. Write comprehension answers in complete sentences.
- **Text-type concepts:** narrative; descriptive; procedural/instructional; fiction; non-fiction.
- **Vocabulary concepts:** synonyms; antonyms; parts of speech; spelling; word meaning.
- **Reading modes and oral-language teaching concepts:** group reading; choral reading; modelled reading; individual reading; topic discussion; oral presentation; dialogue and role-play.
- **PacEdu interpretation / observable evidence (derived, not official wording):** learner identifies a text's type and main idea, locates key information using skimming/scanning, retells or summarises the text, reads with understanding, explains unfamiliar vocabulary, builds related words from a root, and writes a complete-sentence response supported by the passage.
- **Level:** Year 6 explicitly stated.
- **Older lineage:** LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND. Search for the earlier Year 6 English syllabus/prescription and older teacher guides before any worksheet is authorised.

## Record 128 — Historical Fiji primary English syllabus evidence and reading/language lineage lead (1968–1991)

**Purpose:** Record actual English curriculum aims and content architecture reported from the earlier Fiji primary English syllabus. This helps trace the historical lineage of later reading and oral-language concepts, but it does not establish that any specific 2015 Year 6 indicator is identical to an earlier prescribed indicator.

### Source identity

- **Author:** Heather Lotherington-Woloszyn, University of the South Pacific.
- **Title:** *Literacy in ESL: Pedagogical and Cultural Pathfinding in Fiji*.
- **Date/type:** Conference paper, December 1991; ERIC document ED357627.
- **Source:** https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED357627.pdf
- **Source locators:** PDF pp. 3–6; the discussion of the primary English syllabus begins on printed page 3 of the paper (PDF page 4).
- **Source type/status:** Secondary analysis quoting/describing an earlier Fiji primary English syllabus and the SPC/Tate course. It is not the original controlled syllabus. Mark HISTORICAL_LINEAGE_REFERENCE, not PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED.
- **Scope:** Primary English / English as a Second Language; paper says oral work begins in Class 1 and ESL literacy in Class 2.
- **Rights:** ERIC-hosted conference paper; do not copy substantial passages. Use short attributed quotations only where needed and otherwise paraphrase.

### Extracted source evidence

1. **Earlier syllabus aim:** The paper quotes the syllabus as aiming to help children “understand and use the English language with ease and accuracy” (paper p.3; it attributes the quotation to the syllabus, p.1).
2. **Class progression reported:** oral English work starts in Class 1; literacy in English as a second language starts in Class 2 (paper p.3).
3. **Programme content architecture:** the prescribed SPC/Tate materials are described as structurally graded oral-language drills and accompanying graded readers (paper pp.3–4).
4. **Historical programme lineage:** the SPC/Tate course was developed for Cook Islands primary ESL in the 1960s and Fiji adopted it in 1968 (paper p.4). This is the paper's historical account, not a substitute for inspecting Fiji's original adoption circular or syllabus.
5. **Teaching/literacy resource concepts described:** oral language; graded drills; graded readers; reading; storybooks; shared reading; children's literature; rhymes; songs; poetry; experience-based literacy resources (paper pp.4–6).
6. **Later enrichment approach described:** the paper reports the USP Primary Reading Project / Ready to Read as an enrichment approach, with shared reading, story-based language and literacy, children's books, rhymes, songs and poetry (paper pp.5–6). These are reported enrichment approaches, not proof of mandatory Fiji syllabus indicators.

### Lineage relationship to Record 126 — Year 6 English Reading Skills

- **Possible broad continuity:** English language comprehension and the ability to understand/use English are broad predecessor aims relevant to later reading comprehension and vocabulary learning.
- **Possible resource-method continuity:** graded readers and reading materials are historical precursors to later text-based reading instruction.
- **Not established:** no evidence in this paper maps the 2015 Year 6 outcomes EN 6.1.1 or its listed indicators (text types, main ideas, skimming/scanning, summarising, fluency, vocabulary, root words and complete-sentence comprehension answers) to specific 1968/earlier syllabus codes or pages.
- **Required next lineage source:** retrieve the original Fiji primary English syllabus and SPC/Tate implementation materials, then compare exact class-level wording and sequence. Until that is done, keep each Record 126 English indicator's lineage as LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND; Record 128 is a contextual predecessor lead only.

### PacEdu content handling

- Preserve the earlier syllabus aim as a short attributed historical outcome statement, not a current mandatory indicator.
- Do not convert the reported Ready to Read or shared-reading approaches into a mandatory prescription.
- Do not infer modern literacy expectations from this 1991 paper. Use it only to locate older source documents and understand broad predecessor aims.
- No daily worksheet authorised; CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

**Source:** Lotherington-Woloszyn, H. (1991), *Literacy in ESL: Pedagogical and Cultural Pathfinding in Fiji*, ERIC ED357627, pp. 3–6: https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED357627.pdf .

## Record 131 — Fiji Year 1 English Language, Literacy and Communication resource book (2013; revised 2019; reprinted 2020)

**Purpose:** Extract the actual Year 1 learning content and activity concepts visible in the Ministry-issued resource. This is a resource-book extraction, not proof that each activity is a formally approved achievement indicator or that this is the current controlled Year 1 prescription.

### Source identity and controls

- **Title:** *Year 1 English — Language, Literacy and Communication*.
- **Issuer shown in source:** Ministry of Education, Heritage and Arts, Curriculum Development Unit, Fiji.
- **Edition history printed in book:** 2013; revised 2019; re-printed 2020.
- **Source copy inspected:** public FlipHTML5 text-view copy: https://fliphtml5.com/gjgbb/miwv/Year_1_English_-_Language%2C_Literacy_and_Communication/
- **Printed pages inspected:** 1–69 (book pp. 5–69 contain the visible teaching/learning units and phonics activity pages).
- **Source integrity note:** the copy is hosted by a third party, not the Ministry website. Title/copyright pages identify the Ministry/Curriculum Development Unit; obtain the controlled Ministry copy before treating it as authoritative current curriculum.
- **Copyright notice (printed p.2):** CAS owns copyright; schools may reproduce in part or full for classroom purposes only with acknowledgement; other use must be referred to the Senior Education Officer English Primary at CAS. PacEdu digital/commercial adaptation or reproduction is therefore **BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW** pending permission. CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.
- **Classification:** SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY / PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW for PacEdu. Not PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED. This is a resource book and activity sequence, not an independently verified current syllabus/prescription.
- **Level:** Year 1 (explicit in title).

### Extracted concepts and observable learning evidence

The source presents activity prompts rather than coded achievement-indicator statements. The entries below therefore retain the distinction: **source activity/content** is what the book actually asks learners to do; **PacEdu observable evidence** is a separate derived description, not official Ministry wording.

1. **Personal oral language and self-description** — Unit 1, printed p.5. Source activities ask learners to state their name, age, clothing and identity, draw themselves, and answer questions about name, age, favourite colour and clothing. Derived evidence: learner gives simple personal information orally and completes a short patterned self-description. **Concepts:** speaking/listening; personal vocabulary; question-and-answer exchange; simple sentence frames.
2. **Letter-name and letter-form recognition** — printed pp.6–9, 11–14, 16–19, 21–24, 26–29, 32–35, 37–45. Repeated activities trace, rewrite and identify upper/lowercase forms, including single letters and selected digraphs. Derived evidence: learner recognises and forms the displayed graphemes. **Concepts:** alphabetic knowledge; upper/lowercase correspondence; letter formation; visual discrimination.
3. **Initial-sound discrimination** — printed pp.6–9, 11–14, 16–19, 21–24, 26–29, 32–33, 37–45 and phonics activities pp.55–57. Learners circle/colour pictures whose beginning sound matches a target letter/sound. Derived evidence: learner identifies a target initial phoneme in a spoken or pictured word. **Concepts:** phonemic awareness; initial phoneme; sound-symbol association.
4. **Medial and final sound discrimination** — printed pp.29–30, 33–35, 45–54 and phonics activities pp.58–60. Learners identify matching middle/end sounds and complete words using displayed vowel patterns. Derived evidence: learner identifies a target medial/final sound and selects or supplies the corresponding grapheme pattern. **Concepts:** phoneme position; medial/final phoneme; vowel patterns; grapheme–phoneme correspondence.
5. **Selected consonant and vowel patterns** — printed pp.29–30, 33–35, 37–40, 45–54; phonics pp.58–60. Explicit examples include /ai/, /oa/, /ie/, /ee/, /or/, /ng/, /oo/, /ch/, /sh/, /th/, /qu/, /ou/, /oi/, /ue/, /er/ and /ar/, alongside single-letter sounds. Derived evidence: learner recognises, says, writes or locates the target pattern in a word. **Concepts:** digraphs; vowel teams; r-controlled vowel patterns; consonant clusters/digraphs as presented; spelling patterns.
6. **Blending/segmenting and word construction** — printed pp.31–32, 35–40, 49–60, 66. Learners combine segmented sound units to read words, supply missing sound patterns, add endings such as “et” and “ay”, and say completed words aloud. Derived evidence: learner blends supplied sound units into a word and identifies component sound patterns. **Concepts:** phoneme blending; segmentation; onset/rime; word completion; decoding.
7. **Word recognition and early reading vocabulary** — printed pp.15, 25, 30–31, 36, 41, 60–64. Word sets and short text include examples such as “my”, “can”, “find”, “the”, “rain”, “day”, “down”, “again”, “get”, “to”, “see”, “help”, “come”, “is”, “it”, “me”, “away”; later pages include short family and daily-routine sentences. Derived evidence: learner reads selected familiar words in isolation or simple sentences. **Concepts:** high-frequency/familiar words; vocabulary recognition; decoding in context.
8. **Oral comprehension and picture discussion** — printed pp.10, 15, 25, 30, 36, 41–42. Questions invite learners to retrieve details from pictures/text, describe actions, respond to familiar experiences and express preferences. Derived evidence: learner answers literal questions and describes a pictured event using simple oral language. **Concepts:** listening comprehension; picture reading; literal response; oral vocabulary; describing actions.
9. **Recitation, rhyme and rhythm** — printed pp.25 and 30. Learners recite short rain-themed rhymes. Derived evidence: learner joins in or recites a short rhyme with recognisable sequence and phrasing. **Concepts:** rhyme; rhythm; oral fluency; memorised language; sound pattern awareness.
10. **Reading and drawing / text-to-image representation** — printed pp.62–65. Learners read simple family and daily-routine sentences and draw corresponding people/actions. Derived evidence: learner represents the meaning of a short sentence through a relevant drawing. **Concepts:** sentence comprehension; vocabulary in context; connecting written language to meaning.
11. **Sentence construction and picture-based writing** — printed p.70. Learners are asked to write a sentence about a picture. Earlier patterned prompts appear on pp.5 and 20. Derived evidence: learner writes a relevant simple sentence using a model or own words. **Concepts:** sentence meaning; basic written expression; picture prompt; patterned sentence construction.
12. **Following written instructions and sequencing** — printed pp.20 and 67. Learners complete a daily routine using a word bank and order letters alphabetically from A to Z. Derived evidence: learner selects contextually appropriate words for a simple sequence and orders alphabet letters. **Concepts:** routine vocabulary; temporal sequencing; word-bank use; alphabetic order.
13. **Colour, size and comparative vocabulary in reading tasks** — printed pp.5, 67–68. Learners identify colours in written directions and compare longest, tallest and biggest objects. Derived evidence: learner follows a short written direction and identifies the requested colour or comparative attribute. **Concepts:** colour vocabulary; adjectives; comparative/superlative meaning; following instructions.
14. **Everyday themes as language contexts** — Units 1–8, printed pp.5–54 and reading activities pp.62–70: self, friends, school, getting ready for school, rainy day, rainy-day activities, family feast and family routines. These are contexts for oral language, vocabulary, phonics and early reading, not separate formal achievement indicators. Derived evidence depends on the specific language task, not merely naming the theme.

### Older-source lineage check

- **Record 128** (Lotherington-Woloszyn, 1991, pp.3–6) reports the earlier Fiji primary English syllabus aim and describes oral work beginning in Class 1, ESL literacy beginning in Class 2, and the historical SPC/Tate oral course with graded readers. This provides broad historical context for oral language and early reading.
- **Not established:** no exact older syllabus wording or indicator code has yet been found that matches this 2013/2019 Year 1 resource's specific phoneme targets, letter patterns, word lists, unit activities, picture-comprehension prompts or sentence-writing tasks. Do not mark these as lineage-verified.
- **Lineage status:** LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND for each detailed concept above. Record 128 is contextual only, not a verified source for the detailed Year 1 content.

### PacEdu handling decision

- Retain each concept above as a separately traceable source-derived concept, not an official achievement indicator.
- Do not create mandatory daily worksheets from this record until the controlled current Year 1 English prescription/scope-and-sequence and older source lineage are checked.
- Keep the source's printed page references, source wording/activity distinction and rights restriction attached to every derived entry.
- **Status:** SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY; PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW; BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW for reproduction/adaptation; LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND.
- **No worksheet authorised. No CAS contact now.**

**Source:** Ministry of Education, Heritage and Arts, Curriculum Development Unit (2013, revised 2019, reprinted 2020), *Year 1 English — Language, Literacy and Communication*, printed pp. 1–69, third-party text-view copy: https://fliphtml5.com/gjgbb/miwv/Year_1_English_-_Language%2C_Literacy_and_Communication/ .

## Record 132 — South Pacific Commission (SPC) Junior Series Reader Book 1 (1966): inspectable early ESL reading predecessor

**Purpose:** Record actual learning-language content from an inspectable 1966 SPC reader, and test whether it provides an older-source relationship to the later Fiji Year 1 English resource (Record 131). This is a historical regional reader, not a Fiji Ministry prescription and not proof of a formal achievement indicator.

### Source identity and adoption context

- **Author:** G. M. Tate.
- **Title:** *SPC Readers: Junior Series, Book 1*.
- **Publisher/issuer:** South Pacific Commission, Nouméa; 1966.
- **Inspected source:** SPC digital library PDF: https://spccfpstore1.blob.core.windows.net/digitallibrary-docs/files/81/81a111a457261c174bc86bc802e91ad3.pdf
- **Source locators:** reader printed pp. 3–32 (PDF text lines 43–647); introductory notes on PDF lines 4–11.
- **Source's own scope statement:** SPC Readers were produced for primary children learning English as a second/foreign language; they were structurally based on the Tate Oral English Course. The Junior Series contains nine books. Book 1 should not be introduced until pupils have had adequate pre-reading and reached at least the oral-English level at the beginning of Book IV of the Oral English Course (front matter, before printed p.3).
- **Fiji connection:** Lotherington-Woloszyn (1991), Record 128, reports that Fiji adopted the SPC/Tate Oral English Course in 1968. This confirms the programme's historical use in Fiji, but the specific scanned 1966 Reader Book 1 is not itself proven to have been the exact prescribed Fiji reader or a formally adopted indicator document.
- **Status:** HISTORICAL_LINEAGE_REFERENCE; SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY for PacEdu content; not PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED. Copyright © South Pacific Commission 1966. Reproduction/adaptation rights for PacEdu not established; keep source text quotations brief and seek permission before reuse.

### Actual content and concepts extracted

1. **Naming and identifying people/objects** — printed pp.3–10, 16–20. Short patterned statements identify family members, children, common objects and people in illustrations (for example, “This is Father”; “This is a book”). **Concepts:** naming vocabulary; nouns; demonstratives; identification; picture–word association. Derived evidence: learner identifies a pictured person/object and matches a short spoken or written label.
2. **Personal and family vocabulary** — printed pp.3–7, 11–14, 16–20, 28–31. Vocabulary includes family roles and personal names, clothing, household objects and familiar places. **Concepts:** family relationships; people; clothing; home objects; possessive names. Derived evidence: learner recognises and uses familiar vocabulary in short statements.
3. **Oral interaction and classroom directions** — printed pp.4–8, 11–16, 19–21, 23–28. Repeated dialogue uses requests and prompts such as calling someone, asking them to come/look, and responding. **Concepts:** listening and responding; turn-taking; requests; simple commands; conversational routines. Derived evidence: learner follows a familiar one-step oral prompt and responds appropriately.
4. **Simple sentence patterns** — printed pp.3–20, 24–31. The reader repeatedly models “This is…”, “Here is…”, “I am…”, “I want…”, “I can…”, “I can see…”, “He/She is…”, “has/have” and “can/can’t”. **Concepts:** basic sentence structure; subject pronouns; present-tense be; simple present/progressive contrast as modelled; possession; ability/negation; question/answer patterns. These are language structures in the reader, not a verified Fiji syllabus grammar sequence.
5. **Action words and present actions** — printed pp.7–8, 14–15, 17–19, 22–27. Actions include running, walking, laughing, crying, reading, dancing, playing, climbing, singing, drawing, standing and sitting. **Concepts:** action vocabulary; verb meaning; describing visible actions; “can” ability statements; progressive action statements. Derived evidence: learner names or describes a visible action using a modelled phrase.
6. **Yes/no questions and short answers** — printed pp.20–23, 26–27. The reader asks whether objects/people can be seen and whether people can perform actions, with “Yes, I can” / “No, I can’t” responses. **Concepts:** question forms; yes/no comprehension; short answers; can/can’t. Derived evidence: learner answers a simple question using an appropriate short response.
7. **Describing and comparing attributes** — printed pp.14–18, 28–30. Content includes colours, big/little, and identifying who owns an object. **Concepts:** colour words; size adjectives; basic comparison; possessive forms. Derived evidence: learner selects or states an object's colour/size or identifies its owner.
8. **Picture-supported reading and meaning** — throughout printed pp.3–30. Short written sentences are paired with illustrations, and learners are asked to identify or answer questions about what can be seen. **Concepts:** visual context; picture-supported decoding; literal understanding; matching text to image. Derived evidence: learner selects the illustration that matches a simple sentence or answers a literal picture question.
9. **Early word recognition and cumulative vocabulary** — printed pp.31–32 include a word list ordered by occurrence in the reader and a companion teacher-book list for flashcards. The word list includes function words, pronouns, nouns, verbs, adjectives and question words introduced in the reader. **Concepts:** cumulative sight/reading vocabulary; word recognition; oral rehearsal; flashcard practice. The source does not supply a modern phonics progression.
10. **Pre-reading as a prerequisite** — source front matter says Book 1 should follow adequate pre-reading and a specified oral-English course level. **Concepts:** readiness sequencing; oral-language preparation before this reader; staged introduction of print. This is a source-specific prerequisite, not a modern diagnostic threshold for PacEdu learners.

### Comparison with Record 131 (Year 1 English resource book)

- **Broad predecessor links supported:** personal/family vocabulary; oral language and question/answer interaction; action and object vocabulary; short patterned sentences; picture-supported meaning; familiar word recognition. These are broad pedagogical/content continuities between a regional ESL reader used in the period of Fiji's SPC/Tate programme and the later Year 1 resource.
- **Not supported by this source:** the 2013/2019 Year 1 book's letter tracing, initial/medial/final phoneme activities, explicit vowel/digraph patterns, alphabetic order, rhyme work, word-bank sequencing, and its particular unit structure. Do not assign Record 132 as lineage for those Record 131 concepts.
- **Exact Fiji prescription lineage:** still LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND. The 1991 paper's account of Fiji adoption in 1968 plus this 1966 regional reader establish historical programme context, not the exact Fiji controlled syllabus, adoption list or exact class-level sequence.
- **Record 131 lineage update permitted:** for only the broad categories above, add a note “HISTORICAL_PREDECESSOR_SUPPORTED — broad content/method continuity only; not an exact indicator match.” Keep detailed phonics and specific unit activity lineage as LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND.

### PacEdu handling decision

- Treat this reader as historical source evidence, not as a mandatory Fiji curriculum prescription.
- Do not recreate its dated character names, cultural examples or dialogue as current mandatory content; use the concept categories only as historical comparison.
- Do not use its pre-reading threshold to place or test modern learners.
- No daily worksheet authorised from this record; no CAS contact now.

**Sources:** G. M. Tate (1966), *SPC Readers: Junior Series, Book 1*, South Pacific Commission, printed pp.3–32, https://spccfpstore1.blob.core.windows.net/digitallibrary-docs/files/81/81a111a457261c174bc86bc802e91ad3.pdf ; Lotherington-Woloszyn (1991), *Literacy in ESL: Pedagogical and Cultural Pathfinding in Fiji*, ERIC ED357627, pp.3–4, https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED357627.pdf .

## Record 134 — Fiji revised Primary Years 1–8 Literacy and Numeracy curriculum: official implementation and controlled-source access trail (2022–2023)

- **Source:** Fiji Ministry of Education, *Annual Report 2022–2023*, Chapter 5 / curriculum implementation section, printed report pages around 99–101 (PDF text lines 4902–5008): https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Ministry-of-Education-Annual-Report-2022%E2%80%932023.pdf
- **Authority:** Ministry of Education, Fiji; official annual report tabled as Parliamentary Paper No. 109/24.
- **Source type:** OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_IMPLEMENTATION_EVIDENCE / CONTROLLED_SOURCE_ACCESS_LEAD; not a syllabus and not a source of individual achievement indicators.
- **Actual evidence extracted from the report:**
  1. The Ministry initially engaged the Fiji Program Support Facility in 2019 to develop scope-and-sequence documents for Primary Years 1–8 Literacy and Numeracy (report lines 4902–4908).
  2. The stated process reviewed ECE–Year 8 curriculum, scoped and sequenced the existing curriculum to identify gaps/inconsistencies, revised syllabi, developed year-level scope-and-sequence documents with elaborations, and revised teacher guides (lines 4911–4921).
  3. Phase 1 Years 1–4 documents were trialled in 90 schools; the report says final copies were printed and implementation rolled out after teacher and Head of School training (lines 4922–4928).
  4. At the time of the report, Years 5–8 were in Phase 2 trial (line 4929). Do not treat this 2022–23 status as proof of their present status.
  5. The report says the revised documents articulate when CLOs are introduced and consolidated and unpack CLOs into sequential yearly elaborations; they also provide guidance for out-of-phase learners (lines 4955–4966).
  6. It states that curriculum documents such as syllabi were uploaded to FEMIS and Moodle (line 4972). This identifies the Ministry-controlled access route to pursue; it does not establish that PacEdu has access or permission.
  7. The report records 648 final Years 1–4 syllabi and Literacy/Numeracy Guides supplied to primary schools, with 250 draft copies for the 90-school trial phase (line 4979).
  8. It states that Years 1–4 implementation began in all primary schools in 2023 (line 5008).
- **What was not extracted:** No exact English or Mathematics CLO wording, achievement indicator codes, year-level elaborations, contact hours or subject-specific page references are reproduced in this annual report section. None may be invented from the process description.
- **Source status:** OFFICIAL_IMPLEMENTATION_CONFIRMED; PRESCRIPTION_CONTENT_NOT_YET_ACQUIRED. This is stronger evidence than Record 133 that the Years 1–4 final package was implemented, but it still does not provide the actual prescription content.
- **Older-source lineage:** The report says current syllabi were reviewed and scope-and-sequence gaps/inconsistencies identified (lines 4914–4919), but it does not identify the exact older syllabus editions or map any individual outcome to an earlier source. Keep each detailed indicator's lineage LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND until the actual old and revised syllabus texts are compared.
- **PacEdu action:** Next obtain the controlled final Years 1–4 English and Mathematics syllabus, scope-and-sequence and teacher-guide files from the Ministry/FEMIS/Moodle source. For each CLO and elaboration, capture exact text, code, year, strand, page, and the superseded source it replaces or develops. Then repeat the same process for Years 5–8 only after confirming their final approved rollout/version. Do not substitute the 2013/2019 Year 1 English resource book, 2015 Term 3 teacher guide, or third-party curriculum maps for these controlled files.
