## Record 135 — Fiji Ministry Years 9–10 English Syllabus (2014): actual Year 9 CLOs and achievement-indicator concepts extracted

### Source identity, status and rights

- **Title:** *English Syllabi — Years 9 & 10*.
- **Issuer:** Fiji Ministry of Education, Curriculum Development Unit (CDU).
- **Edition:** Fiji, 2014.
- **Inspected source:** PDF hosted by The SEE Project: https://theseeproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/l2_year910_english_syllabi.pdf
- **Printed pages inspected:** pp.3–25 (PDF text lines 38–783).
- **Source integrity:** The title page identifies the Fiji Ministry/CDU as issuer; the PDF is hosted outside the Ministry. Obtain the controlled Ministry copy for current-version verification.
- **Copyright:** The source permits school classroom reproduction with CDU acknowledgement; other use must be referred to the Permanent Secretary through the Director Curriculum Advisory Services. PacEdu reproduction, digital adaptation or commercial reuse is BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.
- **Curriculum status:** HISTORICAL_OFFICIAL_PRESCRIPTION_SOURCE / PRESCRIPTION_CONTENT_EXTRACTED; NOT current prescription verification. The 2014 syllabus itself says its concepts, skills and attitudes were selected from older prescriptions (printed p.3), but it does not identify the old prescription editions or provide an item-by-item lineage table.
- **Important structure:** This source distinguishes CLOs (learning destinations) from achievement indicators (what students do to achieve outcomes) and scope of content (themes/topics), printed p.14. PacEdu must preserve these as separate data fields.

### Year 9 source structure

- Key Learning Area outcome: use language effectively and critically through speaking, listening, viewing, reading, writing and shaping in varied forms and situations to explore and communicate ideas.
- Strands: Listening and Speaking; Reading and Viewing; Writing and Shaping.
- Sub-strands: Text Types; Language Features and Rules; Understanding Socio-cultural Contexts and Situations; Language Learning Processes and Strategies.
- The syllabus says the strands are interrelated and should be integrated rather than taught as isolated blocks (printed pp.5–8).
- **Level:** Year 9 only for the entries below. Do not transfer them to Year 10 or other years without the corresponding syllabus row.

### Year 9 coded CLOs and extracted indicator concepts

The following preserves each source CLO code and records a concise paraphrase of its achievement-indicator actions. It does not reproduce full indicator sentences.

1. **EN 9.1.1.1 — Listening and Speaking / Text Types** (printed p.15; PDF lines 378–410). CLO concerns courteous listening and speaking for varied purposes using media texts. Indicator actions: inspect an audio-media text and its features; discuss purpose, tone, audience and context; compare audio and audio-visual media; create and perform a media text; predict content and connect themes to experience. Scope examples include radio, sports commentary, television broadcast, advertisements, careers interview and weather bulletin. **Concepts:** media literacy; active listening; text features; purpose/audience/tone/context; comparison; prediction; oral composition and performance.
2. **EN 9.1.1.2 — Listening and Speaking / Text Types** (printed pp.15–16; PDF lines 415–442). CLO concerns respectful everyday conversation. Indicator actions: select dialogue, analyse its purpose/audience/context, and demonstrate a suitable everyday conversation. Scope includes greetings, classroom instructions, requests, shopping/market visits, appointments and conversations on buses/playgrounds. **Concepts:** conversational register; listening and turn-taking; respectful interaction; practical dialogue; audience and context.
3. **EN 9.1.1.3 — Listening and Speaking / Text Types** (printed p.16; PDF lines 445–453). CLO concerns attentive listening to literary texts and responding. Indicator actions: examine literary features/functions; compare fiction and non-fiction; evaluate a recently read book through purpose, audience, context, characters, setting and plot; illustrate themes/values. **Concepts:** literary listening; genre comparison; book response; character/setting/plot; theme and values; oral reporting and summarising.
4. **EN 9.1.2.1 — Language Features and Rules** (printed p.16; PDF lines 456–462). CLO concerns explaining grammar relevant to spoken communication. Indicator actions: study parts of speech and explain their functions; examine grammar in oral and written work. Scope: nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, subject–verb agreement, tenses, articles, connectives and word order. **Concepts:** grammatical categories; grammar in context; sentence construction; agreement; tense; cohesion.
5. **EN 9.1.2.2 — Language Features and Rules** (printed p.17; PDF lines 475–484). CLO concerns analysing sentence structures for effective communication. Indicator actions: identify sentence types and discuss their features/functions; examine sentence types in spoken text and converse on a chosen topic. Scope: simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences. **Concepts:** sentence classification; clause relationships; sentence variety; oral application.
6. **EN 9.1.2.3 — Language Features and Rules** (printed p.17; PDF lines 488–499). CLO concerns persuasive techniques used to engage an audience. Indicator actions: explore persuasive techniques and their relevance; investigate and present techniques in a spoken text. Scope: idioms, figures of speech, jargon and emotive vocabulary. **Concepts:** persuasion; rhetorical language; audience impact; idiom; figurative and emotive language.
7. **EN 9.1.3.1 — Socio-cultural Context and Situation** (printed pp.17–18; PDF lines 502–520). CLO concerns evaluating and illustrating oral genres in formal contexts. Indicator actions: appraise language in formal situations; analyse speaker–listener relationship, topic and purpose; present an oral genre in a relevant context. Scope includes oral history, speeches, conferences, debates, impromptu speaking, critique and group/interpersonal communication. **Concepts:** formal register; oral genre; audience relationship; purpose; debate; public speaking; intercultural communication.
8. **EN 9.1.3.2 — Socio-cultural Context and Situation** (printed p.18; PDF lines 522–526). CLO concerns examining and demonstrating informal oral communication. Indicator actions: analyse an informal context and explain its purpose, audience and features; demonstrate suitable language. Scope includes informal registers, talanoa, family gatherings, village functions and celebrations. **Concepts:** informal register; context-sensitive language; talanoa; social interaction; cultural context.
9. **EN 9.1.4.1 — Language Learning Processes and Strategies** (printed pp.18–19; PDF lines 529–540). CLO concerns analysing strategies for making sense of text. Indicator actions include identifying techniques that convey meaning and comparing character traits in a relevant scene. Strategy concepts include pre-listening prediction, guessing, background knowledge; during-listening context clues, listening for detail/main idea/time words; post-listening summarising and interpretation. **Concepts:** before/during/after listening; prediction; inference; selective listening; summarising; interpretation.
10. **EN 9.1.4.2 — Language Learning Processes and Strategies** (printed p.19; PDF lines 544–546). CLO concerns engagement with oral-language learning strategies. Indicator actions: select vocabulary/ideas and formulate sentences for an oral presentation; demonstrate useful oral-language learning strategies. Scope includes posture, eye contact and asking questions. **Concepts:** oral presentation planning; vocabulary selection; non-verbal communication; questioning; self-monitoring.
11. **EN 9.2.1.1 — Reading and Viewing / Text Types** (printed p.21; PDF lines 560–560). CLO concerns careful viewing and critical evaluation of printed media. Indicator actions: interpret different text types in relation to purpose, audience and context; formulate themes/values from textual events. Scope includes newspapers, magazines, newsletters, billboards, posters, stickers, documentaries, articles, comprehension passages and translation. **Concepts:** media reading; purpose/audience/context; critical interpretation; theme and values; multimodal texts.
12. **EN 9.2.1.2 — Reading and Viewing / Text Types** (printed p.21; PDF lines 561–561). CLO concerns explaining purpose, message and theme of prescribed literature. Indicator actions: describe purpose/theme/message and audience; examine vocabulary for comprehension; evaluate and present themes associated with universal values. Scope includes short stories, novels, poems and drama. **Concepts:** literary comprehension; message/theme; vocabulary in context; genre; interpretation and presentation.
13. **EN 9.2.1.3 — Reading and Viewing / Text Types** (printed pp.21–22; PDF lines 562–570). CLO concerns interpreting visuals in literary texts. Indicator actions: interpret visuals; relate literary ideas to real life; discuss literary devices in visual/printed texts; identify and use literary features; compare examples, facts and figures of speech. **Concepts:** visual literacy; image-text relationships; transfer to real-life contexts; literary devices; evidence and comparison.
14. **EN 9.2.2.1 — Reading and Viewing / Language Features and Rules** (printed p.22; PDF lines 575–593). CLO concerns language/literary features and rules in printed and visual texts. Indicator actions: apply grammar, mechanics and rhetorical devices in reading/writing; infer author purpose and relate lessons to experience/culture. Scope includes fiction/non-fiction, documentaries, movies, flashback, alliteration, point of view, irony, metaphor and onomatopoeia. **Concepts:** grammar in authentic texts; authorial purpose; rhetorical/literary techniques; reading-to-writing transfer.
15. **EN 9.2.2.2 — Reading and Viewing / Language Features and Rules** (printed p.22; PDF lines 597–614). CLO concerns language conventions and their contribution to meaning. Indicator actions: explore genre background/context/audience; examine themes, values and beliefs; compare settings and viewpoints and dramatise a relevant scene. Scope includes theme, plot, setting, narrative structure, characters, mood and literary techniques. **Concepts:** conventions; genre context; narrative elements; perspective; comparison; dramatic interpretation.
16. **EN 9.2.3.1 — Reading and Viewing / Socio-cultural Context** (printed p.23; PDF lines 621–627). CLO concerns socio-cultural values, attitudes and beliefs in relation to text, audience, purpose and conventions. Indicator actions: identify characters and characteristics; connect dialogue with character actions. **Concepts:** characterisation; dialogue; actions; values and beliefs; text-context relationship.
17. **EN 9.2.3.2 — Reading and Viewing / Socio-cultural Context** (printed p.23; PDF lines 631–638). CLO concerns the link between dialogue, action and character. Indicator actions: present a scenario illustrating textual values/themes; compare home culture with the culture represented in texts and write about the comparison. **Concepts:** cultural comparison; interpretation; dialogue/action; values; reflective writing.
18. **EN 9.2.4.1 — Reading and Viewing / Language Learning Processes and Strategies** (printed p.24; PDF lines 645–664). CLO concerns key reading/viewing strategies. Indicator actions: practise strategies collaboratively; evaluate reading content and develop/present a summary. Scope includes fiction/non-fiction, poetry, drama, documentaries, newspapers and other print/visual texts. **Concepts:** reading strategies; evaluation; summarising; collaborative interpretation; multiple text forms.
19. **EN 9.3.1.1 — Writing and Shaping / Text Types** (printed p.25; PDF lines 695–717). CLO concerns effective writing for media texts and targeted audiences/purposes. Indicator actions: explain writing strategies/styles; examine purpose/audience/context and publish an essay; compare styles and sentence types. Scope includes paragraphs, expository essays, narratives, descriptions, personal/business letters, applications, emails, diaries, newsletters, stories and print media. **Concepts:** genre selection; audience and purpose; writing style; publishing; comparison of forms.
20. **EN 9.3.1.2 — Writing and Shaping / Text Types** (printed pp.25–26; PDF lines 721–745). CLO concerns planning for visual writing/visual production. Indicator actions: collect relevant information; organise ideas into linked paragraphs; select an appropriate style/sample. Scope includes reports, book reviews, journals, diary entries, articles, recounts, descriptions, explanations, CV/career materials, invitations/thanks/refusals, enquiries, play/movie production, posters and scripts. **Concepts:** research; planning; paragraph organisation; visual communication; multimodal composition.
21. **EN 9.3.2.1 — Writing and Shaping / Language Features and Rules** (printed p.26; PDF lines 748–768). CLO concerns structurally sound and functional sentences. Indicator actions: use vocabulary critically; explain/use prefixes and suffixes; recognise and apply verb tenses; choose style for purpose and publish. Scope includes expressing reasons/concessions, obligations, requests, advice/warnings, comparison, purpose, permission, results/regret, gratitude and conditions. **Concepts:** morphology; tense; functional sentence meaning; register; purpose-driven writing.
22. **EN 9.3.2.2 — Writing and Shaping / Language Features and Rules** (printed pp.26–27; PDF lines 772–790). CLO concerns functional texts for information, messages, invitations and preferences in work/creative contexts. Indicator actions: identify and describe text forms for conveying information; analyse tone and writer–reader relationship; use appropriate figurative language. Scope includes pronouns, verb tenses, possessives, direct/reported speech, prepositions, adjectives, comparatives, superlatives and articles. **Concepts:** functional writing; tone; audience relationship; grammar choices; figurative language.
 
### Older-source lineage and current-status decision

- The 2014 syllabus explicitly states that essential concepts, skills and attitudes were selected from older prescriptions and incorporated with developments in English (printed p.3). It does not name those prescriptions or identify which old item produced each 2014 CLO/indicator.
- Therefore, for every coded entry above, the older lineage remains LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND at item level. The source only confirms that older prescriptions informed the 2014 syllabus generally.
- The 2014 syllabus is not to be used as the current Years 9–10 prescription without current Ministry confirmation. A 2024 Revised Secondary English Curriculum Teacher Guide is separately identified in this bank; it is a later curriculum package lead, but the precise mapping between these 2014 codes and the 2024 CLOs/achievement standards has not yet been established.
- Do not transfer these Year 9 outcomes to Years 10–13 or to primary classes.
- The source is sufficient to populate a historical-source extraction table and support a future old-to-new comparison. It is not sufficient to populate the active current prescription register.

### PacEdu handling

- Store each numbered CLO/indicator mapping as an independent source-linked entry; keep CLO text, achievement-indicator action, scope examples, and PacEdu-derived observable evidence in separate fields.
- Status for each: HISTORICAL_OFFICIAL_PRESCRIPTION_SOURCE; PRESCRIPTION_CONTENT_EXTRACTED; CURRENT_STATUS_UNCONFIRMED; LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND; BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.
- No mandatory current daily worksheet is authorised from this record. CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.


## Record 136 — Older Fiji Forms I–IV English prescription: documentary lineage lead (1980s; source text not yet acquired)

### Evidence actually inspected

- **Secondary research source:** Beatrice Boufoy-Bastick, “Using A Polar Grounded Composite To Describe The Socio-Cultural Determinants Of ESL Teaching In Rural Fijian Schools,” The Qualitative Report, June 2003, pp. 183–192 in the retrieved extract. Searchable full-text mirror: https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=b87d58f282cee547cdb8bf9a3a8fbe68341209c6&repid=rep1&type=pdf ; ResearchGate record: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228486830_Using_A_Polar_Grounded_Composite_To_Describe_The_Socio-Cultural_Determinants_Of_ESL_Teaching_In_Rural_Fijian_Schools
- **What the paper explicitly reports:** the Fiji Ministry of Education Curriculum Development Unit set a Form 1–4 English prescription; the prescription was developed with assistance from overseas advisers; it described broad educational and linguistic objectives of the junior secondary English course. The paper reports that the Ministry-prescribed Link 3 and Link 4 textbooks were used for Forms III and IV, and that teachers relied heavily on selected textbook passages and Fiji Junior Certificate examination preparation.
- **Historical resource leads identified in an external bibliographic list:** Link 3: An English Course for Secondary Schools: Pupil’s Book (Ministry of Education, Suva, 1981) and Link 4: An English Course for Secondary Schools: Pupil’s Book (Ministry of Education, Suva, 1982). A separate bibliography lists Link 1: Functional English for Secondary Schools: Pupil’s Book (Ministry of Education, 1989) and later Link 1/2 rapid-reading and pupil books. Bibliographic source: https://www.nira.or.jp/pdf/0702report.pdf (Fiji textbook bibliography, p.63).
- **Additional documentary clue:** the 2003 paper cites the Link books as Curriculum Development Unit, 1980 and states that the Form 1–4 prescription described broad course objectives. This may refer to the original prescription or a related CDU edition; exact title, publication year and edition have not been independently verified.

### Actual content extraction boundary

- The research paper describes historical implementation and teaching practice, not the full prescription text. It discusses a distinction between language and literature components in the Fiji Junior Certificate course and gives examples of teachers' use of reading passages, comprehension, summaries, grammar/language exercises and literary texts. These are descriptions of practice and examination preparation, not a verified exhaustive list of official achievement indicators.
- No full original Forms I–IV prescription was recovered in this search. No exact older indicator codes, CLOs or prescribed indicator sentences can be extracted from this evidence.
- Do not convert teachers' reported practices, textbook chapters, examination weightings or the 2003 researcher's observations into official curriculum indicators.

### Comparison with Record 135 (2014 Years 9–10 English)

- **Broad historical continuity candidates only:** language/literacy objectives; reading comprehension; language/grammar study; literary texts; oral and written English; use of reading passages and summaries. These broad areas are visible in the 2003 account of the older Forms III–IV course and also occur as broad areas in the 2014 syllabus.
- **Not established:** no exact match has been verified between any of the 22 Year 9 CLO/indicator entries in Record 135 and a specific statement in the older Forms I–IV prescription. Keep all Record 135 entry-level lineage statuses as LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND.
- The 2014 syllabus states that essential concepts, skills and attitudes were selected from older prescriptions, but neither it nor the 2003 paper identifies which exact older item maps to each 2014 indicator.

### Next source retrieval targets

1. Locate the original Ministry/CDU English Prescription Forms I–IV (likely 1980-era) and inspect its objectives, content, language skills, literature, grammar and assessment sections.
2. Locate the original Link 3 (1981) and Link 4 (1982) pupil books and teacher guides. Extract their actual learning content only as textbook/resource concepts, not as a substitute for the prescription.
3. Search for the earlier Forms I–IV prescription editions and amendments that the 2014 syllabus says informed its concepts and skills; preserve edition-specific lineage.
4. Compare each old prescription item to each 2014 Year 9 coded CLO and achievement-indicator action using EXACT_MATCH, PARTIAL_CONCEPT_CONTINUITY, PEDAGOGICAL_CONTINUITY_ONLY, or NO_MATCH_FOUND; require a source locator for every match.

### PacEdu status

- Record type: HISTORICAL_PRESCRIPTION_LINEAGE_LEAD / SECONDARY_SOURCE_AUDIT.
- Status: SOURCE_EVIDENCE_REVIEWED; ORIGINAL_PRESCRIPTION_NOT_ACQUIRED; NO_EXACT_INDICATOR_EXTRACTED.
- Lineage: broad continuity candidates only; no item-level links verified.
- Rights: secondary paper/bibliography used for research and source discovery; do not reproduce Link books or prescription content until rights and controlled-copy status are checked.
- No current prescription activation; no daily worksheet authorised; CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.


## Record 137 — Fiji Ministry Years 10 English Syllabus (2014): Year 10 CLOs and achievement-indicator concepts extracted

### Source identity and status

- **Source:** *English Syllabi Years 9 & 10*, Ministry of Education, Curriculum Development Unit, Fiji, 2014.
- **Inspected copy:** https://theseeproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/l2_year910_english_syllabi.pdf
- **Printed pages inspected:** pp.28–40 (PDF lines 829–1395).
- **Authority and copyright:** Title page identifies Ministry/CDU; Ministry copyright 2014. Classroom reproduction permitted with CDU acknowledgement; other use must be referred to Permanent Secretary through Director CAS. PacEdu adaptation/reproduction remains BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.
- **Status:** HISTORICAL_OFFICIAL_PRESCRIPTION_SOURCE; PRESCRIPTION_CONTENT_EXTRACTED; CURRENT_STATUS_UNCONFIRMED. This is the same 2014 syllabus as Record 135, not a separate edition.
- **Scope:** Year 10 English only. Keep separate from Year 9 (Record 135).

### Year 10 coded CLOs and extracted indicator concepts

The actions below are concise paraphrases of the source's achievement-indicator column. Scope examples are kept separate and are not themselves indicators.

**Strand 1 — Listening and Speaking (printed pp.28–32)**

1. **EN.10.1.1.1 — Media text:** examine media texts; determine tone, purpose, audience, context and jargon; compare features and synthesise meaning. Scope examples: audio/audio-visual texts, TV broadcasts, panel discussions, interviews, YouTube essay-writing videos, movies and mobile phones. Concepts: media listening; critical comparison; register/jargon; audience and purpose.
2. **EN.10.1.1.2 — Everyday communication:** discuss everyday communication; analyse purpose, audience and context; apply effective communication in formal and informal speech. Scope: partner/group work, instructions, procedures, questioning, interviews, church gatherings, dialogue, singing, prayer, oral presentations, recitals, vote of thanks, farewell speech, text messages, email/Skype, voice messages, radio and telephone. Concepts: conversational fluency; formal/informal register; practical oral interaction; digital communication.
3. **EN.10.1.1.3 — Literary text:** plan, research and present oral work; listen attentively; examine literary texts and identify purpose, audience and context; compare fiction and non-fiction characteristics. Scope: storybooks, magazines, articles. Concepts: literary listening; oral research/presentation; genre comparison.
4. **EN.10.1.2.1 — Grammar and persuasion:** identify parts of speech and their functions; apply persuasive techniques in oral and written activities; identify characters, setting, plot and relate themes (the source table carries the final clause across a page break). Scope: nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, subject–verb agreement, tenses, articles, connectives, word order and word forms. Concepts: grammar in context; persuasion; narrative elements.
5. **EN.10.1.2.2 — Sentence and language concepts:** study sentence types and their functions; apply language concepts orally and in writing to create meaning and engage an audience. Scope: simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences; idioms; figures/features of speech; jargon; emotive vocabulary. Concepts: sentence variety; rhetorical language; audience engagement.
6. **EN.10.1.3.1 — Social oral communication:** explore oral communication for social purposes; choose and discuss an oral genre and identify its context. Scope: oral registers, talanoa, family gatherings, village functions, New Year/Christmas celebrations and intercultural gatherings. Concepts: social register; oral genres; cultural context.
7. **Code ambiguity — oral genres and strategies:** the printed table at pp.31–32 labels a row EN.10.1.4.1 for analysing oral genres/register in formal and informal contexts, then repeats EN.10.1.4.1 for selecting strategies to make sense of creative text. Do not silently correct or merge these. Store both rows with SOURCE_CODE_AMBIGUOUS pending controlled-copy verification. Their indicator actions concern (a) addresser/addressee relationship and cultural norms; (b) describing oral genres and registers, analysing purpose/audience/context, and evaluating values/attitudes. Scope includes oral history, speeches, conferences, debates, impromptu speaking, critique, group/interpersonal communication, self-talk/soliloquy, novels, short stories, poems, drama, fiction and non-fiction.
8. **EN.10.1.4.2 — Oral-language strategies:** describe and dramatise oral-language learning processes/strategies; identify and evaluate appropriate strategies. Scope: recounting, storytelling, responding to instructions, giving opinions, replying to requests, asking questions and following instructions. Concepts: oral-language strategy selection; retelling; questioning; instruction-following.

**Strand 2 — Reading and Viewing (printed pp.33–37)**

9. **EN.10.2.1.1 — Media texts:** examine media texts and assess purpose/audience/context; analyse meaning, themes and values; read for pleasure and information. Scope: print/visual texts, newspapers, magazines, newsletters, billboards, posters, documentaries and career articles. Concepts: critical media reading; theme/value interpretation; informational and recreational reading.
10. **EN.10.2.1.2 — Everyday communication:** analyse everyday transactions for purpose/audience/context; dramatise appropriate everyday communication; investigate and describe accounting concepts used in accounting processes (source wording). Scope: classroom instructions, bus conversations, doctor visits and telephone calls. Concepts: functional reading; transaction literacy; role-play; accounting vocabulary in context.
11. **EN.10.2.1.3 — Literary texts:** examine language conventions and explain how they contribute to text meaning and context. Scope: fiction/non-fiction, library books, dictionaries, movies, documentaries, news, articles, passages, summaries and magazines. Concepts: literary comprehension; language conventions; meaning/context.
12. **EN.10.2.2.1 — Figurative/literary features:** explore figurative language in print/visual texts and discuss author intention; evaluate text content/context; connect texts to personal experience. Scope: figures of speech, emotive vocabulary, idioms, slang and jargon. Concepts: figurative language; authorial purpose; context; reader response.
13. **EN.10.2.2.2 — Language conventions:** analyse parts of speech in genres and apply them in reading/writing. Scope: parts of speech, sentence structure, grammar/mechanics, pronouns, prepositions, past/present/future time, direct/reported speech and question tags. Concepts: grammar in genres; mechanics; tense; reported speech; question forms.
14. **EN.10.2.2.3 — Text, audience and purpose:** critically examine the relationship between text, audience and purpose; evaluate mass-media functions and compare features. Scope: mass media, fiction/non-fiction, documentaries, newspaper articles and appropriate print/visual/religious texts. Concepts: media purpose; audience; genre comparison; critical literacy.
15. **EN.10.2.3.1 — Media and audience:** assess how media text types relate to purpose/audience and create an appropriate media text. Scope: print, visual, audio and multimedia. Concepts: media roles; audience design; multimodal literacy.
16. **EN.10.2.4.1 — Literature as integrated reading:** examine literary genres and use an appropriate integrated approach to support reading. Scope: short stories, novels, poems and drama. Concepts: genre selection; integrated reading; literary interpretation.

**Strand 3 — Writing and Shaping (printed pp.38–40)**

17. **EN.10.3.1.1 — Purposeful writing:** examine written materials for purpose/context; write appropriate text types using their features; compare and contrast published writing. Scope: paragraphs, expository essays, narratives, descriptions, personal letters, letters to editor and business letters. Concepts: purpose-driven writing; genre conventions; comparison.
18. **EN.10.3.1.2 — Writing plans:** examine/use planning strategies; use varied sentence types and sequence ideas with examples. Scope: application letters, emails, literature essays, diaries, conversation, newsletters and stories. Concepts: planning; sequencing; sentence variety; supporting examples.
19. **EN.10.3.2.1 — Media conventions:** examine and use media conventions/techniques in writing; compare and contrast texts. Scope: print media, letters to editor, formal writing, reports, book reviews, journals, diary entries and articles. Concepts: media conventions; formal writing; report/review/journal genres.
20. **EN.10.3.2.2 — Precision and elaboration:** elaborate ideas with precise/effective language; use figurative language and emotion in different writing styles. Scope: recount, descriptive and imaginative writing. Concepts: elaboration; precision; figurative language; expressive style.
21. **EN.10.3.3.1 — Context and purpose:** explore reasons for writing in varied situations and use appropriate techniques/styles; study and integrate writing processes and strategies. Scope: invitations, enquiries, letters of thanks and refusals. Concepts: functional writing; audience/context; writing process.
22. **EN.10.3.4.1 — Language varieties:** examine features of language varieties, compare similarities/differences and evaluate context. Scope: conversation, sports commentary, religion, science and research. Concepts: register; language variation; domain-specific language; contextual analysis.

### Source-quality and lineage notes

- The printed table contains apparent structural/code anomalies: EN.10.1.4.1 appears twice with different descriptions; one strand/sub-strand heading appears inconsistent with the row content; some indicator text crosses page breaks. Preserve source codes exactly as printed and flag ambiguity rather than silently repairing it.
- The syllabus says the 2014 Years 9–10 concepts, skills and attitudes were selected from older prescriptions, but does not name the editions or map specific predecessor statements (printed p.3; see Record 135 and Record 136).
- Record 136 supplies only broad historical evidence that a Forms I–IV prescription existed and that Link 3/4 were Ministry-prescribed texts. No exact older indicator match has been verified for any Year 10 entry.
- All 22 Year 10 entries retain LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND at item level. The source's general claim of older-source influence is not item-level lineage evidence.
- The 2024 Revised Secondary English Curriculum Teacher Guide is a later lead, but no exact crosswalk from these 2014 Year 10 CLOs/indicators to 2024 Achievement Standards/CLOs has yet been established.

### PacEdu handling

- Store each Year 10 CLO and its indicator actions as an independently traceable entry, preserving the printed code, strand, sub-strand, page and separate scope examples.
- Status: HISTORICAL_OFFICIAL_PRESCRIPTION_SOURCE; PRESCRIPTION_CONTENT_EXTRACTED; CURRENT_STATUS_UNCONFIRMED; LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND; BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.
- Keep ambiguous code rows flagged SOURCE_CODE_AMBIGUOUS until a controlled source resolves them.
- No current mandatory worksheet authorised. No CAS contact now; CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 138 — 1973 Regional Curriculum Workshop: Forms 1–4 English outline, weekly topics and skills (historical source; draft/workshop evidence)

**Source:** *Regional Curriculum Workshop: Final Workshop Report*, University of the South Pacific, School of Education, Suva; UNESCO-sponsored, January 2–19, 1973; published 1973. English Language Work Group report by D. McKeating, Senior Education Officer, Secondary English, Fiji Department of Education (printed pp.99–118); ERIC ED088771. Full source: https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED088771.pdf. Inspected PDF lines covering printed pp.99–118 and appendices A and D.

**Source authority and limitation:** This is a regional workshop report, not the final Fiji-approved Forms 1–4 syllabus. The report states that an outline Forms 1–4 syllabus had been prepared by a UNDP English specialist before the workshop. Participants discussed and modified the outline and produced trial materials. The workshop's draft and recommendations must not be represented as an approved Fiji prescription. Classification: HISTORICAL_LINEAGE_REFERENCE / WORKSHOP_DRAFT_EVIDENCE; not PRESCRIPTION_VERIFIED. Rights for PacEdu reproduction/adaptation have not been established; BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.

### Extracted curriculum concepts and skills (not current mandatory indicators)

1. **Weekly thematic language learning:** Form 1 topics included self/family, school, houses, natural disasters, animals, illness, hospitals, sports, transport, road safety, town/city life, fishing, sea/leisure, festivals, islands, legends, measurement and careers. Form 2 topics included legends, animals/food/clothing, careers, earthquakes/volcanoes, disability, leisure, cinema, space, food/cooking, sea economy, phosphate mining, time, clothes, examinations, shopping, floods/droughts/fires, sugar production, communications and exploration (printed pp.105–107). These are historical topic contexts, not transferable as current mandatory content without review.
2. **Vocabulary acquisition and revision:** revise known vocabulary from Tate Oral English Course; introduce selected new vocabulary from L. A. Hill's 2,075 headword list based on Michael West's General Service List (printed pp.101–102).
3. **Prepositions and adverbial particles:** revise primary-course items and teach selected new items (p.101).
4. **Grammar and sentence structures:** revise known structures and teach new structures drawing on A. S. Hornby's *A Guide to Patterns and Usage* (p.101).
5. **Error recognition and correction:** identify common errors in pupils' written work and plan corrective work (p.101).
6. **Phonemic discrimination and speech:** ear-and-speech training using contrasting phoneme pairs (p.101).
7. **Aural comprehension:** listen to and understand spoken passages; the outline includes dedicated aural-comprehension work (pp.101–102, 117–118).
8. **Oral language and composition:** teach new vocabulary and structures orally before written work; prepare oral work and then compose/write (pp.102–103, 116–118).
9. **Reading fluency and rapid reading comprehension:** practise rapid/speed reading and answer comprehension tasks (pp.101–102, 104, 117–118).
10. **Intensive reading and close comprehension:** read longer passages and answer searching questions requiring attention to detail and exact meaning (pp.103, 116–118).
11. **Written composition:** develop written composition after preparatory oral work; sample work included composition passages (pp.104, 117–119).
12. **Note-taking:** the questionnaire explicitly asks whether note-taking using simpler material would be useful or possible at Form 1 (p.115); this is a discussion prompt, not a confirmed syllabus requirement.
13. **Reading resource development:** extensive reading materials were recommended to supplement existing published readers (p.117).
14. **Regional and cultural adaptation:** participants recommended including vocabulary of regional significance and preparing alternative units where cultural backgrounds differed (p.117).

### Teaching sequence and time allocation recorded in the draft

The initial weekly allocation assumed seven 40-minute periods: ear/speech training 5 × 10 minutes; aural comprehension 1 × 20 minutes; oral and written composition 2 × 30 minutes; rapid reading comprehension 1 × 30 minutes; revision/corrective work 2 × 30 minutes; new vocabulary/idioms/structures 2 × 30 minutes (printed p.102). The workshop later recommended a sequence integrating oral work, written reinforcement, speed reading, composition, aural comprehension and intensive reading (pp.117–118). These are historical planning recommendations, not current timetable requirements.

### Historical lineage value for Records 135 and 137

- Provides broad historical predecessor evidence for the existence of a Forms 1–4 English outline and for the domains of vocabulary, structures/grammar, phonemic contrast, oral language, listening, reading comprehension, composition and corrective work.
- Record 135/137 (2014 Years 9–10 English syllabus) states that its concepts, skills and attitudes were selected from older prescriptions. This 1973 workshop report is a plausible earlier source in that history, but it does **not** prove that any particular 2014 CLO or achievement indicator descends from a specific 1973 item.
- Keep all 2014 item-level lineage fields as LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND unless a controlled older prescription or an exact textual match is located.
- Record 132 (1966 SPC Junior Series Reader Book 1) and Record 128 (1991 historical ESL paper) provide additional context for oral-language/graded-reader history. Do not infer that the 1973 outline is the exact Fiji final prescription or that its Form 1–2 vocabulary/weekly topics match the later 2014 syllabus.

### PacEdu handling

- Store the 14 concepts separately as historical source entries with page references; keep draft recommendations, workshop discussion prompts and actual syllabus-outline components distinguishable.
- Status: HISTORICAL_LINEAGE_REFERENCE; WORKSHOP_DRAFT_EVIDENCE; SUPPLEMENTARY_ONLY; CURRENT_STATUS_UNCONFIRMED; BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.
- Do not promote any entry to current mandatory curriculum or create daily worksheets from this record alone.
- CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 139 — Fiji Revised Secondary English Curriculum (RSEC), Years 9–10 Teacher Guide 1 (2024): achievement standards, CLOs and KUD learning objectives

**Source:** *Revised Secondary English Curriculum — Teachers Guide 1*, Ministry of Education (Curriculum Advisory Services), prepared in partnership with Fiji Program Support Facility Fiji Education Program; ©2024. Publicly readable third-party FlipHTML5 copy: https://fliphtml5.com/gjgbb/naau/RSEC_Teachers_Guide_Year_9_%26_10/. Inspected printed pp.2–30 and contents/structure. This is a Ministry-authored guide as identified by its title and copyright page, but the inspected copy is hosted by a third party; retrieve a Ministry-controlled copy for final source-control verification.

**Current-status context:** The guide identifies itself as RSEC Years 9 and 10. A 2025 Fiji education programme advisor posting states that the Ministry had developed and rolled out English curriculum frameworks for Years 9 and 10; another public report states Year 9 RSEC rollout began in 2025. These are supporting rollout clues, not a substitute for a current Ministry circular confirming the precise 2026 status of every Year 9 and Year 10 strand. Record status: MINISTRY_AUTHORED_CURRICULUM_GUIDE; CONTENT_EXTRACTED; CURRENT_CONTROLLED_COPY_PENDING; RIGHTS_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Copyright page says no part may be reproduced except in accordance with Fiji Copyright Act 1999. PacEdu reuse/adaptation BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW.

### Curriculum architecture extracted

- Three strands: Language, Text Types, Critical Literacy (printed pp.1, 9–16). The guide numbers them Strands 4, 5 and 6 in the larger curriculum architecture.
- Classroom learning objectives use KUD: Know, Understand and Do; each CLO is unpacked into knowledge, understanding and practical language-use objectives (printed pp.17–34).
- Language strand sub-strands: vocabulary, sentence level, whole text (printed pp.11–14).
- The guide integrates reading, listening, viewing, speaking, writing and multimedia text rather than treating communication modes as isolated.
- Five model units per year level; DTE (Daily Text Engagement) includes short reading/listening/viewing and inferential comprehension discussion. The guide specifies differentiated DTE text versions, SET reading support, and guided reading for students not yet independent readers (printed pp.1–3).
- Formative assessment is embedded in lessons; Dry Run Tasks provide feedback before Performance Tasks, which align to rubrics (printed pp.3, 45–51).

### Achievement standard and KUD concepts extracted (one concept per item in the source bank)

1. **Tiered vocabulary:** Year 9 develops Tier 1 and Tier 2 vocabulary; Year 10 extends to Tier 3 subject-specific vocabulary. Apply vocabulary to social, classroom and academic purposes (printed pp.11–14, 18–19, 26–27).
2. **Vocabulary inference and word relationships:** use context clues, dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses, word walls, roots, prefixes and suffixes; infer new meanings; select synonyms for subtle differences (pp.18–19, 26–27).
3. **Language choice and register:** explain and justify language choices according to text type, tone, audience, purpose and context; recognise how choices affect clarity, credibility and meaning (pp.18–19, 26–27).
4. **Sentence construction:** understand and use simple, compound and complex sentences; distinguish dependent and independent clauses; use introductory clauses, coordinating/subordinating conjunctions and relative clauses (pp.19–20, 27–28).
5. **Grammar for meaning:** use verbs and tenses, pronouns, adverbs, adjectives, prepositional phrases and punctuation to add precision, coherence and circumstance (pp.19–20, 27–28).
6. **Whole-text cohesion and organisation:** use reference items, connectives, topic sentences, paragraph links, consistent style/tone, text structures and layout features; use plot devices such as foreshadowing and flashbacks (pp.20–23).
7. **Text type and genre knowledge:** understand and create varied fictional and non-fictional text types, including narrative, description, recount, argument, discussion, explanation, information report, personal response and media campaign; examine their purpose, audience and typical structure (pp.13–16, 21–24, 29–32; examples pp.69–73).
8. **Multimodal and digital visual literacy:** interpret and create written, spoken, visual and multimedia texts; consider how images, layout, captions, sound and other modes contribute to meaning and audience impact (pp.9–16, 20–23, 33–34).
9. **Critical literacy:** examine perspective, representation, credibility, bias, purpose and the ways texts position audiences; include digital/social media texts and diverse voices (pp.15–16, 24–25, 33–34).
10. **Oral communication and listening:** develop conversation skills, listen for different purposes, participate in group discussion and debate, and adapt spoken language for formality, fluency and audience (pp.2–3, 52–54).
11. **Reading comprehension and strategies:** daily inferential comprehension; prediction, connection-making, graphic organisers, readers' theatre, skimming, scanning, visualising and synthesising (pp.2, 36–37, 58–66).
12. **Writing process and craft:** plan, draft, revise and edit; use text structure, figurative language, persuasive writing and journaling (pp.67–74).
13. **Differentiated learning and guided reading:** use appropriately levelled texts and differentiated tasks while keeping shared learning goals; provide small-group guided reading for learners who are not yet independent readers (pp.2–3, 38–40, 43–44).
14. **Assessment evidence:** formative checks and feedback; Dry Run Tasks; Performance Tasks assessed against five-criterion rubrics (pp.3, 45–51).

### Historical lineage comparison — what can and cannot be claimed

- **Record 136 / 1973 Fiji regional workshop report:** broad continuity is visible in vocabulary, grammar/structures, listening, oral language, reading comprehension and composition. The 1973 report is a workshop draft/recommendation, not a final approved syllabus. These are broad domain similarities, not exact predecessor matches.
- **Record 135/137 / 2014 Years 9–10 syllabus:** both cover language, text forms, audience/purpose, reading, writing and communication, but the 2024 RSEC restructures the framework into Language, Text Types and Critical Literacy with explicit KUDs and achievement standards. Do not claim direct item-level descent without a source crosswalk.
- **2006 Ministry secondary English curriculum:** a secondary academic article summarises a Ministry 2006 reorganisation around listening, speaking, reading, writing and grammar; it reports spiral grammar areas (parts of speech, phrases, clauses, sentences), integrated skills and literature genres. The original Ministry 2006 syllabus/guide has not yet been retrieved. This is secondary-source context only; not a verified original prescription and not item-level lineage.
- All item-level lineage fields remain LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND unless an original older prescription or exact text match is inspected.

### PacEdu handling

- Extracted content is a useful source for the RSEC Years 9–10 curriculum file; preserve source codes and KUD wording exactly when later transcribing full tables. This record summarises concept domains and does not claim to reproduce every CLO/KUD.
- Distinguish official achievement standards, CLOs and KUDs from PacEdu-derived observable evidence and activity design.
- Status: MINISTRY_AUTHORED_CURRICULUM_GUIDE; CURRENT_CONTROLLED_COPY_PENDING; RIGHTS_REVIEW_REQUIRED; LINEAGE_NOT_YET_FOUND at item level.
- No PacEdu daily worksheets authorised until current prescription source control and older-source lineage review are completed, and rights are cleared.
- CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 140 — Fiji National Policy on Open Educational Resources (2016): PacEdu source-use and learning-resource concepts

**Source:** Ministry of Education, Heritage and Arts, *National Policy on Open Educational Resources*, effective 4 January 2016; policy owner identified as Fiji Higher Education Commission. Ministry-hosted PDF: https://www.education.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/OER_National_Policy_Final.pdf. Inspected printed pp.1–6 (PDF pp.2–7).

**Source classification:** Fiji national education policy; not a student subject syllabus and not a set of official learner achievement indicators. It provides a lawful policy basis and practical concepts for PacEdu resource literacy, digital literacy, research skills and learning-resource creation. Exact policy provisions are paraphrased below, not copied as official student outcomes.

### Extracted source concepts for possible PacEdu daily activities

1. **Open educational resource meaning:** identify learning materials in any medium that are public domain or released under an open licence allowing no-cost access, use, adaptation and redistribution (printed p.4, section 4.1).
2. **Licence reading:** locate and interpret the conditions stated on a resource's open licence; distinguish permissions from restrictions (p.4, sections 4.6–4.7).
3. **Reuse and adaptation:** explain the difference between reusing, revising, remixing, redistributing and retaining learning materials (p.2, section 2.3).
4. **Attribution and acknowledgement:** identify creator/source and licence conditions when developing or sharing a learning resource (p.2, section 2.4; p.4).
5. **Resource evaluation:** examine peer review, user ratings and quality assurance as ways of evaluating learning resources (p.2, section 2.5).
6. **Information access and retrieval:** locate and retrieve resources using appropriate open standards and different media formats (p.2, section 2.7).
7. **Digital and multimedia literacy:** distinguish text, graphics, images, audio, video, streaming media and podcasts (p.4, sections 4.3–4.5).
8. **Inclusive access:** identify barriers involving access, cost, language and format, and consider how adaptable resources can reduce them (p.3, section 3.3.1).
9. **Cultural and contextual adaptation:** adapt educational material to local curriculum requirements and Fiji's cultural diversity (pp.2–3, sections 2.2, 2.8, 3.1).
10. **Research and evidence:** explain how research into the production, use and re-contextualisation of OER can inform quality and cost-effectiveness (p.3, section 2.11).
11. **Digital access infrastructure:** recognise the role of mobile technology, broadband, ICT infrastructure and reliable electricity in access to learning (p.2, section 2.6).

**PacEdu use:** these may be developed into PacEdu-created concepts and observable learning targets in appropriate subjects/levels after age and curriculum fit is checked. They must be labelled PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT_FROM_FIJI_POLICY, not Ministry achievement indicators. No student should be taught that the policy itself is a student syllabus.

**Rights note:** the policy describes open licensing and says publicly funded educational materials should generally be openly licensed subject to case-by-case restrictions. That policy does not itself grant PacEdu permission to copy every Ministry resource. Check the licence/copyright notice on each resource separately. USP copyright guidance explains that government works are not automatically public domain and that legislation is treated differently from ordinary government publications. Record status: SOURCE_INSPECTED; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPTS_AVAILABLE; ITEM_LEVEL_RIGHTS_CHECK_REQUIRED.

## Record 141 — Fiji Environment Management Act 2005: Fiji-context science, geography, agriculture, health and civic concepts

Official Ministry of Environment and Climate Change legislation listing and description: https://mecc.gov.fj/legislation/ and https://mecc.gov.fj/environment-management-act-2005-act-no-1-of-2005-an-act-for-the-protection-of-the-natural-resources-and-for-the-control-and-management-of-developments-waste-management-and-pollution-control-and-fo/ . **Source classification:** Fiji primary legislation. It is a legal source for real Fiji concepts and examples, not a Ministry curriculum prescription. The Act is amended by later legislation; before using any legal duty, penalty, agency name or compliance requirement, check the latest consolidated text and amendments. Activities should teach concepts and reading of legal information, not provide individual legal advice.

### Extracted concepts suitable for PacEdu-designed learning activities

1. **Environment as an interacting system:** air, land, water, atmosphere, living organisms and natural/human systems interact (s.2, printed pp.4–5).
2. **Natural-resource categories:** coastal zones, wetlands, lakes, rivers, forests/vegetation, fauna, land, seabed and marine environments (ss.2–3, pp.2–9).
3. **Habitat carrying capacity:** explain how a habitat or land area has limits to the population of life it can support over time (s.2, p.2).
4. **Biodiversity and habitat protection:** recognise indigenous vegetation, fauna, protected species and significant habitats as conservation concerns (ss.2–3, pp.5–9).
5. **Coastal and freshwater protection:** identify why coastal environments, wetlands, lakes and river margins are matters of national importance (s.3(3), pp.8–9).
6. **Human health and environmental quality:** explain links between environmental protection, human life, health and safety (ss.2–3, pp.5–9).
7. **Pollution and pollutants:** classify examples such as sewage, garbage, agricultural/industrial waste, chemical waste, oil residues and exhaust gases (s.2, pp.5–6).
8. **Waste categories and management:** distinguish solid, liquid, hazardous, packaging and special waste; explore reduction, separation and safe management (s.2 and s.14, pp.3–7, 13–14).
9. **Pollution incident and environmental impact:** identify how a pollutant entering the environment can affect marine life, fishing, water, air, soil and human health (s.2, pp.5–6).
10. **Sustainable development:** discuss meeting present needs while preserving the ability of future generations to meet their needs, within resource limits (s.2, pp.7–8).
11. **Environmental impact assessment:** understand that proposed development may need assessment of possible environmental and resource impacts before approval (Part 4; check the current amended Act and regulations for legal process).
12. **Resource ownership and guardianship:** recognise the Act's reference to traditional owners/guardians and the relationship of Fijian communities with ancestral lands, waters, sacred areas and other treasures (s.3(3)–(4), pp.8–9).
13. **Environmental monitoring and evidence:** identify the roles of surveys, inspections, registers, resource inventories and environmental reports in monitoring resources and impacts (ss.11–14, pp.11–14).
14. **Public participation and governance:** identify that environmental decision-making involves government, local authorities, resource owners, business, NGOs and other stakeholders (ss.7–8, pp.9–11).
15. **Development and land-use change:** identify activities such as construction, dredging, reclamation, mining, sand/coral removal and vegetation removal as activities that may alter land or the environment (s.2, pp.2–3).
16. **Finite resources and competing uses:** discuss finite natural resources and possible conflicts between different uses of a resource (ss.2–3, pp.7–9).

### Suggested subject connections (PacEdu planning suggestions, not official Ministry subject placement)

- Elementary/Basic Science: ecosystems, habitats, biodiversity, pollution, water/air/soil, waste and sustainability.
- Social Science/Geography: Fiji's coastal and inland environments, land use, communities, resource ownership, public institutions and decision-making.
- Agriculture: soil/water protection, agricultural waste, resource sustainability and effects of land-use practices.
- Healthy Living: environmental quality, sanitation, pollution and human health.
- Mathematics: classify and tally waste, measure and graph local observations, compare quantities and interpret environmental data.
- English/Vosa Vakaviti/Fiji Hindi: read an age-appropriate information extract, explain cause and effect, compare viewpoints, write a report or persuasive message using evidence.
- Technology/Computer Studies: create a labelled diagram, data table, map or multimedia explanation using cited sources.

**Age and safety controls:** do not ask learners to handle hazardous waste, chemicals, sewage, sharp objects or contaminated water. Use photographs, teacher-prepared data, safe simulations and supervised observation from safe locations. Simplify legal vocabulary without changing legal meaning.

**Rights and legal accuracy:** the Act is primary legislation and the USP copyright guidance notes that Acts and other specified legal instruments are treated differently from ordinary copyright works. Use the official legal text and cite Act/section; do not copy a modern publisher's commentary, annotated edition, layout or third-party teaching material without checking its rights. Verify amendments and current consolidated text before presenting a provision as current law.

**PacEdu status:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE; SOURCE_INSPECTED; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPTS_AVAILABLE; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; CURRENT_LEGAL_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED for each activity; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Do not label these concepts as Ministry achievement indicators. They can support Fiji-context daily activities where curriculum gaps exist, subject to level suitability and review.

## Record 142 — Fiji source-use and concept-development rule (user-approved expansion)

The user has approved using Fiji legal resources, primary texts and other lawful sources when a formal achievement indicator is not available, provided the concept/indicator and source are identified.

**Mandatory distinction in PacEdu records:**
- OFFICIAL_ACHIEVEMENT_INDICATOR: exact indicator from a verified current Ministry prescription.
- OFFICIAL_CLO_OR_ACHIEVEMENT_STANDARD: exact current Ministry CLO/standard, with its own source and page.
- FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT: concept derived from a Fiji Act, regulation, Constitution or official legal text; never represented as a Ministry syllabus indicator.
- FIJI_PRIMARY_TEXT_CONCEPT: concept/skill derived from an inspected Fiji primary text, literary work, historical document, public report or technical text.
- OPEN_EDUCATIONAL_RESOURCE_CONCEPT: concept derived from a source whose licence explicitly allows the intended reuse/adaptation.
- PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT: PacEdu-authored learning target built from one or more cited sources; explicitly not official wording.
- SUPPLEMENTARY_CONTEXT_ONLY: source helps supply examples/context but does not establish a learning target.
- PENDING_SOURCE_REVIEW / BLOCKED_RIGHTS_REVIEW / CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED: use when evidence or permission is incomplete.

**Required fields for every concept:** exact source title; issuing body/author; date/edition; source URL or file identifier; exact page/section/article/clause; quoted extract only when necessary and lawful; PacEdu paraphrase; subject connection; suggested level or LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED; prerequisite; observable learner evidence; source type/status; licence/rights check; current-version/amendment check for laws; and teacher-review status.

**Daily-activity rule:** Where a formal indicator is missing, PacEdu may design a daily activity around a verified Fiji-source concept. The activity objective must be labelled as a PacEdu-derived concept, not a national achievement indicator. One source and section/page must be recorded for each concept before any worksheet is generated. Official indicators retain priority where available; supplementary/legal concepts fill gaps and add local Fiji context without displacing the prescribed curriculum.

**Legal-source hierarchy:** current consolidated Acts and regulations from Parliament/Office of the Attorney-General or responsible Ministry; Fiji Constitution; official Ministry technical publications and datasets; Fiji court judgments where age-appropriate; USP and other Fiji tertiary research; openly licensed Pacific resources. Check amendments, commencement, repeals and source date. Do not rely on a search-result snippet as the extracted text.

**Rights rule:** open access is not the same as open licence. Verify the specific item's licence. Government publication status alone does not establish public-domain status. For Acts, regulations and judgments, cite the official legal source and exact section; distinguish the legal text from third-party editorial material. If licence or rights are unclear, extract concepts and cite the source without copying/adapting protected expression; flag reuse for review.

**Status:** USER_APPROVED_WORKFLOW; applies across ECE–Form 7 with developmental appropriateness checks. No worksheet is automatically authorised by a source's discovery alone; each concept must be extracted, sourced, classified, level-checked and teacher-reviewed. CAS contact remains DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 143 — Constitution of the Republic of Fiji (2013): citizenship, rights, public institutions and democratic participation

**Source identity**
- **Source type:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE
- **Exact title:** *Constitution of the Republic of Fiji*
- **Issuing body:** Government of the Republic of Fiji
- **Date/edition:** 2013 Constitution; official Government-hosted English PDF.
- **Primary source URL:** https://www.pmoffice.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/constitution-2013.pdf
- **Official Government Constitution page / language versions:** https://www.fiji.gov.fj/fijian-constitution/
- **Inspected source:** complete 2013 PDF text; relevant sections inspected include Preamble; ss.1–6; ss.8–18; ss.20–32; ss.35–45; ss.46–53; ss.67–75; ss.81–93; ss.97–100; ss.123–126; ss.139–152.
- **Printed page references:** Preamble and Ch.1 pp.7–10; Bill of Rights Ch.2 pp.11–29; Parliament Ch.3 pp.30–43; Executive Ch.4 begins p.44; Judiciary Ch.5; State Services Ch.6; Revenue/Expenditure Ch.7; Accountability Ch.8. Section numbers are the controlling locators; printed pages are supplementary locators.
- **Source status:** official primary constitutional text inspected. This 2013 PDF is not itself a consolidated statement of every later judicial interpretation or amendment. Fiji’s 2026 constitutional review / Constitution (Amendment) Bill process is ongoing; the 2013 Constitution was still described as in force in the current process source checked on 12 November 2026. Before any lesson states the current legal effect of an individual provision, verify the latest official Gazette, enacted amendments, and relevant court decisions. In particular, do not teach ss.159–160 amendment thresholds from the unannotated 2013 PDF as the current legal position without checking the Supreme Court’s 2025 advisory opinion and any later legal developments.
- **Rights and reuse:** concepts and legal principles are recorded in PacEdu's own words; do not reproduce long constitutional passages. Confirm applicable legal-text reuse rules before copying substantial text or producing facsimiles. No claim is made that the whole PDF or any accompanying editorial material carries an open licence.
- **Classification:** FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; SOURCE_INSPECTED; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED; LEVEL_AND_PREREQUISITE_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Constitution and rule of law** — Source: Preamble; ss.1–3. Concept: a constitution establishes the framework of the State; public authority and laws operate within constitutional rules; rule of law, dignity, equality and freedom are foundational civic ideas. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: rules, authority and community. Observable evidence: learner explains in their own words why public rules apply to institutions as well as individuals.
2. **National identity, cultural diversity and shared citizenship** — Source: Preamble; ss.1 and 5. Concept: the text recognises distinct communities, cultures, customs, traditions and languages while describing common and equal citizenry. Subject links: Social Science, Vosa Vakaviti, Fiji Hindi, English, Arts. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: identity, family and community. Observable evidence: learner identifies examples of cultural heritage and distinguishes cultural identity from shared civic status without stereotyping.
3. **Citizenship and responsibilities** — Source: s.5. Concept: citizenship has defined means of acquisition and includes rights, duties and responsibilities; multiple citizenship is addressed in the constitutional text. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: identity and membership. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes citizenship, residence and community membership using age-appropriate examples. Do not teach application eligibility or immigration advice from this section alone.
4. **Separation of powers and checks and balances** — Source: s.1(f); Chapters 3–5. Concept: legislative, executive and judicial functions are institutionally distinct and interact through defined constitutional procedures. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: roles and responsibilities. Observable evidence: learner sorts examples of law-making, government administration and judicial decision-making into the correct broad branch.
5. **Equality and non-discrimination** — Source: ss.1(d), 26. Concept: equality before the law, equal protection and unfair discrimination; constitutional text lists protected grounds and addresses access to public services and reasonable access for persons with disabilities. Subject links: Social Science, Healthy Living, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: fairness and respectful treatment. Observable evidence: learner analyses a fictional school/community scenario for unequal treatment and proposes a fair, inclusive response.
6. **Freedom of expression and responsible communication** — Source: s.17. Concept: expression includes seeking, receiving and sharing information and ideas; the section also identifies limits, including incitement to violence and certain forms of discriminatory hatred. Subject links: English, Computer Studies, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: opinion, evidence and respectful discussion. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes a supported opinion from harmful or unsupported communication in a safe fictional example.
7. **Peaceful assembly, association and petitions** — Source: ss.18–19; s.72. Concept: peaceful collective participation, joining associations and presenting petitions are recognised; Parliament is required to facilitate public participation in its processes. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: group decision-making and rules. Observable evidence: learner outlines a peaceful, lawful way a community group could raise a concern. Legal procedures must be checked before practical instruction.
8. **Religion, conscience and belief in a secular State** — Source: ss.4 and 22. Concept: religious liberty, personal belief, equal treatment of religions by the State and protections concerning religious instruction are addressed. Subject links: Social Science, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: respect for differences. Observable evidence: learner describes how a shared public setting can respect different beliefs and non-belief. Avoid asking learners to disclose personal beliefs.
9. **Privacy and personal information** — Source: s.24. Concept: privacy includes confidentiality of personal information and communications and respect for private and family life. Subject links: Computer Studies, Technology, English, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: personal information and safe communication. Observable evidence: learner identifies personal information that should not be shared publicly and explains a safe digital choice.
10. **Access to information and correcting inaccurate records** — Source: s.25. Concept: access to public-office information and correction or deletion of untrue or misleading information are addressed in the Constitution, subject to lawful procedures and limits. Subject links: English, Computer Studies, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: reliable information and record checking. Observable evidence: learner compares two information sources, identifies a possible error and explains why evidence is needed before correcting a record.
11. **Land, customary ownership and resource interests** — Source: ss.27–30. Concept: constitutional provisions address property, public-purpose acquisition and compensation, protection of iTaukei, Rotuman and Banaban lands, land interests and mineral royalties. Subject links: Social Science/Geography, History, English, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: land use, ownership and community resources. Observable evidence: learner identifies different interests in a fictional land-use case and distinguishes a constitutional principle from a specific legal procedure. Teach with cultural care; do not generalise across communities.
12. **Education, languages and lifelong learning** — Source: s.31. Concept: the Constitution recognises early childhood, primary, secondary and further education; it addresses progressive realisation of education and names conversational and contemporary iTaukei and Fiji Hindi as compulsory primary-school subjects. Subject links: Social Science, English, Vosa Vakaviti, Fiji Hindi. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: school stages and language awareness. Observable evidence: learner organises education stages and identifies why language learning matters in a multilingual society. Check current education legislation and policy before presenting operational requirements.
13. **Work, economic participation and public wellbeing** — Source: ss.32–38. Concept: constitutional provisions address participation in economic life, work, wages, transport, housing, sanitation, food, water, social security and health. Subject links: Social Science, Business/Commercial Studies, Mathematics, Healthy Living. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: needs, services, work and community resources. Observable evidence: learner groups examples of public services and economic participation and explains how they affect community wellbeing. Distinguish constitutional rights from immediate service entitlements or guaranteed outcomes.
14. **Environmental stewardship and intergenerational responsibility** — Source: ss.1(h), 40. Concept: sustainable relationship with nature and a clean, healthy environment are constitutional themes, including protection for present and future generations. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Social Science/Geography, English, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: living things, habitats and resource use. Observable evidence: learner supports a practical environmental proposal with a reason and evidence.
15. **Children’s rights and best interests** — Source: s.41. Concept: the text addresses children’s identity, basic needs, care, protection from abuse and exploitation, and the best interests of the child as a primary consideration. Subject links: Social Science, Healthy Living, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: safety, needs and trusted support. Observable evidence: learner identifies safe, protective choices in fictional scenarios. Do not use activities that require learners to disclose abuse or personal family circumstances; provide safeguarding pathways through school policy.
16. **Accessibility, disability and communication rights** — Source: s.42. Concept: reasonable access to places, transport and information; sign language, Braille and other communication means; and reasonable adaptation to support participation. Subject links: Social Science, English, Technology, Arts. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: different ways people access information. Observable evidence: learner identifies barriers in a classroom/public-space scenario and proposes accessible alternatives such as clear text, audio, Braille, sign language or physical access.
17. **Courts, fair process and administrative justice** — Source: ss.13–16; ss.44–45; ss.97–100. Concept: constitutional text includes fair-process principles, access to courts, language access, lawful and procedurally fair administrative action, rights enforcement and human-rights oversight. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: fairness, evidence and decision-making. Observable evidence: learner sequences a simplified fictional complaint process and identifies why reasons, impartiality and understandable communication matter. Do not simulate real criminal cases or give legal advice.
18. **Parliament and law-making** — Source: ss.46–51. Concept: Parliament’s legislative authority, Bills, debate, assent, publication, commencement and delegated regulations are set out in constitutional form. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: rules and how decisions are made. Observable evidence: learner arranges a simplified Bill-to-Act sequence and distinguishes a proposal from a law in force.
19. **Representation, elections and voting systems** — Source: ss.52–66; s.75. Concept: constitutional provisions address representation, secret ballot, elections, voter registration, proportional representation and electoral administration. Subject links: Social Science, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: counting, representation and decision-making. Observable evidence: learner interprets a fictional simple vote tally or proportional representation illustration. Do not teach current voter eligibility or live election rules without checking current electoral legislation.
20. **Public scrutiny, committees and participation** — Source: ss.70–74. Concept: parliamentary committees scrutinise administration and legislation; parliamentary business is generally open; public participation, petitions and evidence-gathering are provided for. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: evidence, questions and public discussion. Observable evidence: learner prepares a short evidence-based question or petition about a fictional community issue.
21. **Executive government and ministerial accountability** — Source: ss.81–96. Concept: constitutional roles of the President, Prime Minister and Cabinet; government confidence in Parliament; and ministerial accountability, reporting and answering questions. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: leadership and institutional roles. Observable evidence: learner matches broad executive roles to responsibilities and explains accountability in a simple scenario.
22. **Judicial independence and public institutions** — Source: ss.97–122. Concept: courts and judicial officers, independent judicial/legal institutions and constitutional commissions are established or described. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: fairness, rules and institutions. Observable evidence: learner explains why a court deciding a dispute should be independent from the parties to that dispute.
23. **Public service values and state responsibilities** — Source: ss.123–138. Concept: constitutional principles for public service, public officers and disciplined forces; functions and oversight of public service institutions. Subject links: Social Science, Business/Commercial Studies, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: public and private services. Observable evidence: learner identifies examples of impartial, accountable and service-oriented conduct in fictional public-service situations.
24. **Public finance, budgets and accountability** — Source: ss.139–152. Concept: public revenue, consolidated funds, legal authorisation of expenditure, annual budgets, accounting for public money, freedom of information and audit oversight. Subject links: Mathematics, Business/Commercial Studies, Social Science, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: money, income, expenditure and tables. Observable evidence: learner reads a simplified public-budget table, classifies revenue/expenditure and explains why public accounts need checking.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Social Science/Civics:** concepts 1–5, 7–8, 11–13, 17–23.
- **English:** explain, compare, summarise, debate respectfully, interpret evidence and write a fictional petition/report across the concepts.
- **Mathematics:** fictional election tallies, proportions, public-budget tables, resource-use graphs and simple data interpretation (concepts 19 and 24, plus environmental/resource concepts).
- **Computer Studies/Technology:** privacy, information accuracy, access to information and accessible communication (concepts 9–10 and 16).
- **Healthy Living:** children’s rights, access, sanitation, food, water and health concepts (concepts 13, 15–16).
- **Science/Agriculture:** environmental stewardship and resource management (concept 14); connect to Record 141's Environment Management Act concepts.
- **Languages/Arts:** cultural and linguistic diversity, respectful representation and accessible communication (concepts 2, 8, 12 and 16).

### Teaching and legal safeguards
- These are source-derived concepts, not a substitute for official Fiji curriculum indicators, scope-and-sequence documents or Ministry/CAS guidance. Keep the official indicator field blank where none has been verified; record the PacEdu-derived target in a separate field.
- Do not infer year-level placement from the constitutional section. Assign ECE–Form 7 levels only after developmental, reading-load, prior-knowledge and curriculum alignment checks. Most constitutional concepts require age-appropriate paraphrase; younger learners should work with simple classroom/community examples, not legal interpretation.
- Avoid partisan persuasion and party-political advocacy. Civic activities must be balanced, evidence-based, non-partisan and accessible.
- Do not ask learners to disclose citizenship status, religion, ethnicity, disability, family circumstances, political preference, immigration history or personal experiences of discrimination.
- Current legal effect must be checked against the latest official text, Gazette and judicial interpretation before making claims about present-day duties, rights procedures, electoral rules or constitutional amendment. Treat the 2026 amendment process as a separate, time-sensitive source record if used in later lessons.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. A concept can proceed to a daily-activity design only after level/prerequisite mapping, official-curriculum comparison, source/version check, rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.
