## Record 144 — Fiji Food Safety Act 2003 and Food Safety Regulations 2009: food hygiene, consumer information and food systems

**Source identity**
- **Primary Act:** *Food Safety Act 2003*, Act No. 10 of 2003, Parliament of the Fiji Islands; assented 26 August 2003.
- **Official Fiji Trade Portal record:** https://www.fijitradeportal.gov.fj/en-gb/site/display/165 (lists Act No. 10 of 2003 and identifies the Food Unit, Ministry of Health and Medical Services as responsible agency).
- **Act text inspected:** FAOLEX-hosted PDF mirror of the Fiji Act: https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/fij50969.pdf. This is a text mirror, not the preferred official hosting location; the official portal's PDF download link was identified but could not be opened during this inspection.
- **Regulations:** *Food Safety Regulations 2009*, Legal Notice No. 20, made under the Act; Ministry of Health and Medical Services-hosted PDF: https://www.health.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Food-Safety-Regulations-2009.pdf.
- **Official Trade Portal Regulations record:** https://www.fijitradeportal.gov.fj/en-gb/site/display/166.
- **Inspected Act sections:** ss.2–14, 16–23 and 28–54, plus contents of Parts 4–7.
- **Inspected Regulations:** regs.1–7; 14–18; 21–26; 29–34; 47–53; Fourth Schedule (general hygiene), and selected commodity-specific schedules. Relevant text inspected includes definitions and purpose, unsafe/adulterated food, consumer protection, misleading claims, labelling, food establishment licensing, hygiene, cleaning, pest control, water, waste and temperature control.
- **Source type:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE; FIJI_REGULATORY_SOURCE.
- **Current-version caution:** The Act and Regulations are historical base texts, not confirmed consolidated current law. The Regulations include transitional dates (including historical 2015 and 2020 dates) and technical provisions that may have been amended or superseded. The Trade Portal lists the Act and Regulations, but that listing alone does not prove that every provision in these PDFs remains current. Before teaching any current legal duty, licence requirement, numerical food-safety threshold, penalty, enforcement role or official agency name, obtain the latest consolidated legislation/Gazette and Ministry guidance. For learner activities, use stable general concepts and avoid stating unverified technical thresholds as current law.
- **Rights and reuse:** concepts are paraphrased; no long legal passages reproduced. Open access to a PDF does not establish an open licence for the whole file or third-party content.
- **Classification:** FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; SOURCE_INSPECTED; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Food as a system of substances and ingredients** — Source: Act s.2; Regulations reg.3. Concept: food includes substances and ingredients intended for human consumption, including drinking water and food-processing water. Subject links: Healthy Living, Science, Agriculture, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: food groups and basic needs. Observable evidence: learner classifies examples of food, ingredients and drinking water in a simple food-system diagram.
2. **Food safety and public health** — Source: Act ss.3 and 10; Regulations regs.2–3. Concept: unsafe, unhygienic or unfit food can create risks to health; hygiene protects consumers. Subject links: Healthy Living, Science, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: hygiene and health. Observable evidence: learner identifies safe and unsafe conditions in fictional food-handling pictures and explains the risk.
3. **Contamination and adulteration** — Source: Act ss.3–4; Regulations regs.29–34. Concept: contamination can involve harmful substances, microorganisms, foreign matter or unsuitable handling; adulteration includes misleading composition or unauthorised substances. Subject links: Science, Healthy Living, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: clean/dirty, living/non-living and cause/effect. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes a contamination hazard from a quality or composition issue using safe, teacher-prepared examples. No tasting or handling of suspect food.
4. **Food hygiene and sanitation** — Source: Act s.10; Regulations reg.14 and Fourth Schedule. Concept: hygienic premises, equipment, handling practices and sanitation reduce contamination risks. Subject links: Healthy Living, Home Economics, Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: personal hygiene and clean environments. Observable evidence: learner creates a safe sequence/checklist for cleaning a classroom food-preparation area using teacher-approved materials.
5. **Handwashing and personal cleanliness** — Source: Regulations Fourth Schedule and specific hygiene provisions for food businesses; selected detailed requirements in fish-processing schedules. Concept: suitable handwashing facilities and personal hygiene are part of preventing contamination. Subject links: Healthy Living, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: hygiene routines. Observable evidence: learner orders illustrated handwashing steps and identifies when handwashing is needed. Avoid treating the detailed fish-processing facility requirements as a household rule.
6. **Cleaning, disinfection and safe chemical handling** — Source: Regulations reg.16 (cleaning and disinfection) and Fourth Schedule. Concept: cleaning removes food residues and dirt; disinfection may be needed; cleaning chemicals must be stored and used to prevent contamination. Subject links: Healthy Living, Science, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: materials and safe routines. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes cleaning from disinfection in a simple scenario and selects a safe adult-supervised storage rule. Learners must not handle disinfectants or other chemicals for an activity.
7. **Pest prevention and waste management** — Source: Regulations reg.17 and Fourth Schedule. Concept: keeping premises clean, protecting stored food, preventing pest access and containing waste reduce food contamination. Subject links: Healthy Living, Science, Agriculture, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: pests, habitats and waste sorting. Observable evidence: learner proposes a safe storage/waste arrangement from a diagram and explains how it reduces pest access.
8. **Safe water and ice** — Source: Act s.2 (water intended for consumption is included as food); Regulations Fourth Schedule and reg.3 (potable water definition). Concept: water used for drinking and food preparation must be suitable for human consumption; safe water is part of food hygiene. Subject links: Science, Healthy Living, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: water sources and clean/contaminated. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes a protected water source from a possible contamination pathway using teacher-provided diagrams. Do not conduct experiments using unsafe or untreated water.
9. **Time and temperature as food-safety controls** — Source: Regulations reg.18 and relevant commodity schedules. Concept: temperature and time can affect food safety; refrigeration and suitable thawing methods are controls described in the source. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Healthy Living, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: temperature measurement, time and graphs. Observable evidence: learner reads a teacher-provided temperature/time data table and explains why food storage conditions matter. Do not teach the exact historical 5°C–66°C / four-hour wording as current legal advice until amendments and current Ministry guidance are verified.
10. **Food storage, transport and cross-contamination** — Source: Regulations regs.14–18 and relevant schedules; Act ss.2–3. Concept: storage, packaging, transport and separation of foods can help prevent contamination; raw and ready-to-eat foods require careful handling. Subject links: Healthy Living, Home Economics, Science, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: grouping and hygiene. Observable evidence: learner identifies contamination pathways on a fictional kitchen/storage diagram and suggests separation measures.
11. **Food labels and traceability** — Source: Act s.13; Regulations regs.21–23. Concept: labels communicate food identity and required consumer information; batch/lot identification supports traceability; date and storage information help consumers make decisions. Subject links: English, Mathematics, Healthy Living, Business/Commercial Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: reading labels, dates, units and product information. Observable evidence: learner locates product name, ingredients, quantity, date marking and storage instructions on a teacher-selected label and records information accurately. Verify current labelling requirements before claiming a field is legally mandatory.
12. **Ingredients, quantities and measurement** — Source: Act s.13; Regulations regs.21–23 and food commodity standards. Concept: ingredient lists and net quantity use ordering, measurement and comparison; ingredient proportions can be represented mathematically. Subject links: Mathematics, Home Economics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: mass, volume, ordering and fractions/percentages as age-appropriate. Observable evidence: learner compares two fictional labels, orders listed ingredients and solves a simple quantity problem.
13. **Nutrition information and food claims** — Source: Act ss.8 and 14; Regulations regs.22–25. Concept: food information and claims should not mislead; nutrient and health claims have defined meanings and conditions in the regulatory text. Subject links: Healthy Living, Science, English, Mathematics, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: evidence, advertising language and basic nutrition. Observable evidence: learner separates a factual label statement from an unsupported promotional claim using fictional examples. Do not give individual dietary or medical advice.
14. **Consumer rights, informed choices and fair trading** — Source: Act ss.7–9 and 13–14. Concept: purchasers should receive food that meets applicable standards and should not be misled by false, deceptive or incomplete representations. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, English, Mathematics, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: needs, wants, price and advertising. Observable evidence: learner compares fictional product descriptions and explains which information is useful for a fair consumer choice.
15. **Food processing and preservation** — Source: Act s.2; Regulations regs.15–20 and commodity-specific schedules. Concept: processing may include mixing, heating, cooling, freezing, fermenting and preserving; different food types have different handling and quality considerations. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Home Economics, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: changes in materials and food sources. Observable evidence: learner sorts examples by processing method and describes a simple change in food without performing risky preservation procedures.
16. **Food sampling, testing and evidence** — Source: Act ss.32 and 43–47; Regulations regs.8–13. Concept: authorised officers and analysts use controlled sampling, sample identification, laboratory analysis and documented results to assess food. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: observation, fair tests, measurement and recording. Observable evidence: learner interprets a fictional sample label and a simple test-result table. Only teacher-prepared, safe, non-food or simulated data; learners do not collect suspect food or conduct microbiological testing.
17. **Food businesses and accountability** — Source: Act ss.16–23 and 28–34; Regulations regs.47–50. Concept: food establishments, licensing, record-keeping, inspections and authorised public-health roles are part of the regulatory system. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, Social Science, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: business roles and workplace responsibility. Observable evidence: learner identifies the responsibilities of a fictional food business and explains why records and inspections support safety. Verify current licensing process and agency names before teaching operational details.
18. **Fiji food supply chains and commodity diversity** — Source: Regulations Parts IV and VIII and commodity schedules; Act ss.2 and 24–27. Concept: the regulatory text treats fish, meat, eggs, milk, fruit, vegetables, cereals, spices, oils and beverages as distinct food categories with different product standards and handling needs. Subject links: Agriculture, Science, Social Science, Mathematics, Home Economics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: local food sources and classification. Observable evidence: learner maps a familiar food from producer to seller/consumer and identifies one safe handling point at each stage.
19. **Food safety and trade** — Source: Act ss.24–27 and 69; Regulations regs.4–7 and export sampling provisions. Concept: food standards connect domestic safety with import/export controls and international standards; the text references Codex Alimentarius. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, Social Science, Science, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: trade, standards and quality. Observable evidence: learner explains why a food product may need to meet standards before it is sold or traded. Do not infer current export/import permit steps from these historic base texts alone.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Healthy Living:** hygiene, contamination, safe water, storage, consumer information and food choices (concepts 1–14).
- **Science:** contamination, microorganisms as a concept (without culturing), temperature, measurement, processing and evidence (concepts 2–3, 8–10, 15–16).
- **Agriculture:** food sources, water, storage, pests and supply chains (concepts 7–8, 18).
- **Home Economics:** personal hygiene, cleaning, food preparation, storage, labels and food handling (concepts 4–12, 15).
- **Mathematics:** mass/volume, ingredient order, quantities, dates, temperature/time tables and simple data analysis (concepts 9, 11–12, 16).
- **English:** instructions, labels, persuasive claims, evidence-based reports and consumer explanations (concepts 11–14, 16).
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** food businesses, customer information, fair claims, quality, records and trade (concepts 13–14, 17–19).

### Safety and legal safeguards
- This record does not authorise learner handling of spoiled food, raw meat/seafood, unknown samples, chemicals, disinfectants, pesticides, contaminated water or microbiological cultures. Use diagrams, photographs, fictional labels, teacher-prepared datasets and safe classroom simulations.
- Do not ask learners to taste foods to determine safety or to diagnose foodborne illness.
- Exact temperatures, time limits, technical standards, mandatory label fields, licensing requirements, enforcement powers, fees and penalties must not be stated as current law until the latest consolidated Act, Regulations and Ministry guidance have been checked.
- Food and nutrition activities must remain educational and non-clinical; do not prescribe diets or make individual medical recommendations.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Level/prerequisite mapping, official-curriculum comparison, current-version check, rights review and teacher review are still required.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 145 — Fiji Climate Change Act 2021 (Act No. 43 of 2021): climate science, adaptation, mitigation, oceans and community resilience

**Source identity**
- **Exact title:** *Climate Change Act 2021* (Act No. 43 of 2021).
- **Issuing body:** Parliament of the Republic of Fiji.
- **Assent:** 23 September 2021; Act is 112 sections in 17 Parts.
- **Primary official source:** Parliament of Fiji PDF: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Act-No.-43-Climate-Change.pdf
- **Responsible-government information portal:** Fiji Climate Change Portal: https://fijiclimatechangeportal.gov.fj/home/
- **Inspected sections:** ss.2–6 (definitions, objectives and principles); ss.7–8 (Paris Agreement/NDC); ss.18–26 (state entities, decision-making, EIA, procurement and curriculum); ss.27–37 (policy, emissions inventory, data and Information Platform); ss.38–44 (emissions target, carbon budgets, sectors and transport); ss.45–64 (carbon sequestration and emissions projects); ss.65–74 (adaptation, rights, risk scenarios and resilient infrastructure); ss.75–78 (climate displacement and planned relocation); ss.79–86 (oceans); ss.87–100 (finance and private-sector engagement).
- **Printed page references:** ss.2–6 printed pp.412–425; ss.18–26 pp.434–440; ss.27–37 pp.440–446; ss.38–44 pp.446–450; ss.65–74 pp.464–469; ss.75–78 pp.469–471; ss.79–86 pp.472–476; ss.87–100 pp.477–481. Use section numbers as the principal locator.
- **Official context:** Fiji Climate Change Portal identifies the Act as the legal basis for long-term climate measures and links the National Climate Change Policy, National Adaptation Plan, National Ocean Policy and Low Emission Development Strategy.
- **Current-version status:** Official Parliament Act text inspected; the Fiji Climate Change Portal continues to list the Act. This inspection did not establish a consolidated amendment history or verify every regulation, policy or target currently made under it. Do not present any carbon budget, numerical target, agency portfolio, reporting threshold or legal obligation as current operational fact without checking subsequent Gazette notices, amendments, regulations and current official policy/data. In particular, distinguish the Act's statutory long-term target and planned periods from the latest implementation data.
- **Rights:** Concepts below are paraphrased. No substantial constitutional/legislative text is reproduced. No open licence is claimed for the PDF or portal materials.
- **Classification:** FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; SOURCE_INSPECTED; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED; LEVEL_AND_PREREQUISITE_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Weather, climate and climate change** — Source: s.2 (definitions), ss.4–6. Concept: distinguish short-term weather from longer-term climate patterns; climate change in the Act concerns changes attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alter atmospheric composition beyond natural variability over comparable periods. Subject links: Elementary/Basic Science, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: weather observations and patterns. Observable evidence: learner sorts examples into weather events and long-term climate patterns and explains the distinction.
2. **Greenhouse gases and atmospheric emissions** — Source: s.2 (greenhouse gas, emissions, anthropogenic emissions); ss.29–33. Concept: greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane and other gases identified in the Act; emissions are releases over a specified area and period. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: air, gases and measurement. Observable evidence: learner identifies examples of human activities that release greenhouse gases and reads a simple, teacher-provided emissions dataset.
3. **Human causes and natural variability** — Source: s.2 (climate change, anthropogenic emissions); ss.4–6. Concept: examine human activities and distinguish human-caused changes from natural climate variability without assuming every individual weather event is caused solely by climate change. Subject links: Science, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: weather/climate distinction and cause/effect. Observable evidence: learner evaluates a fictional claim and identifies the evidence needed before attributing an event to climate change.
4. **Climate mitigation** — Source: s.2 (mitigation); ss.38–44. Concept: mitigation means limiting or preventing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing natural or other sinks; examples in the Act include energy, transport, industry, agriculture, forestry, fisheries, waste, tourism, aviation and shipping. Subject links: Science, Technology, Agriculture, Business, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: energy use and resource use. Observable evidence: learner classifies a set of actions as potential emissions-reduction measures and explains why.
5. **Climate adaptation** — Source: s.2 (adaptation); ss.65–74. Concept: adaptation is adjustment in natural or human systems to actual or expected climate effects in order to moderate harm or make use of beneficial opportunities. Subject links: Science, Geography, Agriculture, Technology, Healthy Living. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: hazards, needs and problem-solving. Observable evidence: learner proposes a practical adaptation for a fictional school, farm or coastal community and explains the hazard addressed.
6. **Climate vulnerability, exposure and resilience** — Source: s.2 (at-risk community, climate resilience, vulnerability); ss.67–71. Concept: vulnerability relates to susceptibility or inability to withstand adverse effects; resilience concerns the ability of communities, built environments and ecosystems to respond, withstand and recover. Subject links: Science, Geography, Social Science, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: systems and hazards. Observable evidence: learner compares two fictional communities with different exposure, resources and protective measures and justifies which is more vulnerable.
7. **Sustainable development and intergenerational equity** — Source: s.2 (sustainable development); s.5. Concept: meet present needs without compromising future generations; decision-making balances environmental, social and economic considerations and recognises precaution and intergenerational equity. Subject links: Social Science, Science, English, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: needs, resources and future consequences. Observable evidence: learner evaluates a fictional development choice from present and future community perspectives.
8. **Precautionary principle and evidence-informed decisions** — Source: ss.2 and 5; ss.19–20. Concept: where serious or irreversible harm is possible, uncertainty does not automatically justify inaction; decisions should consider best available science, risks and cost-effectiveness. Subject links: Science, English, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: evidence, uncertainty and risk. Observable evidence: learner compares two proposals and explains what evidence and precautions should be considered.
9. **Fiji's climate emergency and island vulnerability** — Source: s.6. Concept: the Act recognises climate risks to Fiji, including extreme weather, sea-level rise, food and water security, public health, infrastructure, communities and the economy. Subject links: Science, Geography, Healthy Living, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: natural hazards and community needs. Observable evidence: learner links a climate hazard to possible effects on people, ecosystems and infrastructure using a source-based cause-and-effect diagram.
10. **Climate impacts on food and water systems** — Source: ss.6 and 65–67. Concept: climate impacts can affect food production, water availability, health and livelihoods; adaptation planning includes water resources, agriculture, forestry, fisheries and aquaculture. Subject links: Agriculture, Science, Healthy Living, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: food chains, water cycle and farming. Observable evidence: learner maps a fictional drought/flood/coastal-saltwater scenario through effects on crops, water and household needs.
11. **Emissions sources and sector data** — Source: ss.29–33. Concept: national emissions information is organised by sectors including energy, transport, industrial processes, agriculture/forestry/other land use and waste; reliable estimates depend on consistent data collection. Subject links: Mathematics, Science, Business, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: tables, categories and data collection. Observable evidence: learner sorts a sample activity dataset by sector and checks totals and units.
12. **Measurement, reporting, verification and data quality** — Source: ss.29–37. Concept: inventories, sector data, research, reports, information platforms and verification support transparent climate decision-making; data should be consistent, accurate and documented. Subject links: Mathematics, Science, English, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: measurement, recording and checking. Observable evidence: learner identifies missing units, dates or source details in a sample dataset and improves its record.
13. **Climate information and digital access** — Source: ss.34–37. Concept: climate communication and a public information platform support access to emissions data, climate projections, vulnerability and research; the Act expressly requires disability accessibility and data protection/security planning. Subject links: Computer Studies, English, Technology, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: information literacy and accessible formats. Observable evidence: learner finds and summarises information in a teacher-selected public climate dataset and suggests an accessible presentation format.
14. **Carbon sinks and sequestration** — Source: s.2 (carbon sequestration, carbon stocks, blue carbon, sink); ss.45–60. Concept: carbon can be stored in vegetation, soils, sediments and coastal/marine ecosystems; mangroves, salt marshes and seagrasses are examples of blue-carbon ecosystems. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: photosynthesis, ecosystems and matter cycles. Observable evidence: learner diagrams how carbon moves between atmosphere, vegetation, soil or marine sediments using a simplified model.
15. **Forests, mangroves and nature-based solutions** — Source: ss.2, 43, 45–60 and 79–85. Concept: forest conservation, reforestation, mangrove protection and nature-based coastal protection can contribute to carbon storage, ecosystem health and climate adaptation. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Geography, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: habitats, plants and coastal processes. Observable evidence: learner compares a natural coastal buffer and a fictional built intervention, identifying possible benefits and limitations.
16. **Energy efficiency, renewable energy and transport** — Source: ss.23, 38–44. Concept: low-emission energy, efficient buildings, transport decarbonisation and sustainable procurement are possible parts of mitigation. Subject links: Science, Technology, Mathematics, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: energy sources, transport and efficiency. Observable evidence: learner compares two fictional school transport or energy options using a simple cost/energy/emissions table.
17. **Carbon budgets, baselines and trends** — Source: ss.38–42. Concept: a carbon budget sets a planned limit or reduction pathway over a defined period; the Act relates reductions to a 2013 emissions baseline and describes successive five-year budget periods. Subject links: Mathematics, Science, Business, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: baseline, percentage change, time series and graphs. Observable evidence: learner reads a fictional baseline and plots a simple emissions trend. Use fictional numbers unless current official budgets and verified datasets have been sourced; the Act's statutory target is not a substitute for actual reported performance.
18. **Environmental impact and climate risk assessment** — Source: ss.19, 22 and 69–71. Concept: decisions and proposed infrastructure can be assessed for direct, indirect, cumulative, short- and long-term climate effects, vulnerability and resilience. Subject links: Science, Geography, Technology, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: cause/effect, systems and risk. Observable evidence: learner completes a simple risk matrix for a fictional school building or community project.
19. **Climate-resilient infrastructure and built environments** — Source: ss.70–72. Concept: infrastructure resilience includes assessing exposure, vulnerability, replacement needs and the ability of buildings and assets to withstand climate impacts. Subject links: Technology, Science, Mathematics, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: materials, structures and measurement. Observable evidence: learner identifies design features that could reduce risk in a fictional school or community facility; all design work remains conceptual and teacher-supervised.
20. **Climate displacement and planned relocation: rights and participation** — Source: ss.75–78. Concept: planned relocation is treated as a last-resort process after other adaptation measures, requiring community participation, free and prior informed consent, dignity, non-discrimination, livelihoods, and attention to both relocating and host communities. Subject links: Social Science, Geography, English, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: community decision-making, rights and empathy. Observable evidence: learner analyses a fictional scenario and lists questions that affected and host communities should be able to raise. Never use a real learner's community relocation, land claim or family history as a classroom case without consent.
21. **Healthy oceans and marine climate impacts** — Source: ss.79–86. Concept: oceans are connected to livelihoods and identity; climate impacts include coral bleaching, ocean acidification, biodiversity loss and deoxygenation; pollution, sedimentation and unsustainable fishing can add stress. Subject links: Science, Geography, Agriculture, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: marine ecosystems and food webs. Observable evidence: learner explains one pathway by which a stressor affects a marine ecosystem using a labelled diagram.
22. **Ocean sustainability, marine protected areas and traditional knowledge** — Source: ss.81–85. Concept: ocean management involves targets, marine protected areas, scientific evidence, consultation and traditional knowledge; the Act identifies the role of sustainable ocean management. Subject links: Science, Social Science, Geography, Vosa Vakaviti, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: marine habitats and community resources. Observable evidence: learner compares scientific observations and a teacher-approved community knowledge example, with attribution and respect, to explain a marine stewardship proposal. Do not extract or publish restricted/traditional knowledge without appropriate permission.
23. **Climate finance and resource allocation** — Source: ss.87–91. Concept: climate action requires financial resources, planning and mechanisms for funding mitigation and adaptation; projects can be evaluated for intended public benefits and accountability. Subject links: Mathematics, Business/Commercial Studies, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: budgeting and needs. Observable evidence: learner allocates a fictional limited budget across adaptation options and explains trade-offs.
24. **Business climate risks, opportunities and disclosure** — Source: ss.92–100. Concept: businesses and financial institutions may need to consider and disclose climate-related financial risks and measures to reduce them; climate change can affect assets, operations, investment and opportunities. Subject links: Business Administration, Commercial Studies, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: business operations, risk and financial records. Observable evidence: learner identifies climate-related risks to a fictional business and proposes a basic continuity or adaptation measure. Do not present these sections as a general legal disclosure checklist for every small business.
25. **Public consultation, Talanoa and inclusive decision-making** — Source: s.2 (Talanoa); ss.5, 9–10, 27–28, 67, 77 and 83. Concept: transparent, inclusive dialogue and consultation help share information, consider different views and support collective decisions; participation should include youth and vulnerable or at-risk groups. Subject links: English, Social Science, Vosa Vakaviti, Arts. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: listening, turn-taking and respectful discussion. Observable evidence: learner records a balanced set of viewpoints from a fictional community discussion and summarises common concerns.
26. **Climate change education across the curriculum** — Source: s.25. Concept: the Act directs the education minister, in consultation with the climate minister, to integrate evidence-based climate learning into a variety of subjects of the Fiji National Curriculum Framework at all curriculum levels. This is a legal curriculum-integration direction, not a list of learner achievement indicators or an independently specified lesson sequence. Subject links: cross-curricular. Level: ECE–Form 7 as a statutory policy scope; age-appropriate objectives still require curriculum mapping. Observable evidence: a PacEdu mapping record links verified climate concepts to the relevant official subject and level indicator where one exists, or labels the target as PacEdu-derived where none has been verified.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Elementary/Basic Science:** concepts 1–10, 14–15, 18, 21–22.
- **Social Science/Geography:** concepts 6–10, 18, 20–25.
- **Agriculture:** concepts 10–11, 14–15, 21–22.
- **Mathematics:** concepts 11–12, 17, 18, 23–24.
- **Technology/Computer Studies:** concepts 12–13, 16, 18–19.
- **Healthy Living:** concepts 9–10, 20–21.
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** concepts 11, 16–17, 23–24.
- **English and Fiji languages:** vocabulary, reading, explanation, evidence, data commentary, debate, Talanoa and reporting across all suitable concepts.

### Teaching, safety and legal safeguards
- Section 25 is especially relevant to PacEdu's curriculum mapping: it provides a statutory direction for evidence-based climate learning across subjects and all levels of the Fiji National Curriculum Framework. It does not itself supply detailed year-level achievement indicators. PacEdu must still map to the official curriculum and clearly label derived learning targets.
- Avoid climate fatalism, alarmist messaging and claims that every disaster is caused only by climate change. Teach evidence, uncertainty, local adaptation, community knowledge and constructive agency.
- Do not ask learners to disclose personal displacement, land ownership, financial vulnerability, disaster trauma or family circumstances. Use fictional or public case studies and protect community knowledge.
- Do not send learners into hazardous coastal areas, floodwater, storms, damaged infrastructure or mangroves for fieldwork. Use teacher-approved safe observation sites, public datasets, maps, photographs and simulations.
- Carbon-credit markets, property rights, emissions registries, offences, penalties, institutional powers and relocation procedures are specialist legal matters; do not turn these into learner compliance advice.
- Any numerical carbon budget, emission factor, sea-level trend, vulnerability statistic or current government target used in an activity must have its own current dated source and units. The Act's 2050 target in s.38 is a statutory target, not a claim about measured progress.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Official curriculum comparison, developmental level/prerequisite mapping, current source/policy check, rights review and teacher review remain required.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 146 — Fisheries (Amendment) Act 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025): aquatic biodiversity, fishing systems, monitoring and regulatory accountability

**Source identity**
- **Exact title:** *Fisheries (Amendment) Act 2025*, Act No. 24 of 2025. It is an amendment to the *Fisheries Act 1941*, not a standalone replacement Fisheries Act.
- **Issuing body:** Parliament of the Republic of Fiji.
- **Assent:** 26 November 2025. Passed by Parliament on 6 November 2025.
- **Primary official source:** Parliament of Fiji PDF: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Act-24-Fisheries-Act-2025.pdf
- **Base Act official-law reference:** Fisheries Act 1941, Laws of Fiji / Office of the Attorney-General, surfaced through the Fiji Trade Portal: https://www.fijitradeportal.gov.fj/en-gb/site/display/180
- **Commencement verified:** Parliament's 2023–2026 sitting statistics identify commencement on 18 February 2026 by Legal Notice No. 25 of 2026. Source: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Compiled-Parliament-Sitting-Statistics%E2%80%93May-2026.pdf
- **Inspected provisions in the amendment:** s.1 (short title/commencement); s.2 (definitions, including expanded definition of fish, fishing gear, fishing vessel and taking fish); s.3 (terminology); s.4 (appointment of authorised officers); s.5 (search, examination and detention powers); ss.6–7 (licence suspension/cancellation, appeals and fixed penalty notices); ss.8–9 (regulations and licence-condition offences).
- **Source lines/pages:** official Act PDF printed pp.119–124; section references above are primary locators. PDF text inspected in full.
- **Current-version status:** This amendment came into force on 18 February 2026. It amends the 1941 principal Act; therefore it must be read together with the latest consolidated principal Act and any later amendments/regulations. This record is not a complete consolidated Fisheries Act. The official Parliament Acts index also lists later Acts through 2026, so recheck it before any future lesson about current fisheries law. Do not teach detailed offence, penalty, search, seizure, licensing or appeal procedures as learner advice.
- **Rights:** paraphrased concepts only; no substantial legal passages copied. No open licence is claimed for the PDF.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE; FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; SOURCE_INSPECTED; COMMENCEMENT_VERIFIED; CONSOLIDATED_CURRENT_TEXT_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Aquatic biodiversity and the meaning of fish** — Source: Fisheries (Amendment) Act 2025, s.2 (amends Fisheries Act 1941, s.2 definition of “fish”). Concept: the statutory definition covers aquatic plants and animals, not only finfish; examples named include molluscs, crustaceans, coral, sponges, sea cucumbers (holothurians), echinoderms, turtles and aquatic mammals, as well as eggs and juvenile stages. Subject links: Elementary/Basic Science, Social Science/Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: living/non-living, animal groups and habitats. Observable evidence: learner sorts illustrated marine organisms into broad groups and explains why marine biodiversity includes more than finfish.
2. **Life cycles and vulnerable life stages** — Source: Act s.2 (amended “fish” definition expressly includes eggs, spawn, spat and juvenile stages). Concept: aquatic species have different life stages, and protecting breeding and juvenile stages is relevant to maintaining populations. Subject links: Science, Agriculture/Aquaculture, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: life cycles and reproduction. Observable evidence: learner orders a teacher-provided marine species life-cycle diagram and identifies a stage that could be vulnerable to disturbance. The conservation implication is a PacEdu learning inference, not a quoted legal rule in this amendment.
3. **Fishing as a connected activity and supply chain** — Source: Act s.2 (amended definition of “taking fish”). Concept: fishing activity can include searching, attempted catching, harvesting and operations that support or prepare for taking fish. Subject links: Social Science, Business/Commercial Studies, Science, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: occupations, production and supply chains. Observable evidence: learner maps a fictional fishing supply chain from locating/catching through handling, transport and sale. Do not teach legal boundaries of an offence from this simplified concept.
4. **Fishing gear, tools and technology** — Source: Act s.2 (definition of “fishing gear”). Concept: fishing equipment includes lines, hooks, nets, spears, reels and mechanical/electrical assistance; tools influence how fishing is carried out. Subject links: Technology, Science, Social Science, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: tools, materials and simple machines. Observable evidence: learner classifies safe photographs of fishing tools by purpose and describes one possible effect of gear choice on fishing activity. No learner handling of spears, hooks, nets or powered gear.
5. **Vessels, marine transport and fishing operations** — Source: Act s.2 (definitions of “vessel” and “fishing vessel”). Concept: water-going craft are part of fishing operations; vessels and equipment can be considered as a connected system. Subject links: Technology, Science, Social Science, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: transport types and systems. Observable evidence: learner labels a fictional fishing-vessel diagram and identifies how vessel, crew, gear and catch interact. Avoid unsafe boat or sea activities.
6. **Fisheries management and public institutions** — Source: Act ss.2 and 4 (new s.6A appointing authorised officers). Concept: fisheries management involves defined public roles and authorised personnel; institutional responsibilities and oversight can be studied as part of resource governance. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: community roles and public services. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes a resource user, a business operator and a public officer in a fictional governance diagram. Do not imply that any person may exercise statutory powers.
7. **Monitoring, inspection and evidence records** — Source: Act s.5 (substituted Fisheries Act 1941, s.7). Concept: the amendment provides for inspection of licences, fishing gear and fish, and examination of relevant vessels/premises by authorised officers; this illustrates monitoring, evidence collection and compliance systems. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: observation, classification and accurate recording. Observable evidence: learner completes a fictional observation log with date, location, category and evidence source. Do not simulate searches, detentions or enforcement encounters.
8. **Licences, conditions and accountable resource use** — Source: Act s.6 (substituted Fisheries Act 1941, s.8). Concept: commercial/regulated fishing activity may be subject to licences and conditions, and the law provides for suspension or cancellation where specified grounds apply. Subject links: Social Science, Business/Commercial Studies, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: rules, permissions and responsibilities. Observable evidence: learner explains the difference between permission to undertake an activity and responsibility to follow its conditions, using a fictional non-legal example. Current licensing requirements must be sourced separately.
9. **Fair process, written reasons and appeal pathways** — Source: Act s.7 (new Fisheries Act 1941, s.8A). Concept: the amendment provides a formal appeal route for specified licensing decisions and requires notification of licence suspension/cancellation to be in writing with grounds. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: decisions, reasons and respectful disagreement. Observable evidence: learner identifies the decision, reason and review route in a fictional school-club permission scenario. Do not present the fisheries appeal deadline or process as general legal advice.
10. **Rules, notices and procedural accountability** — Source: Act s.7 (new ss.8B–8C) and s.8. Concept: legislation can establish procedures for notices, time limits, documentation and communication between officers and courts; this provides an example of why public procedures must be written and traceable. Subject links: English, Social Science/Civics, Mathematics, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: dates, sequence, formal notices and records. Observable evidence: learner arranges a fictional administrative notice sequence and checks that required fields are present. Do not reproduce penalty notice templates or teach real penalty amounts, deadlines or court consequences as personal guidance.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Science:** aquatic biodiversity, life cycles, habitats and marine food webs (concepts 1–2).
- **Social Science/Geography:** fisheries as a livelihood, resource governance, public institutions and community use (concepts 3, 6, 8–9).
- **Technology:** fishing gear, vessels and safe technology classification (concepts 4–5).
- **Mathematics:** classify catch datasets, tally species groups, compare fictional time-series or supply-chain quantities (concepts 1–5, 7, 10).
- **English and Fiji languages:** descriptions, explanations, observation logs, balanced viewpoints and procedural sequencing (concepts 3, 6–10).
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** fishing value chains, permissions, operating conditions and accountability (concepts 3, 8).

### Teaching, safety and legal safeguards
- This amendment broadens the legal definition of fish, but does not itself provide a full marine ecology syllabus or a complete set of conservation rules. Use separate verified ecological sources for food webs, protected species, closed seasons, size limits and sustainable harvest concepts.
- Do not present the 1941 Act as fully consolidated from this amendment alone. Check the latest Laws of Fiji principal Act, all subsequent amendments, regulations and Gazette notices before any lesson about current legal duties or fisheries rules.
- Do not teach offence penalties, enforcement powers, searches, vessel detention, fixed penalty amounts, licence eligibility or statutory appeal deadlines as practical advice to learners or fishers.
- No learner handling of hooks, spears, nets, live catch, marine mammals, turtles, coral, sea cucumbers, fishing vessels or powered gear. Use teacher-approved images, diagrams, fictional datasets and safe classroom models.
- Do not send learners to sea, reefs, mangroves, river mouths or fishing operations without a formal school safety assessment and supervision. Protect community and traditional knowledge; obtain permission and attribute sources appropriately.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Official curriculum comparison, level/prerequisite mapping, consolidated law check, rights review and teacher review remain required.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 147 — Forestry Act 2025 (Act No. 28 of 2025): Fiji forest ecosystems, customary rights, sustainable resource management and forest industry

**Source identity and legal status**
- **Exact title:** *Forestry Act 2025*, Act No. 28 of 2025.
- **Issuing body:** Parliament of the Republic of Fiji.
- **Enacted:** 1 December 2025.
- **Commencement:** 1 December 2025, by Legal Notice No. 11 of 2026. Commencement is confirmed in Parliament's 2023–2026 Sitting Statistics updated following the May 2026 sitting.
- **Primary official enacted source:** Parliament of Fiji, *Forestry Act 2025*, 52-page PDF: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Act-28-Forestry.pdf
- **Official Parliament Acts index:** https://www.parliament.gov.fj/acts/ (Act No. 28 of 2025 is listed under Act 2025).
- **Supplementary legislative history:** Forestry Bill No. 36 of 2025: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Bill-No.-36a-Forestry-Bill-2025.pdf. The Bill is background only; this record uses the enacted Act for substantive section references.
- **Commencement verification source:** Parliament, *2023–2026 Parliament Sitting Stats*, updated May 2026: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Compiled-Parliament-Sitting-Statistics%E2%80%93May-2026.pdf
- **Inspected enacted provisions:** ss.1–6; ss.7–21; ss.22–26; ss.27–34; ss.35–43; ss.44–48; ss.49–54; selected definitions in s.2. The 52-page enacted Act PDF was inspected for these provisions.
- **Exact section/page locators:** s.2 (printed pp.150–157; PDF pp.3–10); ss.4–6 (printed pp.158–160; PDF pp.11–13); ss.8–17 (printed pp.162–166; PDF pp.15–19); ss.18–21 (printed pp.166–168; PDF pp.19–21); ss.22–26 (printed pp.168–171; PDF pp.21–24); ss.33–34 (printed pp.173–174; PDF pp.26–27); ss.44–50 (printed pp.178–180; PDF pp.31–33); ss.51–54 (printed pp.180–182; PDF pp.33–35). Page locators use the printed pagination visible in the Act; section numbers are the controlling locator.
- **Version check:** Parliament's index and May 2026 sitting statistics confirm Act 28 and its commencement. This review did not establish whether later 2026 amendments, subsidiary legislation, forest practice codes, Gazette declarations, or revised National Forest Policy have since changed operational details. Before teaching current protected areas, licensing, customary rights, harvesting conditions, species lists, fire restrictions, penalties, royalties or certification, recheck current Gazette notices, regulations, codes and official Ministry guidance.
- **Rights:** This record paraphrases legal concepts and does not reproduce substantial passages. No open licence is claimed for the Act PDF.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE; FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; ENACTED_ACT_INSPECTED; COMMENCEMENT_VERIFIED; CURRENT_SUBSIDIARY_LAW_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **What counts as a forest and forest ecosystem** — Source: Forestry Act 2025, s.2 (definitions of “forest”, “forest ecosystem”, “forest cover” and related terms; printed pp.150–152). Concept: forest areas can include natural and planted vegetation, mangrove forest and certain connected areas; a forest is more than a group of timber trees and can be studied as a living system. Subject links: Elementary/Basic Science, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: plants, habitats and living/non-living components. Observable evidence: learner labels a teacher-provided forest ecosystem diagram, identifying vegetation, soil, water and organisms. Avoid teaching the statutory canopy thresholds as universal ecological definitions without a science source.
2. **Forest ecosystem services** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “ecosystem services” (printed pp.152–153). Concept: forests provide products and functions including food, timber and non-timber products, carbon storage, climate regulation, water purification, erosion control, nutrient cycling, soil formation, biodiversity, recreation and cultural values. Subject links: Science, Geography, Agriculture, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: needs, resources and ecosystems. Observable evidence: learner groups examples into provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural benefits; these category labels are a PacEdu teaching framework, not a statutory classification.
3. **Conservation, deforestation and forest degradation** — Source: Act s.2 definitions (printed pp.151–153), read with ss.4–6 (printed pp.158–160). Concept: conservation means planned management and sustainable use for long-term natural and cultural values; deforestation is conversion from forested to non-forested land; degradation is reduced ability to provide goods and ecosystem services even without full conversion. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: land cover, change over time and cause/effect. Observable evidence: learner compares two fictional forest-cover diagrams and distinguishes clearing from declining forest condition.
4. **Indigenous, invasive and protected species** — Source: Act s.2 (definitions of “indigenous species” and “invasive species”; printed pp.154–155); ss.48–49 (printed pp.180–181). Concept: species naturally originating in Fiji are distinguished from introduced species; introduced species may be invasive where they cause or are likely to cause harm to the economy, environment, health or biodiversity; forest species protection and pest prevention are part of forest health. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: native/introduced organisms, habitats and biodiversity. Observable evidence: learner classifies a supplied, verified species case study and explains why origin alone does not establish that a species is invasive. Do not invent species classifications; use a current Ministry/Biosecurity species source.
5. **Mangrove forests and coastal habitats** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “mangrove forest” (printed p.155) and ss.18–20 (printed pp.166–167). Concept: mangroves are forest types adapted to saline and tidal coastal habitats and can be included in protected forest categories. Subject links: Science, Geography, Climate Education, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: coastal habitats, tides and plant adaptations. Observable evidence: learner labels a mangrove habitat cross-section and describes how tidal conditions shape the habitat. Do not assume all mangrove locations have the same legal protection status; verify Gazette declarations.
6. **Sustainable forest management and ecosystem-based decisions** — Source: Act ss.4–5 (printed pp.158–160). Concept: forest management decisions balance long-term ecological health and productivity with economic and social considerations; ecosystem-based management, precaution, monitoring and intergenerational equity are guiding principles. Subject links: Science, Social Science, Agriculture, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: resource use, needs and consequences. Observable evidence: learner compares two fictional forest-use proposals against ecological, social and economic criteria.
7. **Restoration, reforestation and afforestation** — Source: Act s.2 definitions and ss.4, 6, 8 (printed pp.150–160 and 162–163). Concept: restoration seeks to recover damaged forest condition; reforestation increases forest cover on land that was previously forested; afforestation establishes forest on land not forested for the period specified in the Act. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Mathematics, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: plant growth, life cycles and land-use change. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes restoration, reforestation and afforestation using labelled scenarios. The statutory time definition for afforestation must be quoted accurately if taught.
8. **Trees outside forests and agroforestry** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “trees outside of forests” (printed p.157), s.4(i), and s.8(g) (printed pp.158–159 and 162–163). Concept: trees and shrubs in farms, towns and along roads are relevant to tree cover and can provide environmental, economic and social benefits; agroforestry combines trees with agricultural land uses. Subject links: Agriculture, Science, Technology, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: plant needs, farm systems and land use. Observable evidence: learner draws a simple farm layout showing trees, crops, boundaries and possible benefits without assuming that one design suits every site.
9. **Forest classification and protected areas** — Source: Act s.18 (printed pp.166–167), ss.19–20 (printed p.167). Concept: forests may be classified by function, ecological characteristics and management regime, including multiple-use forests, plantations and protected forests; reserve declarations define boundaries, purposes and permitted/prohibited activities. Subject links: Science, Geography, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: maps, land-use categories and habitats. Observable evidence: learner sorts fictional forest-area profiles into categories using the Act's definitions and explains why a map legend and boundary matter. Do not label a real site as a reserve without checking its current Gazette declaration.
10. **Forest resource assessment, mapping and remote sensing** — Source: Act ss.17–18 and s.21 (printed pp.166–168). Concept: satellite imagery and remote sensing can monitor forest cover, condition and change; national resource assessments collect data for forest management, timber supply, catchments, biodiversity habitat and restoration needs. Subject links: Mathematics, Computer Studies, Science, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: maps, graphs, data tables and comparing observations. Observable evidence: learner compares two dated, teacher-supplied forest-cover images, records visible change and states one limitation of image interpretation. Use approved public imagery; do not present a classroom estimate as an official national forest assessment.
11. **Scientific evidence, research and adaptive management** — Source: Act ss.5, 15–17 and 43 (printed pp.160, 165–166, 177). Concept: forest policy and planning draw on evolving scientific knowledge, stakeholder input and changing environmental conditions; monitoring results can lead to revised plans; research evaluates whether management measures are effective. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: observation, evidence, variables and revision. Observable evidence: learner uses a fictional monitoring dataset to recommend a cautious management adjustment and identifies what further evidence is needed.
12. **Forest products, non-timber products and processing** — Source: Act s.2 definitions of “forest products”, “non-timber forest products” and “wood processing” (printed pp.153–157). Concept: forest resources include timber and a wide range of non-timber products such as fruits, nuts, seeds, leaves, roots, fibres, resins, honey and fungi; wood can be processed into sawn timber, poles, chips, pulp and engineered products. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Technology, Home Economics, Business/Commercial Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: materials, raw materials and production. Observable evidence: learner classifies safe pictured products as timber or non-timber and maps a simple raw-material-to-product chain. Avoid collection or consumption of wild products for classroom tasks.
13. **Forest industry, value addition and sustainable trade** — Source: Act ss.4(n)–(q), ss.27–31 and s.47 (printed pp.159–160, pp.168–171 and p.180). Concept: forest industry includes harvesting, processing, product quality, value addition, certification, supply chains and access to markets; sustainable trade depends on lawful sourcing and reliable records. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, Mathematics, Technology, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: production, costs, measurement and markets. Observable evidence: learner maps a fictional timber value chain and identifies where quality checks and source records could be used. Do not teach current licence conditions, export rules or certification claims without current operational sources.
14. **Traditional knowledge, customary rights and participation** — Source: Act ss.4(c), 4(g), 5(a), 12–13, 46 and 79 (printed pp.158–160, pp.164–165, pp.178–180 and pp.182). Concept: forest governance includes participation, recognition of traditional knowledge, customary rights and benefit-sharing; legal decisions may require specific prior consents depending on land status and the proposed licence or plan. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: rights, responsibilities, consultation and respectful listening. Observable evidence: learner identifies stakeholders in a fictional forest-planning case and explains why consultation and permission must be checked. Do not ask learners to disclose family land status, customary rights, clan knowledge or private community disputes; do not generalise the statutory provisions as a complete account of iTaukei land law.
15. **Community benefits, royalties and forest livelihoods** — Source: Act ss.4(c), 4(m)–(n), 45–46 and 53 (printed pp.158–160, pp.178–180 and pp.181–182). Concept: forest-based livelihoods include employment, processing and enterprise; benefit-sharing, royalties and finance mechanisms can influence who benefits from resource use and who bears environmental costs. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, Mathematics, Social Science, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: income, costs, fairness and community needs. Observable evidence: learner compares fictional benefit-sharing options and calculates simple percentage or quantity examples. Never use a real landowning group's private royalty figures or imply that statutory rates are known from this Act alone.
16. **Forest pests, invasive organisms and forest health** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “pests” (printed pp.155–156) and s.49 (printed p.181). Concept: pests can damage forest ecosystem components including soil, water, plants, animals and forest products; prevention and monitoring support forest health. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: organisms, plant health and observation. Observable evidence: learner records symptoms in a fictional case and distinguishes observation from an unverified diagnosis. No handling or release of pests, invasive organisms, plant pathogens or chemicals.
17. **Forest fires, hazard awareness and prevention** — Source: Act ss.50–52 (printed pp.180–181). Concept: forest fire risk is a forest-management concern and the Act provides for fire-hazard areas, authorised fire controls and fire response roles. Subject links: Science, Geography, Healthy Living, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: fire triangle, weather and safety rules. Observable evidence: learner identifies safe prevention actions from a teacher-approved scenario and explains why people should report a fire to responsible adults/emergency services. No learner fire-lighting, fire suppression exercises, entry into fire zones or handling of firefighting equipment.
18. **Climate mitigation, carbon storage and forest finance** — Source: Act ss.2, 4(e), 53–54 (printed pp.152–153, pp.158–159 and pp.181–182). Concept: forests store carbon and can contribute to climate mitigation; forest restoration, conservation and sustainable management may be supported by finance mechanisms, including ecosystem-service and emissions-reduction arrangements governed by other laws. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Business, Climate Education. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: carbon cycle, graphs and money/finance concepts. Observable evidence: learner interprets a fictional carbon-storage diagram and distinguishes a measured carbon result from a financial credit. Do not teach carbon-credit values, project eligibility or claims of offsetting without current technical and regulatory sources.
19. **Monitoring reports, transparency and public information** — Source: Act ss.5(b), 13, 17(5), 21 and 25–26 (printed pp.160, pp.164–168 and pp.170–171). Concept: public forest information, monitoring results, compliance reports and assessments support accountability and informed decisions. Subject links: English, Mathematics, Computer Studies, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: reading tables, report structure and source checking. Observable evidence: learner extracts a stated fact from a teacher-provided public report, records its date/source and distinguishes the report's observation from their own inference.
20. **Forest governance, planning and regulatory roles** — Source: Act ss.7–16 and ss.23–26 (printed pp.161–171). Concept: forest management involves defined institutional roles, committees, an advisory council, forest practices plans, reporting and review; this can be studied as a public-governance system. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, Business, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: roles, responsibilities, planning and records. Observable evidence: learner completes a simple fictional governance flowchart distinguishing landowners, forest users, technical officers and advisory bodies. Do not simulate enforcement powers, searches, seizures, penalties or licensing decisions.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Elementary/Basic Science:** forest ecosystems, species and habitats, ecosystem services, mangroves, pests, fire ecology and carbon storage (concepts 1–7, 16–18).
- **Geography/Social Science:** land cover, protected areas, land use, customary rights, participation, governance and community livelihoods (concepts 3, 5, 8–11, 14–15, 20).
- **Agriculture:** agroforestry, restoration, plant health and non-timber products (concepts 7–8, 12, 16).
- **Mathematics:** forest-cover comparisons, sampling, charts, resource inventories, value chains and fictional benefit-sharing calculations (concepts 10–13, 15, 18–19).
- **Technology/Computer Studies:** remote sensing, mapping, wood processing and traceable records (concepts 10–13, 19).
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** value addition, legal sourcing, forestry livelihoods, finance and benefit-sharing (concepts 12–15, 18).
- **English and Fiji languages:** observation reports, explanations, evidence-based arguments, stakeholder viewpoints and procedural reading (concepts 9–11, 14, 19–20).

### Teaching, safety, rights and curriculum safeguards
- The Forestry Act is a legal governance source, not a Fiji Ministry subject syllabus and not a list of official learner achievement indicators. All 20 entries above are PacEdu-derived concepts. Do not relabel them as official CLOs or achievement standards.
- Do not teach current forestry rules, licence requirements, protected-area boundaries, species lists, fire restrictions, penalties, royalty rates or consent procedures without checking the latest regulations, Gazette notices, code of forest practices, relevant land laws and Ministry guidance.
- The Act's recognition of iTaukei customary rights and consent requirements is not a complete statement of customary land law. Respect cultural authority and do not collect, publish or expose confidential traditional knowledge.
- No learner tree felling, logging, chainsaw operation, burning, entry into forest fire zones, collection of protected species, handling of pests/pathogens, or unsupervised fieldwork. Use approved maps, photographs, fictional datasets and classroom models.
- Field activities require a school risk assessment, landowner/community permission where applicable, supervision, safe access and protection of habitats. Do not direct learners to enter protected areas or harvest forest products.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Compare against the approved Fiji NCF and current Ministry indicators; map actual levels and prerequisites; verify any operational regulations and policy; complete rights review and teacher review before creating daily activities.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.
