## Record 148 — Fiji National Disaster Risk Management: concepts extracted from the 2024 parliamentary Bill text; enacted Act text cross-check pending

**Source identity — strict source distinction**
- **Enacted law:** *National Disaster Risk Management Act 2024*, Act No. 14 of 2024. Parliament's 2023–2026 Sitting Statistics identify Bill No. 6 of 2024 as enacted on 3 October 2024 and the Act as commencing on **5 November 2024** under Legal Notice No. 94 of 2024.
- **Official enacted-law listing:** Parliament of Fiji, Acts index: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/acts/ (the page's 2024 list does not currently expose a clickable Act 14 PDF in the sequence; it lists Act 12 then Act 15).
- **Official commencement and enactment evidence:** Parliament, *2023–2026 Parliament Sitting Statistics – May 2026*: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Compiled-Parliament-Sitting-Statistics%E2%80%93May-2026.pdf; Parliament, *3rd Term of Parliament – Acts*: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/1Acts.pdf.
- **Text actually inspected for concepts:** Parliament's official *National Disaster Risk Management Bill 2024*, Bill No. 6 of 2024, amended version (October 2024): https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Amended-Bill-No.-6a-National-Disaster-Risk-Management-Bill-2024-1.pdf. This is a **Bill/draft text**, not the enacted Act. The Bill was tabled 23 May 2024, referred to the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights, committee report tabled 1 October 2024, and passed/enacted 3 October 2024 (Parliament records above).
- **Secondary enacted-text locator:** IFRC Disaster Law Database lists *National Disaster Risk Management Act (Act No. 14 of 2024)* and a PDF download, updated in its repository in July 2026: https://disasterlaw.ifrc.org/disaster-law-database/national-documents. The download endpoint could not be retrieved for line-by-line comparison during this review. Therefore the concepts below are expressly attributed to the **official amended Bill text inspected**, not represented as verified verbatim provisions of the final Act.
- **Bill provisions inspected:** clauses/sections 1–5; 6–16; 17–30; 34–35; 45–59; 61–90; 91–109; 110–125 and schedules 1–9. The official PDF has printed page numbers 1–65; the detailed concept locators below use section numbers and printed pages.
- **Current-version status:** Act 14 of 2024 commenced 5 November 2024. This source record does not establish the current content of every regulation, plan, operational procedure, later amendment or current hazard warning. Before any lesson on live warning arrangements, evacuation centres, emergency contacts, current agency roles, hazard maps, relief eligibility, privacy or access to government risk information, use current NDRMO, Fiji Meteorological and Hydrological Services, Police, Fire, Health, local authority and other responsible-agency material. Do not treat the Bill draft's wording as proof that every clause survived enactment unchanged.
- **Rights:** concept paraphrases only; no substantial legislative text reproduced. No open licence is claimed for the PDF.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGISLATIVE_SOURCE; FIJI_PARLIAMENTARY_BILL_TEXT_INSPECTED; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; ACT_ENACTMENT_AND_COMMENCEMENT_VERIFIED; FINAL_ENACTED_TEXT_CLAUSE_CROSSCHECK_PENDING; OPERATIONAL_GUIDANCE_CURRENT_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (derived from the inspected amended Bill text; not official Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Hazards, disasters and risk** — Source: Bill No. 6 of 2024, cl.2, definitions of “hazard”, “disaster”, “exposure”, “vulnerability” and “capacity” (printed pp.8–11). Concept: a hazard is a process, phenomenon or human activity that may cause harm; a disaster occurs when a hazardous event interacts with exposure, vulnerability and capacity and causes serious disruption and loss. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: cause/effect, environments and community systems. Observable evidence: learner sorts fictional examples into hazard, exposure, vulnerability, capacity and impact, explaining that a hazard does not automatically become a disaster.
2. **Multiple hazards and interconnected risk** — Source: Bill cls.4(j), 7(a), 12 and 61 (printed pp.12–16 and pp.31–32). Concept: risk planning needs to consider more than one hazard and how warning, response and community actions may need coordination. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: weather, earth processes and simple systems. Observable evidence: learner reads a teacher-provided multi-hazard scenario and identifies two hazards and one possible interaction. Use verified local hazard information, not speculation.
3. **Disaster risk reduction and prevention** — Source: Bill cls.2, 4(b)–(d), 5(c), 12–13 (printed pp.8–13 and pp.15–16). Concept: risk can be reduced by preventing new risks, reducing existing risks and managing remaining risks through planned measures, resilient development and climate adaptation. Subject links: Science, Geography, Technology, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: safety, land use and cause/effect. Observable evidence: learner compares fictional community-development choices and identifies which choices reduce exposure or vulnerability.
4. **Preparedness and readiness** — Source: Bill cls.2 and 14–16 (printed pp.9–10 and pp.15–16). Concept: preparedness includes advance warning, precautionary action, planning, awareness, training and readiness to respond. Subject links: Healthy Living, English, Social Science, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: instructions, sequencing and safe decision-making. Observable evidence: learner orders a teacher-approved preparedness sequence and identifies which information should come from an official warning source.
5. **Early warning and early action** — Source: Bill cls.4(j), 7(a)–(b), 12(2)(d), 61–64 (printed pp.12–16 and pp.31–32). Concept: warning systems connect hazard monitoring, impact forecasting, mapping, communication and pre-agreed actions so people can act before impacts worsen. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Computer Studies, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: interpreting symbols, dates, maps and messages. Observable evidence: learner interprets a fictional warning card, identifies its source, affected area and stated action, and distinguishes a warning from a prediction or rumour. Do not invent alert levels or current warning wording.
6. **Forecasts, monitoring and hazard-impact mapping** — Source: Bill cls.61–62 and 82 (printed pp.31–32 and pp.36–37). Concept: hazard monitoring and impact forecasting can combine meteorological, hydrological, earthquake, tsunami, landslide and environmental information with maps and assessments. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: maps, graphs, observation and data sources. Observable evidence: learner reads a teacher-provided map legend and identifies what a mapped hazard layer does and does not show.
7. **Accessible and inclusive disaster information** — Source: Bill cls.5(a), 7(h), 66 and 69(a) (printed pp.12–13 and pp.32–34). Concept: disaster plans should respect rights and include accessibility, protection and the participation of people who may face heightened barriers or risks. Subject links: Social Science, English, Healthy Living, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: inclusion, communication and different access needs. Observable evidence: learner improves a fictional public safety message by adding clear language, readable layout, audio/visual alternatives and an accessible route instruction. Never ask learners to disclose disability, poverty, displacement or other personal circumstances.
8. **Fiji-specific culture, customary land and language** — Source: Bill cl.5(b) (printed p.13). Concept: disaster risk work in Fiji should recognise iTaukei and Rotuman landowners and respect their cultures, customs, traditions and languages. Subject links: Social Science, English, Vosa Vakaviti, Rotuman, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: respectful listening and cultural diversity. Observable evidence: learner identifies why community-approved local language and culturally respectful consultation matter in a fictional planning example. Do not ask learners to reveal land ownership, chiefly status, private custom or restricted traditional knowledge.
9. **Climate adaptation and resilient development** — Source: Bill cls.4(d), 5(c), 69 and 108 (printed pp.12–13, pp.33–34 and pp.43–44). Concept: disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation can be integrated into development, rehabilitation and reconstruction so future risks are not rebuilt into community systems. Subject links: Science, Geography, Technology, Agriculture, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: climate change, infrastructure and sustainable development. Observable evidence: learner compares fictional reconstruction options and explains which one is more resilient to the stated hazard.
10. **Retrofitting and safer infrastructure** — Source: Bill cl.2 definition of “retrofitting” and cls.66, 108 (printed pp.10–11, pp.32–33 and pp.43–44). Concept: existing structures may be reinforced or upgraded to better withstand hazard impacts; safe and accessible location and building suitability matter in evacuation planning. Subject links: Technology, Science, Mathematics, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: materials, structures and measurement. Observable evidence: learner labels a teacher-provided building diagram with general resilience features and identifies why structural assessments must be performed by qualified professionals. No learner structural inspections or testing.
11. **Evacuation-centre suitability and universal access** — Source: Bill cls.65–67 (printed pp.32–33). Concept: evacuation centres require consideration of safe location, structural suitability, capacity, water, sanitation, hygiene, protection, cooking, power and communication; access for people with different needs matters. Subject links: Healthy Living, Science, Mathematics, Technology, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: needs, facilities, hygiene and accessible design. Observable evidence: learner evaluates a fictional centre checklist and identifies missing facilities. The Bill does not provide a school-specific evacuation instruction; use current official plans.
12. **Community and subnational coordination** — Source: Bill cls.45–51 (printed pp.26–29). Concept: disaster planning and coordination operate at divisional, provincial, district, municipal and community levels, with roles for committees and local structures. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: local government, community roles and maps. Observable evidence: learner matches fictional planning tasks to the correct level of coordination without assuming that every local structure has the same current membership.
13. **Whole-of-society and humanitarian partnerships** — Source: Bill cls.4(c), 34–43 and 68 (printed pp.12, pp.23–25 and pp.33–34). Concept: Government, communities, civil society, private organisations and humanitarian actors may contribute different capacities, but coordination, registration and accountability are important. Subject links: Social Science, Business, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: organisations, roles and cooperation. Observable evidence: learner maps a fictional relief partnership and identifies the need to coordinate supplies and avoid duplication. Do not imply that an unregistered group can automatically carry out regulated humanitarian work.
14. **Emergency operations, relief and basic needs** — Source: Bill cls.91–109 (printed pp.38–44). Concept: emergency operations coordinate monitoring, response, public safety, immediate relief, basic needs and early recovery; response arrangements involve designated agencies and operational centres. Subject links: Healthy Living, Social Science, English, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: basic needs, communication and safe procedures. Observable evidence: learner classifies fictional needs into immediate safety, relief and early recovery categories. Do not simulate emergency command, rescue, medical treatment or real incident reporting.
15. **Recovery and “build back better”** — Source: Bill cl.2 definitions of “recovery” and “build back better”, and cls.107–109 (printed pp.9–11 and pp.43–44). Concept: recovery includes restoring or improving health, livelihoods, infrastructure, social and cultural systems and the environment while reducing future risk. Subject links: Science, Geography, Social Science, Business, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: community needs, systems and sustainable development. Observable evidence: learner compares two fictional recovery plans and identifies how one reduces future risk rather than simply replacing damaged assets.
16. **Risk information systems, geospatial data and privacy** — Source: Bill cls.81–90 (printed pp.36–38). Concept: a central risk information system may combine hazard, damage, exposure and vulnerability information with geospatial and ICT tools to support decisions and accountability; access is controlled and unique identifiers require security. Subject links: Mathematics, Computer Studies, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: data classification, maps, digital safety and privacy. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes public hazard-map information from restricted personal records and identifies why access credentials must be protected. Never use real disaster-affected persons' identifiable data in classroom exercises.
17. **Disaster risk financing and public accountability** — Source: Bill cls.52–60 (printed pp.29–31). Concept: public budgets and a dedicated fund can support prevention, preparedness, response, recovery, training and risk-reduction activities; accounting, audit and annual reporting support accountability. Subject links: Mathematics, Business/Commercial Studies, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: budgets, income, expenditure and records. Observable evidence: learner allocates a fictional classroom budget across preparedness, response and recovery and explains why spending records are needed. Do not present fictional figures as Fiji government allocations.
18. **International assistance and logistics** — Source: Bill cls.31–33 and 110–121 (printed pp.22–23 and pp.45–49). Concept: international assistance requires coordination of personnel, goods, equipment, transport, customs, communications and agreed procedures; local priorities and responsible agencies remain important. Subject links: Geography, Business, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: supply chains, transport and cooperation. Observable evidence: learner maps a fictional relief-supply route and identifies two coordination checks. Do not teach real border exemptions, immigration procedures or import permissions from the draft.
19. **Training, drills and after-action learning** — Source: Bill cls.14–16, 19, 28(j) and 109 (printed pp.15–17, pp.20–21 and pp.43–44). Concept: awareness, approved training, simulations and reviews can help organisations learn from exercises and real events. Subject links: English, Mathematics, Healthy Living, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: reflection, sequencing and observation. Observable evidence: learner completes a fictional exercise review identifying what worked, what needs improvement and what evidence supports the conclusion. Any real school drill must follow the school's current official plan and must not be improvised from this curriculum record.
20. **Rights, dignity and protection during disasters** — Source: Bill cls.2, 5(a), 7(h), 68–69 and 103–108 (printed pp.8–13, pp.33–34 and pp.41–44). Concept: people affected by disasters may experience direct and indirect impacts; disaster plans and relief should respect rights, inclusion, protection, dignity and access to basic support. Subject links: Social Science, English, Healthy Living. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: empathy, rights and respectful communication. Observable evidence: learner identifies respectful and non-stigmatising language in fictional relief messages. Avoid trauma simulations, personal disclosure or asking learners to recount real disaster experiences.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Science and Geography:** hazards, exposure, vulnerability, climate adaptation, forecasting, hazard mapping, resilient environments (concepts 1–6, 9–10).
- **Mathematics:** rainfall/river-level datasets from approved sources, map scales, fictional impact tables, capacity calculations and budget allocation (concepts 5–6, 11, 16–17).
- **Computer Studies:** geospatial systems, data provenance, access control, privacy and secure identifiers (concept 16).
- **Healthy Living:** preparedness information, evacuation-centre facilities, hygiene and safe communication (concepts 4, 7, 11, 14).
- **Social Science/Civics:** governance, customary and cultural respect, community roles, rights, inclusion and humanitarian coordination (concepts 7–8, 12–15, 20).
- **Technology:** safer infrastructure, retrofitting concepts and accessible communication systems (concepts 5, 10–11).
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** supply chains, public budgeting, resource coordination and recovery livelihoods (concepts 13, 15, 17–18).
- **English and Fiji languages:** interpreting official notices, explaining evidence, accessible public information and post-exercise reflection (concepts 4–5, 7–8, 16, 19–20).

### Teaching, safety and legal safeguards
- This is a source-derived concept bank, not a disaster-response manual and not a set of official Fiji Ministry achievement indicators.
- **Draft-to-Act caution is mandatory:** the inspected detailed text is the amended Bill, not the final enacted Act. Before promoting any clause as a current legal requirement, compare it against the final Act No. 14 of 2024 and current regulations. The IFRC database confirms a separately catalogued Act text, but line-by-line comparison was not completed in this pass.
- Use current Fiji Meteorological and Hydrological Services and NDRMO warnings and plans for any real-time hazard information. Do not create invented alert levels, evacuation orders, shelter addresses or emergency contacts.
- No learner-led evacuation, rescue, first aid, fire, floodwater, landslide, coastal surge, damaged-building, electrical or hazardous-material exercises. No entering hazard areas or approaching real incidents to collect data.
- Keep disaster learning non-traumatising: use fictional scenarios, maps and anonymised datasets; never require learners to disclose displacement, loss, disability, poverty, land status, family circumstances or trauma.
- Accessible communication is required in lesson design: plain language, clear visual layout, spoken alternatives and teacher-verified accessible formats; do not assume one format meets every learner's needs.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Final enacted Act comparison, current operational guidance, approved Fiji curriculum mapping, level/prerequisite mapping, rights review and teacher review remain required.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 149 — Meteorological and Hydrological Services Act 2024 (Act No. 2 of 2024): observations, forecasting, climate information and public warning systems

**Source identity and legal status**
- **Exact title:** *Meteorological and Hydrological Services Act 2024*, Act No. 2 of 2024.
- **Issuing body:** Parliament of the Republic of Fiji.
- **Assent/enactment:** 23 May 2024.
- **Official enacted Act:** Parliament of Fiji, Act No. 2 of 2024: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Act-2-Meteorological-and-Hydrological-Services-Act-2024.pdf
- **Commencement:** The Parliament Acts register updated September 2024 states that the Act came into force on **28 June 2024**, except section 4(a), which came into force on **1 August 2024**. The Act itself delegates commencement to Gazette notice; this commencement detail is taken from Parliament's official Acts register, not inferred from assent date. Source: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/1Acts.pdf
- **Official current service source:** Fiji Meteorological and Hydrological Services website: https://www.met.gov.fj/ . Current public products include weather bulletins, warnings, rainfall observations, climate summaries, climate outlooks, marine information and hydrological services. The site is operational information, not a curriculum document.
- **Inspected Act provisions:** ss.1–3 (preliminary, definitions and objectives); ss.4–6 (Service, functions and Director's powers); ss.7–12 (warning authorisation, funding, technical audit, liability, regulations and consequential amendment).
- **Exact section/page locators:** s.1, printed p.7; s.2 definitions, printed pp.7–8; s.3, printed p.8; ss.4–5, printed pp.8–9; s.6, printed p.10; ss.7–9, printed p.10; ss.10–12, printed p.11. Official Parliament PDF pages and section numbers were inspected.
- **Current-version status:** This record is based on the enacted Act. Parliament's Acts register records commencement as above. No later amendment to this Act was identified in the Parliament Acts index during this review, but the latest Gazette and regulations should still be checked before teaching legal duties, offences, penalties, authorisation or commercial fees. Current operational warning products and technical methods may change; use the latest Fiji Met product guides and bulletins.
- **Rights:** paraphrased concepts only; no substantial statutory text reproduced. No open licence is claimed for the Act PDF or Fiji Met products. Use public data with source/date attribution and respect any product-specific terms.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE; ENACTED_ACT_INSPECTED; COMMENCEMENT_VERIFIED_FROM_PARLIAMENT_REGISTER; FIJI_MET_OFFICIAL_OPERATIONAL_SOURCE_IDENTIFIED; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; CURRENT_PRODUCT_GUIDE_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Weather and atmospheric conditions** — Source: Act s.2, definition of “meteorological services” (printed pp.7–8). Concept: meteorological services include forecasts and nowcasts for short, medium and long time periods, marine forecasts, weather information, bulletins and analysis of weather patterns. Subject links: Elementary/Basic Science, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: observations of sky, wind, cloud and rain. Observable evidence: learner describes a day's observed weather using agreed vocabulary and distinguishes an observation from a forecast.
2. **Weather versus climate and climate trends** — Source: Act s.2, meteorological-services definition, and s.5(1)(h) (printed pp.7–9). Concept: day-to-day weather information and analysis of long-term climate trends are related but different kinds of information; climate trend analysis uses records over time. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: time, averages, tables and graphs. Observable evidence: learner sorts examples into weather observation, weather forecast and long-term climate information, explaining the time-scale difference.
3. **Hydrology and the water system** — Source: Act s.2, definition of “hydrological services” (printed p.7). Concept: hydrological services involve collecting, analysing, storing and modelling water-related data and forecasting water availability, flooding and drought. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: water cycle, catchments and measurement. Observable evidence: learner labels a simple catchment diagram and identifies where rainfall, river flow and water availability information may be relevant.
4. **Systematic observation and measurement** — Source: Act s.5(1)(a)–(b) (printed p.9). Concept: reliable services depend on systematic collection, recording, management and analysis of observations, supported by maintained observation networks, infrastructure and equipment. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Technology, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: units, careful observation and record keeping. Observable evidence: learner records a teacher-provided rainfall or temperature dataset with date, unit, location and source, and checks for missing entries.
5. **Weather and hydrological instruments and networks** — Source: Act s.5(1)(b) and s.6(a) (printed pp.9–10). Concept: observation networks use equipment and infrastructure to gather meteorological and hydrological information; instruments need maintenance and renewal to support dependable records. Subject links: Science, Technology, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: measurement tools and instrument purpose. Observable evidence: learner matches safe images of a rain gauge, thermometer, wind instrument and river-level gauge to the quantity each measures. Do not require learners to install or access operational equipment.
6. **Forecasting and nowcasting** — Source: Act s.2 and s.5(1)(c) (printed pp.7–9). Concept: forecasts describe expected future weather or ocean conditions; nowcasts focus on very near-term conditions; forecast time horizons affect how information is used. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: time sequence, observations and probability language. Observable evidence: learner identifies the forecast period and location in a fictional forecast and distinguishes it from a recorded observation.
7. **Ocean and marine weather conditions** — Source: Act s.5(1)(c) and s.2(a) (printed pp.7–9). Concept: official meteorological services include forecasts of ocean conditions and marine weather, important to maritime activities and coastal communities. Subject links: Science, Geography, Technology, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: wind, waves, tides and maps. Observable evidence: learner interprets a teacher-approved marine bulletin's stated area, issue time and described conditions. Do not use a classroom exercise to authorise boating or sea travel.
8. **Rainfall, river flow, flood and drought information** — Source: Act s.2 hydrological-services definition and s.5(1)(e) (printed pp.7–9). Concept: rainfall and hydrological records can inform understanding of water availability, flooding and drought; these are connected but distinct phenomena. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: water cycle, rainfall measurement and graphs. Observable evidence: learner compares a fictional rainfall table with a river-level series and explains why one measure alone may not describe the full catchment condition.
9. **Hazard warnings and public safety information** — Source: Act s.5(1)(e) (printed p.9). Concept: the Service's functions include warnings for gales, storms and weather conditions that may endanger life or property, including conditions associated with floods, forest fires, droughts and storm surges. Subject links: Science, Geography, Healthy Living, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: hazard vocabulary, source checking and safe response instructions. Observable evidence: learner identifies the issuing agency, issue time, affected area, hazard and stated advice in a current or teacher-selected official warning. Always follow current official instructions; a classroom task never replaces an alert.
10. **Impact-based forecasting and exposure** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “impact-based forecast” and s.3(c), s.5(1)(d) (printed pp.7–9). Concept: impact-based forecasts connect a meteorological or hydrological hazard with the people, places or assets exposed; they support Fiji's multiple-hazard early warning system. The Act's definition expressly distinguishes exposure from vulnerability and risk, so do not collapse those terms into one. Subject links: Science, Geography, Mathematics, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: hazard, map, population/place and basic data concepts. Observable evidence: learner uses a fictional map to identify a hazard and exposed location, while separately identifying vulnerability as another consideration.
11. **Communication and dissemination of information** — Source: Act s.5(1)(f)–(g), (m)–(n) (printed pp.9–10). Concept: meteorological and hydrological information is gathered, published and transmitted through communication arrangements; clear, timely and traceable communication supports public use of information. Subject links: English, Computer Studies, Science, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: reading notices, identifying sources and digital communication. Observable evidence: learner prepares a short, source-attributed summary of a teacher-provided bulletin without changing its meaning or inventing advice.
12. **Long-term climate records and climate summaries** — Source: Act s.5(1)(h) (printed p.9); supplementary official service examples: Fiji Met Climate Data and Climate Summaries, https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/climate-data/ and https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/fiji-climate-summaries/. Concept: long-term records allow analysis of rainfall, temperature, wind, sea-surface conditions and other climate patterns; monthly summaries describe observed conditions for a defined period. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Geography, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: data tables, averages, range and graphs. Observable evidence: learner extracts a stated result from a dated Fiji Met climate summary and distinguishes the source's finding from their own explanation.
13. **Research, investigation and evidence quality** — Source: Act s.5(1)(j) and s.9 (printed pp.9–10). Concept: meteorology and hydrology advance through research and investigation; technical audits are required at least once every two years to support maintenance of international standards. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: fair testing, evidence and quality checks. Observable evidence: learner identifies the date, source, units and limitations of a supplied weather dataset and explains why quality checks matter. Do not treat a classroom exercise as a formal technical audit.
14. **International cooperation and shared scientific standards** — Source: Act s.2 (World Meteorological Organization definition) and s.5(1)(l), (p) (printed pp.8–10). Concept: Fiji's service collaborates with other national services and contributes to international meteorological and hydrological cooperation; shared standards and data exchange support regional forecasting and safety. Subject links: Geography, Science, Social Science, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: maps, countries, communication networks and shared measurements. Observable evidence: learner explains why weather systems and ocean conditions crossing national boundaries require regional information sharing.
15. **Aviation weather and specialised forecasts** — Source: Act s.5(1)(i) (printed p.9). Concept: meteorological information supports the safety, regularity and efficiency of air navigation in Fiji's flight information region and selected Southwest Pacific aerodromes. Subject links: Science, Geography, Technology, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: wind, visibility, clouds and transport systems. Observable evidence: learner identifies, from a teacher-approved example, why pilots and airports need specialised weather information. No learner should use the material for operational flight decisions.
16. **Authorised warnings, verification and responsible sharing** — Source: Act s.6(e) and s.7 (printed p.10). Concept: the Director has statutory authority concerning issuance or cancellation of weather warnings and alerts, including flood alerts; the Act distinguishes unauthorised issue from subsequent media or telecommunications sharing of an authorised warning. Subject links: English, Computer Studies, Social Science/Civics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: misinformation, source verification and responsible communication. Observable evidence: learner checks that a warning is from the official Fiji Met source before sharing it and preserves its original issue time and wording. Do not teach or reproduce offence penalties.
17. **Public, private and commercial service provision** — Source: Act s.3(b), s.5(1)(o) and s.5(2) (printed pp.8–10). Concept: the Act supports public-private engagement and allows the Service to provide commercial meteorological and hydrological services for remuneration; complementary services must be understood in relation to the Service's public functions. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, Social Science, English, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: public services, businesses, costs and customer needs. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes a public safety warning from a fictional paid specialist data service. Do not infer actual fees or private-provider authority from this concept.
18. **Public service funding and accountability** — Source: Act s.8 and s.9 (printed p.10). Concept: Service funding can include parliamentary appropriations, prescribed fees and commercial-service income; technical audits provide an additional accountability and standards mechanism. Subject links: Mathematics, Business, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: budgets, revenue and accountability. Observable evidence: learner classifies fictional service income sources and explains why public technical services require transparent quality assurance. Do not present fictional figures as actual Fiji budget allocations.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Elementary/Basic Science:** atmosphere, weather observations, water systems, rainfall, wind, ocean conditions and climate patterns (concepts 1–9, 12–15).
- **Mathematics:** measurement units, tables, rainfall totals, averages, time-series graphs, river-level comparisons and data quality (concepts 2–8, 12–13, 18).
- **Geography:** Fiji's islands and regions, catchments, marine areas, exposure, regional weather systems and climate patterns (concepts 3, 7–10, 12, 14).
- **Agriculture:** rainfall, water availability, drought information and climate outlook interpretation using official sources (concepts 3, 8, 12).
- **Computer Studies:** data recording, source verification, communication, digital bulletin interpretation and responsible sharing (concepts 4, 11, 12, 16).
- **Healthy Living:** recognising official hazard warnings and following current adult/authority instructions (concepts 9, 16).
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** public service, specialist data services, service funding and accountability (concepts 17–18).
- **English and Fiji languages:** weather descriptions, forecast interpretation, clear bulletin summaries, vocabulary and source-attributed reporting (concepts 1, 6, 9, 11, 16).

### Supplementary official operational sources for future lesson examples
These are changing service products, not fixed curriculum indicators:
- Fiji Met alerts and warnings: https://www.met.gov.fj/warnings/
- Fiji Met public weather bulletins: https://www.met.gov.fj/fiji-weather/public/
- Fiji Met product guides: https://www.met.gov.fj/about-fiji-met/product-guides/
- Fiji Met climate data: https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/climate-data/
- Fiji Met climate summaries: https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/fiji-climate-summaries/
- Fiji Met climate outlooks: https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/climate-outlooks/
- Fiji Met early action rainfall watch: https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/early-action-rainfall-watch/
- Fiji Met climate data products: https://www.met.gov.fj/climate-services/climate-data-products/
Use the current issue date and original source with every dataset; distinguish observations, forecasts, outlooks, warnings and summaries. Do not reuse an old warning as a current alert.

### Teaching, safety and curriculum safeguards
- The Act provides a legal framework for the Service; it is not a Fiji Ministry syllabus and does not contain student achievement indicators. All 18 entries are PacEdu-derived concepts.
- Do not teach unauthorised warning issuance, offence provisions, penalties, fees, Director powers or operational legal duties as learner instructions. Use official Fiji Met warning products and guides for current public information.
- Never ask learners to make their own weather warnings, cancel alerts, predict cyclone landfall, or issue advice for real travel, fishing, aviation or evacuation decisions.
- Do not send learners to rivers, floodwater, coastlines, reefs, exposed weather stations, airports, towers or other hazardous sites to collect observations. Use classroom instruments in safe locations, approved public datasets, maps, photographs and simulations.
- Weather and climate data need provenance: location, date/time, units, instrument/source, missing data and whether values are preliminary or quality-controlled. Do not compare unlike stations or periods without explaining limitations.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Map each concept to approved Fiji NCF and current Ministry indicators, identify year-level scope and prerequisites, verify current Fiji Met product guides, complete rights review and teacher review before daily worksheets.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 150 — Aquaculture Act 2024 (Act No. 20 of 2024): aquatic farming systems, sustainability, biosecurity, environmental assessment and aquaculture value chains

**Source identity and legal-status caution**
- **Exact title:** *Aquaculture Act 2024*, Act No. 20 of 2024.
- **Issuing body:** Parliament of the Republic of Fiji.
- **Enacted/assented:** 5 December 2024 parliamentary enactment; presidential assent dated 6 December 2024.
- **Primary official enacted text:** Parliament of Fiji, Act No. 20 of 2024, 71-page PDF: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Act-20-Aquaculture-Act-2024.pdf
- **Office of the Attorney-General hosted text:** https://www.laws.gov.fj/LawsAsMade/GetFile/1718
- **Parliament Acts register:** https://www.parliament.gov.fj/acts/ (lists Act No. 20 of 2024).
- **Commencement clause:** s.1(2) says the Act comes into force on a date or dates appointed by the Minister by notice in the Gazette. The December 2024 Parliament sitting statistics also list commencement as a future Gazette-appointed date. **No specific commencement Gazette notice or effective date was verified in this review.** Accordingly, do not state that the Act is in force, do not describe its licence or offence provisions as currently operative, and do not use it as current legal advice. This is an enacted statute with commencement unverified, not a draft Bill.
- **Government policy context:** Fiji Government, “Aquaculture Act 2024 for Economic, Environmental, and Social Future”, 6 December 2024: https://www.fiji.gov.fj/aquaculture-act-2024-for-economic-environmental-and-social-future/ . This reports the Government's policy rationale: sustainable and biosecure aquaculture, designated areas, environmental protection, industry development, livelihoods and food security. It is contextual government communication, not proof of commencement.
- **Current operational context:** Fiji Government, “Milestones in Aquaculture: Legislative Progress and Pearl Farming Initiatives in Fiji”, 18 December 2024: https://www.fiji.gov.fj/milestones-in-aquaculture-legislative-progress-and-pearl-farming-initiatives-in-fiji/ . The Ministry reported regulations were still being developed at that time. This is historical status only; recheck current regulations and Gazette notices.
- **Inspected provisions in the enacted Act:** ss.1–5 (preliminary, definitions, objectives, application, principles); ss.6–8 (administration); ss.9–26 (Advisory, Licensing and Scientific Committees); ss.27–29 (area designation and management plans); ss.30–39 (licensing and other legal compliance); ss.40–43 (restricted products, genetically modified organisms, live-organism import and registration); ss.44–49 (monitoring and enforcement); ss.50–68 (evidence, liability, fixed penalties, confidentiality and offences); ss.69–70 (consequential and transitional provisions).
- **Exact section/page locators:** s.2 definitions, printed pp.237–242; ss.3–5, pp.242–243; ss.6–8, pp.243–244; ss.9–26, pp.244–248; ss.27–29, pp.248–249; ss.30–39, pp.249–252; ss.40–43, pp.252–253; ss.44–49, pp.253–255; ss.50–68, pp.255–260; ss.69–70 and Schedule, pp.260–263. Section numbers are controlling locators.
- **Current-version and implementation status:** The enacted text was inspected, but this review did not verify a commencement notice, commencement date, complete subsidiary regulations, operational licensing forms/fees, current approved species lists, designated aquaculture areas, prohibited areas, or current administrative arrangements. Parliament's public Gazette page is not a complete searchable Gazette archive. Obtain the relevant Gazette notice and current Fisheries/Biosecurity/Environment directions before any practical or legal aquaculture project. Do not assume a Bill, Act assent, Government announcement or a current-looking portal listing proves commencement.
- **Rights:** concepts are paraphrased; no substantial statutory text copied. No open licence is claimed for the Act PDF, government articles or operational materials.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_LEGAL_SOURCE; ENACTED_ACT_TEXT_INSPECTED; COMMENCEMENT_NOT_VERIFIED; PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; NOT_OFFICIAL_CURRICULUM_INDICATORS; CURRENT_REGULATIONS_AND_OPERATIONAL_STATUS_CHECK_REQUIRED; TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

### Extracted concepts (PacEdu-derived; not Ministry achievement indicators)

1. **Aquaculture and aquatic farming** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “aquaculture” (printed p.237). Concept: aquaculture is the cultivation, propagation or farming of aquatic organisms from eggs, spawn, spat or seed, including the rearing of organisms lawfully sourced from the wild or imported, for trade, business or research. Subject links: Elementary/Basic Science, Agriculture, Technology, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: living things, life cycles and farming. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes aquatic farming from capture fishing using safe, fictional examples. Do not infer that every household fish tank or subsistence activity falls within the Act's scope.
2. **Freshwater, brackish-water and marine environments** — Source: Act s.2 definitions of “fresh water” and “aquaculture”; ss.1 and 4 (printed pp.237, 240 and 242). Concept: aquatic farming may occur in freshwater, brackish water or marine environments, each with different salinity, organisms and environmental conditions. Subject links: Science, Geography, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: water cycle, habitats and basic salinity concepts. Observable evidence: learner classifies teacher-provided pond, estuary and coastal-farm diagrams by water type and explains one environmental difference.
3. **Aquatic biodiversity and organism life stages** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “aquatic organism” (printed pp.237–238). Concept: aquatic organisms include aquatic plants and animals, not only finfish; the definition names molluscs, crustaceans, coral, sponges, sea cucumbers, echinoderms, turtles and marine mammals, as well as eggs, spawn, spat and juvenile stages. Subject links: Science, Geography, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: classification, habitats and life cycles. Observable evidence: learner groups illustrated aquatic organisms and orders a supplied life-cycle sequence. Do not handle live or protected organisms.
4. **Aquaculture production systems and facilities** — Source: Act s.2 definitions of “aquaculture premises”, “aquaculture equipment/gear” and “vessel” (printed pp.237–238 and p.242). Concept: aquaculture uses a facility or area, enclosures and equipment; systems can include cages, nets, ropes, floats, tanks or other infrastructure. Subject links: Science, Technology, Mathematics, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: structures, materials and systems. Observable evidence: learner labels a fictional land-based tank or floating-cage diagram and identifies inputs, growing area and outputs. No construction or installation of operational aquatic equipment by learners.
5. **Aquaculture inputs, feed and equipment** — Source: Act s.2 definitions of “aquaculture equipment/gear” and “aquaculture industry” (printed pp.237–238); s.5(f) (printed p.243). Concept: aquaculture production depends on suitable equipment, feed, materials and techniques; selection should consider environmental safety, selectivity and cost effectiveness. Subject links: Science, Technology, Agriculture, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: needs of living organisms, materials and safe tool use. Observable evidence: learner categorises safe images of equipment and identifies the function of feed, enclosure and water-management equipment. Do not handle chemicals, powered equipment, hooks or live stock.
6. **Water quality and environmental conditions** — Source: Act ss.5(d)–(g) and 29(2)(a), (f) (printed pp.243 and 248–249). Concept: aquaculture planning must consider environmental factors and impacts, land characteristics, soil, topography, land use, pollution and biodiversity. Water quality parameters such as temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, salinity, turbidity and nutrients are relevant scientific teaching extensions, but those individual parameters are **not listed as an express checklist in these provisions** and need a separate technical source before teaching measurement ranges or target values. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: measurement, water properties and ecosystems. Observable evidence: learner reads a fictional water-quality data card and identifies why multiple measurements and site context matter. No learner sampling of unsafe or unknown water.
7. **Aquaculture and ecosystem impacts** — Source: Act s.5(d)–(g) and s.29(2)(f) (printed pp.243 and 248–249). Concept: aquaculture development must consider effects on fisheries resources, biodiversity, significant habitats, pollution and waste; environmental impacts and risks need assessment and mitigation. Subject links: Science, Geography, Climate Education, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: ecosystems, cause/effect and pollution. Observable evidence: learner compares fictional farm designs and identifies possible waste pathways and habitat impacts.
8. **Precautionary approach and scientific evidence** — Source: Act s.5(b)–(c) and s.22 (printed pp.243 and 247–248). Concept: decisions should use the best available scientific evidence; where evidence is missing and serious or irreversible environmental harm is threatened, a precautionary approach is relevant. Scientific advice is part of the governance structure. Subject links: Science, Mathematics, English, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: evidence, uncertainty and decision-making. Observable evidence: learner distinguishes a measured result, an assumption and an unanswered question in a fictional aquaculture proposal.
9. **Waste minimisation and pollution prevention** — Source: Act s.5(e) (printed p.243). Concept: aquaculture management should minimise waste and pollution from premises and reduce impacts on fisheries resources, particularly endangered species. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Technology, Healthy Living. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: waste categories, pollution and resource conservation. Observable evidence: learner traces a fictional waste pathway and proposes safe prevention or containment measures. No handling of farm chemicals, untreated effluent, dead stock or contaminated materials.
10. **Sustainable use and intergenerational needs** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “sustainable use” (printed pp.241–242) and s.5 (printed p.243). Concept: sustainable use balances social, economic and cultural wellbeing with the capacity of aquatic resources to meet foreseeable future needs and with avoiding, remedying or mitigating environmental harm. Subject links: Science, Social Science, Business, Geography. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: resources, needs, trade-offs and future generations. Observable evidence: learner evaluates a fictional aquaculture option using ecological, social and economic criteria.
11. **Aquaculture site selection and land characteristics** — Source: Act ss.27–29, particularly s.29(2)(a)–(b) (printed pp.248–249). Concept: site planning considers land tenure, soil, topography, land-use patterns and which types of aquaculture are suitable for the area. Subject links: Geography, Science, Agriculture, Mathematics. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: maps, landforms, soil and land use. Observable evidence: learner compares fictional site profiles using a teacher-provided suitability matrix. Do not ask learners to disclose family or customary land interests or to select real land for development.
12. **Aquaculture development and management planning** — Source: Act s.29 (printed pp.248–249). Concept: a management plan sets objectives, identifies suitable activities, establishes management measures, considers environmental risks and mitigation, and protects the interests of artisanal, subsistence and small-scale fishers. Subject links: Social Science, Science, Business, English. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: planning, stakeholder perspectives and cause/effect. Observable evidence: learner creates a simple fictional plan with objective, site description, potential impacts, mitigation and affected stakeholder groups.
13. **Aquaculture areas and competing uses** — Source: Act ss.27–28 (printed p.248). Concept: designated aquaculture areas and areas where aquaculture is prohibited are governance tools; decisions should consider scientific, legal, social, economic and environmental factors. Subject links: Geography, Social Science, Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: maps, land/water use and public decision-making. Observable evidence: learner interprets a fictional map showing different water/land uses and explains why boundaries and consultation matter. No actual area should be labelled designated or prohibited without a current Gazette source.
14. **Biosecurity and movement of live aquatic organisms** — Source: Act ss.2 and 40–42 (printed pp.237–242 and pp.252–253). Concept: movement of live aquatic organisms, especially exotic or restricted organisms, creates risks that require identification, controls and traceability; introduction or release into natural waters is a serious biosecurity concern. Subject links: Science, Agriculture, Geography, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: native/exotic species, ecosystems and disease transmission. Observable evidence: learner explains, using a fictional case, why a new species should not be released into a river, lake or sea without expert assessment and official authorisation. Do not import, transport, release or culture organisms for class activities.
15. **Genetically modified aquatic organisms and responsible science** — Source: Act s.2 definition of “genetically modified aquatic organism” and s.41 (printed pp.240 and 252). Concept: genetic modification changes an organism's genetic material; its use in aquaculture raises scientific, environmental, ethical and governance questions and is subject to a separate authorisation provision in the Act. Subject links: Science, English, Social Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: heredity, genes and evidence-based discussion. Observable evidence: learner defines genetic modification at an age-appropriate level and separates scientific claims from ethical opinions. Do not use live GM organisms or present unsupported risk claims.
16. **Aquaculture value chains and related industries** — Source: Act s.2 definitions of “aquaculture industry”, “aquaculture product” and “related activities” (printed pp.237–241). Concept: aquaculture is connected to hatcheries/production, feed and equipment suppliers, processing, storage, transport, sale, export, consultancy and other support services. Subject links: Business/Commercial Studies, Mathematics, Technology, Agriculture. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: production, services, transport and markets. Observable evidence: learner maps a fictional product from seed/juvenile stock through growing, processing, storage and sale.
17. **Product handling, storage, processing and traceability** — Source: Act s.2 definitions of “carry”, “document”, “related activities” and “trade” (printed pp.238–242); ss.43 and 51–53 (printed pp.252–256). Concept: aquaculture products and related activities involve handling, storage, processing, transport and records; documents can include electronic records and logbooks. Subject links: Science, Business, Mathematics, Computer Studies. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: food chains, data recording and safe handling principles. Observable evidence: learner completes a fictional traceability record with product batch, date, source and destination. Food safety temperatures and handling limits must come from current food-safety guidance, not this Act.
18. **Aquaculture research, education and training** — Source: Act s.8(1)(d)–(e) and s.22 (printed pp.243–244 and p.247). Concept: research, training, education and scientific advice support aquaculture development, management and assessment. Subject links: Science, English, Mathematics, Technology. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: inquiry, question formation and observation. Observable evidence: learner proposes a safe research question and identifies what evidence would be needed, without conducting live organism trials.
19. **Stakeholders, participation and customary land interests** — Source: Act ss.9–11, 23 and 27 (printed pp.244–248). Concept: aquaculture governance includes public institutions, land-owning units, industry representatives, NGOs, environmental and biosecurity expertise and other stakeholders; participation and representation are part of decision-making. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English, Geography, Business. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: roles, representation, consultation and respectful dialogue. Observable evidence: learner maps fictional stakeholder roles and identifies why land tenure and community participation must be considered. Do not solicit private land details or claim the Act resolves all customary land questions.
20. **Scientific, licensing and advisory governance** — Source: Act ss.9–26 (printed pp.244–248). Concept: the Act establishes advisory, licensing and scientific committees with different functions; this illustrates how policy advice, licence consideration and scientific assessment can be separated within a governance system. Subject links: Social Science/Civics, English, Science. Level: LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Prerequisite: public institutions, roles and evidence. Observable evidence: learner matches fictional policy, scientific and licensing questions to the relevant type of committee. Do not present current membership or administrative operation as verified without current official information.

### Subject-use map (planning suggestions only)
- **Elementary/Basic Science:** aquatic organisms, life cycles, freshwater/brackish/marine habitats, water conditions, biodiversity, waste and biosecurity (concepts 1–10, 14–15).
- **Agriculture:** aquatic farming systems, production inputs, site suitability, sustainable production and value chains (concepts 1–7, 11–12, 16–18).
- **Geography:** water environments, site mapping, land/water use and aquaculture areas (concepts 2, 11–13, 19).
- **Mathematics:** fictional growth/production datasets, feed quantities, water-quality tables, production costs and traceability records; use technical reference ranges only from a separately verified source (concepts 4–6, 16–17).
- **Technology/Computer Studies:** farm-system diagrams, equipment purposes, record keeping and traceability (concepts 4–5, 16–17).
- **Business/Commercial Studies:** production-to-market value chains, service providers, processing, storage and trade (concepts 5, 16–17).
- **Social Science/Civics:** stakeholder representation, land-use decisions, public planning and governance (concepts 11–13, 19–20).
- **English and Fiji languages:** scientific explanations, evidence summaries, fictional management plans, stakeholder viewpoints and traceability descriptions (concepts 8, 10, 12, 17–20).

### Teaching, safety, legal and curriculum safeguards
- The Act is enacted, but its **commencement has not been verified** in this source review. Teach the scientific and production concepts as PacEdu-derived subject content, not as operative legal duties. Do not say aquaculture licences, prohibited-area declarations, import controls, penalties or enforcement powers are currently in force until the relevant Gazette commencement notice and current regulations are confirmed.
- The Act is not a Fiji Ministry syllabus and contains no official student achievement indicators. All 20 entries above are PacEdu-derived concepts, not official CLOs or achievement standards.
- Aquaculture-specific technical claims require separate sources: safe water-quality ranges, species-specific stocking density, feed formulation, growth rates, disease signs, treatment, hatchery practice, food safety and harvest standards must not be invented or derived from the legal text alone.
- No learner importation, release, breeding, culture, capture, feeding or handling of live aquatic organisms; no use of exotic, restricted, protected or genetically modified organisms; no live coral handling; no chemicals, veterinary medicines, untreated effluent, unsafe water, hooks, nets or powered equipment.
- Use fictional case studies, safe photographs, diagrams and anonymised datasets. Do not direct learners to ponds, rivers, estuaries, reefs, cages, hatcheries or farms without a formal school risk assessment, landowner/community permission where relevant, safe access and competent supervision.
- Protect customary and community knowledge. Do not collect learners' family land tenure, customary rights, private business information or sensitive community disputes.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. First verify Act commencement and current regulations, obtain current Fiji Ministry technical aquaculture materials, map each concept to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry indicators, set year levels and prerequisites, complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 151 — Fiji water resources, water services, rural WASH and sanitation concepts

**Record status:** SOURCE-EXTRACTED; PACEDU-DERIVED CONCEPTS ONLY; NOT OFFICIAL STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT INDICATORS  
**Subject coverage:** Elementary Science; Basic Science; Social Science; Healthy Living; Agriculture; Technology; Mathematics; English; Computer Studies  
**Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending mapping to approved Fiji NCF and Ministry year-level indicators  
**CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT

### Source A — Water Authority of Fiji Promulgation 2007 (Promulgation No. 25 of 2007)

- **Issuer/source:** Government of Fiji; Extraordinary Government Gazette, Vol. 7, No. 62, 22 August 2007.
- **Official PDF:** https://www.health.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/WAF-Promulgation-2007.pdf
- **Inspected provisions:** ss.1–3; ss.5–8; ss.24–28; ss.30–35; s.42; ss.43–44.
- **Exact source locations:** printed pp.1581–1583 (preliminary, definitions and functions); pp.1589–1590 (service operations and water quality); pp.1591–1593 (supply, finance, regulation and transitional provisions).
- **Amendment/version caution:** FAOLEX identifies amendments in 2013, 2014 and 2022. The 2022 Water Authority of Fiji (Budget Amendment) Act No.46 of 2022 expressly amends a principal law described as the Water Authority of Fiji Act 2007 and adds liquid trade waste and infringement-notice provisions. This review did not obtain a current consolidated principal text or verify every amendment and commencement notice. Treat the 2007 Gazette text as a historical primary legal source, not a complete current consolidation.
- **Commencement caution:** section 1(2) requires a ministerial Gazette notice. WAF's official history says the Authority took over operations on 1 January 2010, but that institutional history is not a substitute for the original commencement notice. Do not state a precise legal commencement date without the notice.
- **Source classification:** FIJI_LEGAL_SOURCE_CONCEPT; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source A**
1. **Water supply as a managed system** — harvesting, treatment, reticulation and delivery are linked stages; source s.7(a), printed p.1583. Evidence: learner orders a supplied diagram of a water-supply pathway and explains each stage.
2. **Water treatment and quality standards** — treatment and water-quality standards are distinct but connected; source ss.7(b), 28, printed pp.1583, 1589–1590. Evidence: learner distinguishes a treatment step from a quality check using a safe, teacher-provided diagram.
3. **Wastewater collection and treatment** — collection, transport, treatment and discharge form a managed chain; source s.7(c), printed p.1583. Evidence: learner labels a wastewater pathway and identifies where treatment occurs.
4. **Water and sewerage infrastructure** — systems require facilities, equipment, operation and maintenance; source ss.7(d), 8(a), printed p.1583. Evidence: learner identifies pipes, pumps, storage and treatment components on a non-sensitive schematic.
5. **Water sources and resource conservation** — water-source rights, protection, management and conservation are connected to public supply; source ss.7(i), 8(b), printed p.1583. Evidence: learner sorts examples of water sources and describes one non-harmful conservation action.
6. **Water bodies and land-use planning** — water-resource decisions connect with land-use planning and protection of water bodies; source s.7(j), printed p.1583. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional land-use map and marks possible pathways from land to water.
7. **Water rationing and limited supply** — supply can be managed when availability is constrained; source s.8(g), printed p.1583. Evidence: learner solves a fictional allocation problem using supplied quantities, without issuing real-world restrictions.
8. **Water service access and connection** — water and sewerage service connections are planned and controlled; source ss.26–27, printed p.1589. Evidence: learner explains why a service connection is part of an organised network, not an improvised classroom activity.
9. **Measurement and water meters** — metering can record water supplied; source s.27(4), printed p.1589. Evidence: learner reads a fictional meter illustration and calculates a simple difference between two readings.
10. **Public health and water-quality protection** — standards address water quality and treatment assets; source s.28, printed pp.1589–1590. Evidence: learner explains why clear-looking water cannot be assumed safe and why qualified testing is required.
11. **Service conditions and customer communication** — water services involve conditions and communication between provider and customer; source s.30, printed p.1590. Evidence: learner identifies essential information in a fictional service notice.
12. **Emergency supply and water scarcity** — the legal text recognises control or rationing of supply; source s.8(g), printed p.1583, read with s.31, printed p.1590. Evidence: learner analyses a fictional drought or supply-shortage scenario and identifies safe household conservation options.

### Source B — Fiji Rural Water and Sanitation: Practical Guidelines for Rural Water Supply Management Plan (May 2012)

- **Issuer/source:** Government of Fiji, Ministry of Works, Transport and Public Utilities, Water and Sewerage Department.
- **Date/edition:** May 2012.
- **Official-hosted PDF:** https://www.mims.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/WSD-Practical-Guidelines-for-Rural-Water-Supply-Management-Plan.pdf
- **Inspected source locations:** pp.3–4 (policy context and purpose); pp.7–10 (community description, demand, sources, hazards, extraction and supply design); appendices 6–8, pp.31–35 (rainwater, groundwater and surface-water contamination); appendix 9, p.36 (maintenance); appendix 10, pp.37–38 (treatment concepts); appendix 11, p.39 (planning checklist).
- **Status and limitations:** This is a 2012 implementation guide, not a current drinking-water standard or a learner syllabus. The 2026 National Water Resources Management and Sanitation Policy refers to the 2021 Rural Water Supply Policy and to these practical guidelines for rural scheme planning. Do not treat the 2012 numerical demand, dosing, testing or maintenance values as current universal household instructions. Verify all operational values against current Ministry of Health standards and qualified water-service advice before any teaching use.
- **Source classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_TECHNICAL_GUIDE; HISTORICAL_TECHNICAL_CONTEXT; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source B**
13. **Community water-demand estimation** — population and patterns of use affect estimated demand; source §3, printed pp.7–8. Evidence: learner calculates a fictional community total from supplied population and per-person figures, with units shown.
14. **Wastewater generation and categories** — water use creates wastewater, including greywater and blackwater; source §3.4, printed p.7. Evidence: learner sorts fictional examples into greywater and blackwater categories.
15. **Comparing water-source types** — rainwater, springs, surface water, aquifers and desalinated seawater are distinct source types; source §4.1, printed p.8. Evidence: learner classifies labelled source diagrams and states one relevant consideration for each.
16. **Water quantity and quality evidence** — source assessments need both quantity and quality checks; source §§4.1–4.2, printed p.8. Evidence: learner reads a supplied mock data table and distinguishes quantity results from quality results.
17. **Water-source hazards and risk reduction** — flooding, contaminated sites, animal areas and wastewater disposal can threaten sources; source §4.3, printed p.8. Evidence: learner identifies hazards on a fictional catchment diagram and matches them to prevention concepts.
18. **Water extraction and source limits** — source, extraction type, amount and limits are separate data fields; source §5.1, printed p.8. Evidence: learner completes a fictional data table and compares extraction amounts without making real extraction decisions.
19. **Water-supply system design** — collection, pumps, storage, treatment, filters and pipelines form connected infrastructure; source §6.1, printed p.9. Evidence: learner sequences labelled components on a simple flow diagram.
20. **Technical data and design constraints** — plans require accurate survey and technical information and must account for local capacity and resources; source §§6.2–6.4, printed pp.9–10. Evidence: learner identifies missing information in a fictional project brief.
21. **Rainwater contamination pathways** — roof debris, animal droppings, spray drift, tank entry points and sediment can affect stored rainwater; source appendix 6, printed pp.31–32. Evidence: learner traces a contamination pathway on a drawing and selects a safe prevention concept.
22. **Groundwater contamination pathways** — runoff and nearby sanitation or waste sources can threaten groundwater; source appendix 7, printed pp.32–33. Evidence: learner labels a fictional cross-section showing how contaminants could reach a bore.
23. **Surface-water contamination pathways** — land use and runoff can affect streams and other surface-water sources; source appendix 8, printed pp.34–35. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional catchment picture and identifies upstream/downstream relationships.
24. **Water-system maintenance as prevention** — inspection and maintenance help reduce failure and contamination risks; source appendix 9, printed p.36. Evidence: learner sorts maintenance examples by component using a teacher-provided checklist.
25. **Treatment processes have different purposes** — filtration, UV and chlorine disinfection are different processes; source appendix 10, printed pp.37–38. Evidence: learner matches each process to its general purpose and identifies that no single method removes every contaminant.
26. **Monitoring, testing and evidence** — test results must be compared with the applicable current standard; source appendix 9, printed p.36. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional test report while clearly marking it as practice data, not a real safety determination.

### Source C — National Water Resources Management and Sanitation Policy 2026

- **Issuer/source:** Government of Fiji, Department of Water and Sewerage; national policy publication.
- **Date/edition:** 2026; 55-page policy.
- **Official document library:** https://library-fiji-dws.akvo.org/
- **Direct policy PDF:** https://library-fiji-dws.akvo.org/documents/national-water-resources-management-and-sanitation-policy-2026.pdf
- **Inspected source locations:** pp.3–4 (policy purpose and national context); pp.16–19 (principles, urban water services and conservation); pp.22–26 (sanitation and rural water services); pp.28–30 (water information and monitoring); pp.34–35 (catchment protection); pp.45–46 (water quality and pollution); pp.50–52 (legislative programme, implementation and source protection).
- **Status caution:** This is a policy, not an Act or a set of student achievement standards. The policy describes future regulatory and legislative reforms, including a proposed Water and Sewerage Services Act and regulator. Such proposals must be labelled proposed policy actions, not existing legal powers or completed reforms.
- **Source classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_POLICY; CURRENT_POLICY_SOURCE; NOT_LEGISLATION.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source C**
27. **Universal access, equity and water justice** — safe water, sanitation and hygiene are public wellbeing concerns; source pp.3–4. Evidence: learner explains, using a fictional case, why access needs can differ between communities.
28. **Water security and sustainable management** — availability, service reliability, protection and long-term needs are linked; source pp.3–4 and 16–19. Evidence: learner distinguishes immediate water use from long-term resource security.
29. **Water conservation and demand management** — water-saving practices and consumer awareness are policy priorities; source pp.19–20. Evidence: learner compares fictional household or school conservation options using supplied data.
30. **Rural water-service planning and community participation** — rural schemes involve planning, design, management and community participation; source pp.22–24. Evidence: learner identifies roles in a fictional community planning scenario without assigning real obligations to their own family or village.
31. **Sanitation and wastewater management** — safe disposal and treatment protect health and the environment; source pp.24–26. Evidence: learner distinguishes safe sanitation concepts from unsafe disposal examples in fictional illustrations.
32. **Water-resource data and evidence quality** — surface-water, groundwater, hydrology, water-quality and pollution records support decisions; source pp.28–30. Evidence: learner identifies date, place, unit, method and source in a mock dataset.
33. **Data validation, monitoring and trends** — regular quality checks and long-term monitoring help identify change and risk; source pp.28–30. Evidence: learner compares two fictional datasets, identifies missing values and describes a trend cautiously.
34. **Geospatial information and mapping** — water and flood-risk information can be integrated into GIS and environmental databases; source pp.29–30. Evidence: learner reads a simple, non-sensitive map key and interprets a fictional water-resource map.
35. **Catchment and watershed relationships** — land cover, erosion, pollution and water quality are connected across a catchment; source pp.34–35 and 45–46. Evidence: learner traces a fictional upstream-to-downstream pathway.
36. **Point-source and diffuse pollution** — pollution can come from identifiable discharge points or dispersed land-based sources; source pp.45–46. Evidence: learner classifies fictional pollution examples and explains the difference.
37. **Erosion, sediment and water quality** — vegetation loss and land degradation can increase sediment in water; source pp.45–46. Evidence: learner interprets a teacher-provided diagram linking exposed soil, runoff and suspended sediment.
38. **Groundwater protection** — bore areas and recharge environments require protection from contamination; source pp.45–46 and 51–52. Evidence: learner marks protective concepts on a fictional bore-site diagram.
39. **Climate resilience, flood and drought preparedness** — water planning connects with climate adaptation and disaster-risk reduction; source pp.16–19 and 28–30. Evidence: learner compares fictional planning choices for dry and wet conditions without making real hazard forecasts.
40. **Integrated water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH)** — water supply, sanitation and hygiene are linked but distinct service areas; source pp.3–4 and 22–26. Evidence: learner sorts examples into water, sanitation and hygiene categories and explains one connection.
41. **Environmental safeguards and biodiversity** — water-sector planning should consider ecosystems, biodiversity and environmental impacts; source pp.16–19 and 34–35. Evidence: learner identifies possible ecosystem effects in a fictional infrastructure case.
42. **Community knowledge and source stewardship** — policy recognises community participation and traditional water-source protection; source pp.22–24 and 51–52. Evidence: learner explains respectful consultation and stewardship using a fictional scenario without collecting sensitive customary knowledge.
43. **Public reporting and accountable decisions** — reliable data and transparent reporting support planning and public understanding; source pp.28–30. Evidence: learner writes a short evidence-based summary that separates observation from recommendation.

### Source links and source hierarchy

- The 2007 Promulgation supplies the legal framework concepts only; the 2012 guide supplies technical planning concepts; the 2026 policy supplies current policy direction. Do not merge these source types into one purported curriculum syllabus.
- Official Water Authority water-quality information: https://waterauthority.com.fj/awareness-safety/water-safety/ . WAF describes its National Water Quality Laboratory's sampling, analysis and role in maintaining drinking-water quality against WHO guidance or Fiji National Drinking Water Quality Standards. Use the current standard itself for any numerical or parameter-specific learning task.
- Official WAF water production and GIS information: https://waterauthority.com.fj/waf-production/ . Use current source dates and dataset metadata before adapting any figures.
- 2022 amendment source: https://www.parliament.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Act-46-Water-Authority-of-Fiji-Budget-Amendment-1.pdf . This amendment changes provisions including liquid trade waste and infringement notices; do not teach offences, penalties, notices or enforcement procedure as learner duties.

### Teaching, safety, legal and curriculum safeguards

- None of the three sources is a Fiji Ministry student syllabus or a list of official year-level achievement indicators. Every entry 1–43 above is a PacEdu-derived concept. The policy's strategies and the legal provisions must not be mislabelled as CLOs.
- Do not use the 2012 guide's historic litres-per-person, chlorine dose, pH, residual chlorine, test frequency, tank dimensions or maintenance intervals as current universal advice. They are source-specific historical guidance and require verification against current Ministry of Health standards and qualified technical advice.
- Never ask learners to taste, drink, collect, chemically treat or certify unknown water. Do not ask learners to handle chlorine, disinfectants, UV equipment, wastewater, sewage, contaminated samples, bore equipment or treatment machinery.
- No learner should enter tanks, wells, bores, rivers, drains, treatment plants, sewerage sites, floodwater or restricted catchments for an activity. Use mock data, diagrams, photographs and supervised classroom demonstrations that involve no hazardous materials.
- Do not ask learners to repair, connect, disconnect, ration or operate actual water infrastructure, or issue public health or water-safety notices.
- Respect privacy and customary/community knowledge. Use fictional or anonymised locations and avoid collecting household water bills, addresses, water-source security details or sensitive customary information.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. First verify current consolidated legislation and commencement/amendment notices; obtain the current Fiji National Drinking Water Quality Standards and relevant current technical guidance; map each concept to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry indicators; set year levels and prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.
