## Record 152 — Fiji Ministry of Education: Minimum Standards on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) in Schools Infrastructure

**Record status:** SOURCE-EXTRACTED; PACEDU-DERIVED LEARNING CONCEPTS; NOT OFFICIAL STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT INDICATORS  
**Source title:** *Minimum Standards on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) in Schools Infrastructure*  
**Issuer:** Ministry of Education, National Heritage, Culture & Arts, Government of Fiji  
**Lead author:** Eng. Liliane Sandra Kente  
**Date:** September 2012  
**Source copy:** https://livelearn.org/assets/media/docs/resources/Fiji_MEHA_WinS_Standards.pdf  
**Source quality:** Ministry-authored document, located in a non-Ministry host. Obtain a controlled Ministry copy and confirm current status before relying on it as a current school-facility standard.  
**Inspected source locations:** pp.8–13 (purpose, policy context, school health, learning, gender, community and lifelong skills); pp.14–16 (water); pp.17–22 (sanitation, accessibility, waste and drainage); pp.23 (hygiene promotion); pp.24–28 (assessment checklist); pp.31–35 (water-quality parameter tables).  
**Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_TECHNICAL_GUIDE; HISTORICAL_SCHOOL_WASH_STANDARD; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED; RIGHTS_REVIEW_REQUIRED.  
**Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending mapping to approved Fiji NCF and current Ministry year-level indicators.  
**Subjects:** Healthy Living; Elementary Science; Basic Science; Social Science; Mathematics; English; Technology; Arts; Agriculture.

### Source-derived concepts and observable evidence

1. **Water sources in Fiji** — the guide identifies WAF supply, wells, springs, rainwater, rivers, streams and oceans as water sources; source §3.1, printed p.14. Evidence: learner classifies illustrated source types and distinguishes surface water, groundwater and harvested rainwater.
2. **Water quantity and water quality are different** — the guide treats availability in quantity and quality as separate planning concerns; source §3.1, printed p.14. Evidence: learner explains the difference using a fictional data table with litres and test results.
3. **Potable and non-potable water** — drinking water and water intended for other uses must not be confused; source §§3.1.1–3.1.2, printed pp.14–15. Evidence: learner classifies labelled fictional water-use scenarios and explains why a non-drinking-water label matters.
4. **Safe drinking-water access at school** — the guide calls for safe drinking-water access and hygienic drinking arrangements; source §3.1.1, Standard 1, printed p.14. Evidence: learner identifies safe-access features on an illustrated school plan; learners do not inspect or certify real water.
5. **Water-quality indicators** — the guide refers to physical and microbiological parameters and directs readers to its annex; source §3.1.1, Standard 2, and Annex 1, printed pp.14, 31–35. Evidence: learner groups supplied example results into physical appearance, chemical/physical measurements and microbiological evidence without deciding that real water is safe.
6. **Contamination and risk contexts** — the guide identifies suspected contamination and risk contexts such as flooding, mining and intensive agriculture; source §3.1.1, printed p.14. Evidence: learner traces a fictional contamination pathway from land use to a water source.
7. **Non-potable water purposes** — water not intended for drinking may be used for handwashing, body washing and cleaning; source §3.1.2, printed p.15. Evidence: learner matches non-drinking uses to a labelled water supply in a fictional school diagram.
8. **Clear identification of non-potable water** — the guide requires non-potable supplies to be clearly identified and warns against drinking them; source §3.1.2, printed p.15. Evidence: learner interprets a clear pictorial sign and explains its purpose.
9. **Water storage and supply resilience** — school water supply systems include storage and may incorporate rainwater harvesting; source §3.1.3, Standard 5, printed p.16. Evidence: learner labels a rainwater harvesting and storage diagram and identifies the purpose of a reserve.
10. **Rainfall variability and water planning** — the guide connects rainwater supply with Fiji's variable rainfall cycle; source §3.1, printed p.14, and §3.1.3, printed p.16. Evidence: learner reads a fictional monthly rainfall chart and describes how seasonal variation affects stored water.
11. **Sanitation and health** — sanitation facilities support health, attendance, learning and staff working conditions; source §3.2, printed p.17. Evidence: learner explains a simple cause-and-effect relationship between sanitation access, health and school participation.
12. **Sanitation facility planning and ratios** — the guide discusses facility quantities in relation to school populations; source §3.2.1, Standard 6, printed pp.17–18. Evidence: learner solves a fictional ratio/counting task. Historic facility ratios are not to be presented as current mandatory construction rules.
13. **Privacy, dignity and equal access** — separate and private sanitation arrangements are addressed for girls and boys; source §3.2.1, printed p.17. Evidence: learner identifies privacy and dignity features in a fictional facility plan using respectful, non-stigmatising language.
14. **Accessible sanitation design** — the guide includes an accessible toilet cubicle for children with special needs and accessible hygiene facilities; source §3.2.1 and Annex 3, printed pp.17, 37–38. Evidence: learner identifies access barriers and proposes a design improvement on a diagram. The 2012 wheelchair-specific example must not be treated as a complete current accessibility standard.
15. **Age-appropriate facility design** — the guide addresses child-sized toilet and washbasin dimensions for Classes 1–3; source §3.2.1, printed pp.17–18. Evidence: learner compares labelled design drawings and explains why facilities should be usable by children of different ages. Do not use the historical dimensions as current building specifications.
16. **Menstrual hygiene facilities and dignity** — the guide discusses sanitary materials, disposal and shower provision; source §§3.2.1–3.2.2 and §3.3, printed pp.18–19, 23. Evidence: learner identifies respectful, private and hygienic facility features in an age-appropriate, non-stigmatising scenario.
17. **Cleanable, ventilated and well-lit facilities** — sanitation quality includes hygiene, cleanable surfaces, ventilation and lighting; source §3.2.2, Standard 9, printed p.19. Evidence: learner identifies features that make a fictional facility safer and easier to maintain.
18. **Drainage and stagnant-water prevention** — the guide addresses runoff, drainage and avoiding stagnant water; source §3.2.2 and Standard 12, printed pp.19, 22. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional site diagram and identifies where drainage problems could create stagnant pools.
19. **Waste separation** — the guide calls for separation of biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste; source §3.2.4, Standard 11, printed p.21. Evidence: learner sorts clean, safe picture cards into waste categories and explains the difference.
20. **Composting and waste recovery** — composting is identified as a possible approach for biodegradable waste; source §3.2.4, Standard 11, printed p.21. Evidence: learner sequences a diagram showing how suitable plant material can become compost. No handling of unknown or contaminated waste.
21. **Hygiene practices as teachable skills** — hygiene education includes handwashing, toilet use, cleaning, hygienic items and waste disposal; source §3.3, Standard 13, printed p.23. Evidence: learner sequences illustrated handwashing steps and selects appropriate hygiene actions for a fictional routine.
22. **Hygiene behaviour and role modelling** — the guide discusses monitoring hygiene practices and positive examples from adults; source §3.3, Standard 14, printed p.23. Evidence: learner identifies supportive hygiene role-modelling in a short scenario without publicly judging or shaming classmates.
23. **Fairness and non-discrimination in shared tasks** — cleaning and waste activities should be organised fairly, transparently and without discrimination; source §3.3, printed p.23. Evidence: learner reviews a fictional duty rota and identifies unequal allocation or unfair treatment.
24. **Hygiene tasks must not be punishment** — the guide explicitly says school cleaning activities should not be used as punishment; source §3.3, printed p.23. Evidence: learner distinguishes a fair shared-care routine from a punitive or humiliating task in a fictional case.
25. **School WASH assessment and evidence** — the assessment checklist asks about water quality, quantity, toilets, cleaning, waste and hygiene promotion; source §4, printed pp.24–28. Evidence: learner categorises sample checklist questions and distinguishes observation from a technical test.
26. **Water-quality data and units** — Annex 1 names parameters including pH, colour, turbidity, residual chlorine, total dissolved solids, conductivity, thermotolerant coliforms, E. coli and total coliforms; source Annex 1, printed p.31. Evidence: learner matches parameter names to supplied units or plain-language descriptions using mock data only.
27. **Microorganisms and health** — the glossary and water-quality annex distinguish microorganisms and microbiological indicators; source definitions, printed pp.6–7, and Annex 1, printed p.31. Evidence: learner explains that microorganisms are not all visible and that laboratory testing is needed for microbiological safety.
28. **School environment and solid-waste management** — the guide includes cleanliness, waste disposal and environmental management; source §§3.2.2–3.2.4 and checklist §4.4, printed pp.19–22, 27. Evidence: learner identifies safe waste-management features on a fictional school-site illustration.
29. **Water, sanitation and learning conditions** — the guide links adequate facilities to attendance, learning and lifelong skills; source §§2.1–2.6, printed pp.12–13. Evidence: learner constructs a simple cause-and-effect map showing how WASH supports participation and wellbeing.
30. **Gender-responsive and inclusive WASH planning** — the guide includes a dedicated gender discussion and considers different school users; source §2.4 and §3.2.1, printed pp.13, 17–18. Evidence: learner evaluates a fictional school plan for privacy, equal access and inclusion without stereotyping.

### Separate classification: school-facility standards versus learner learning concepts

- The document's Standards 1–14 and its assessment checklist are **school infrastructure/service standards and facility assessment criteria**, not student learning achievement indicators.
- The 30 numbered concepts above are PacEdu paraphrases for possible curriculum mapping. They are not official Ministry CLOs, year-level outcomes or assessment standards.
- Annex 1 contains historical water-quality values adopted from the Fiji National Drinking Water Quality Standards as cited by the 2012 guide. Do not copy those numerical limits into new learner materials as current standards until the current Ministry of Health standard and any revisions are obtained and checked.
- The guide's construction dimensions, toilet ratios, storage tank capacities and water-quantity recommendations are historical technical requirements. Do not use them as current design or compliance advice without confirmation by the relevant Fiji authorities.
- The source itself lists the Fiji National Drinking Water Standards as a 2011 reference (printed p.29). This record does not claim that the 2011 standard or the 2012 WASH document remains current.

### Current corroboration and follow-up sources

- Water Authority of Fiji, current public water-quality information: https://waterauthority.com.fj/awareness-safety/water-safety/ . WAF says its National Water Quality Laboratory collects samples, analyses results and monitors drinking-water quality against WHO guidance or Fiji National Drinking Water Quality Standards. This is a current institutional description, not the numerical standard itself.
- Ministry of Health and Medical Services, *Guidelines for Climate-Resilient and Environmentally Sustainable Health Care Facilities in Fiji* (©2020): https://www.health.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Guide-for-CRESHCF.pdf . This is a healthcare-facility guide, not a school standard, but its WASH sections provide supplementary concepts about water safety plans, storage, emergency monitoring, maintenance and climate resilience. Do not apply healthcare-facility checklist requirements directly to schools.
- Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Public Advisory #40, 21 September 2026, Batiki water crisis: https://www.health.gov.fj/rise-in-diarrhoea-cases-on-batiki-island-sparks-emergency-ministry-of-health-response-to-el-nino-water-crisis/ . This is a dated current-affairs case study for drought, rainwater storage, water supply resilience, hygiene and public-health communication. The advisory's instructions are time- and event-specific; do not generalise them as a permanent national protocol.

### Safety, rights, curriculum and review safeguards

- No learner should test, certify, taste or drink unknown water; handle sewage, wastewater, sanitary waste, chemicals, disinfectants or contaminated samples; enter tanks, wells, drains, septic systems or treatment sites; or inspect private toilet facilities.
- Use safe classroom diagrams, mock water-quality datasets, photographs with appropriate rights, fictional school plans and non-sensitive case studies. All hygiene instruction must protect dignity and privacy.
- Never make a learner responsible for auditing classmates' bodies, menstrual status, hygiene, disability or family circumstances. No public rankings, shame, punishment or discriminatory cleaning rota.
- Any school WASH assessment must be carried out by authorised adults using current approved standards, not by children.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. First obtain a controlled current Ministry copy and determine whether the 2012 school WASH standards have been superseded; obtain current Fiji National Drinking Water Quality Standards; map concepts to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry indicators; confirm levels and prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 153 — Fiji Ministry of Health: Communicable-disease surveillance, outbreak communication and environmental-health concepts

**Record status:** SOURCE-EXTRACTED; PACEDU-DERIVED CONCEPTS; NOT OFFICIAL STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT INDICATORS  
**Subject coverage:** Healthy Living; Elementary Science; Basic Science; Social Science; Mathematics; English; Computer Studies  
**Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending approved Fiji NCF and Ministry mapping  
**CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT

### Source A — Fiji Communicable Disease Surveillance and Outbreak Response Guidelines (December 2016)

- **Issuer:** Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Republic of Fiji.
- **Technical revision:** December 2016; the Ministry PDF cover identifies the 2016 edition. The PDF is hosted on the official Ministry domain.
- **Official PDF:** https://www.health.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Fiji-Communicable-Disease-Surveillance-and-Outbreak-Response-Guidelines-2016-1.pdf
- **Inspected locations:** §1.3–1.5, printed pp.16–24; §2.1–2.4, printed pp.28–38; §2.12, printed pp.53–54; §3.3, printed pp.74–78; §3.5, printed pp.82–84; §4.5, printed pp.101–104; §4.7, printed pp.107–110; selected disease transmission tables in §§4.3, 4.6 and 4.12.
- **Version caution:** This is a 2016 operational public-health guideline, not a current clinical manual or student syllabus. The Ministry's current Guidelines index also lists a separate 2016 Communicable Disease Surveillance and Outbreak Response Guidelines entry, but the continued current operational status and subsequent amendments or replacement must be confirmed with the Ministry before operational use. Do not use old disease thresholds, diagnostic criteria, treatment details, or case definitions as current health advice.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_PUBLIC_HEALTH_GUIDELINE; HISTORICAL_TECHNICAL_SOURCE; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source A**
1. **Communicable disease and prevention** — the guideline distinguishes communicable disease prevention, surveillance and response; source §1 and §2.1, printed pp.15–16, 28. Evidence: learner distinguishes prevention, monitoring and response in a fictional scenario.
2. **Outbreak as a change from expected patterns** — outbreak recognition depends on comparison with expected disease occurrence and verified information; source §1.1–1.3, printed pp.16–17. Evidence: learner compares fictional weekly counts and describes an unusual increase without declaring an outbreak.
3. **Surveillance as systematic observation** — disease surveillance collects information over time to identify patterns and guide public-health work; source §2.1, printed p.28. Evidence: learner explains why consistent records over time are more useful than isolated anecdotes.
4. **Data quality and verification** — increases must be checked for data-quality issues, reporting changes and changed definitions; source §1.3, printed pp.16–17. Evidence: learner identifies missing dates, duplicate records and changed categories in a mock dataset.
5. **Time, place and person as data dimensions** — descriptive epidemiology organises information by when, where and who; source §1.5, printed pp.20–22. Evidence: learner sorts fictional, anonymised records into time, place and person fields.
6. **Tables and line lists** — structured tables organise observations for comparison; source §1.5, printed pp.20–21. Evidence: learner completes a fictional table using anonymous case IDs and non-identifying variables.
7. **Epidemic curves and time-series graphs** — a curve plots counts over time and can help describe a pattern; source §1.5, printed pp.21–22. Evidence: learner constructs and interprets a simple bar chart from fictional data, with labelled axes and units.
8. **Spot maps and spatial patterns** — maps can display where events are reported relative to landmarks; source §1.5, printed p.22. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional map using invented locations and a legend, without plotting real patient addresses.
9. **Rates, counts and averages are different** — the guideline discusses incidence and moving averages; source §1.3, printed pp.16–17. Evidence: learner distinguishes a count from a rate and calculates a simple average from mock values.
10. **Local patterns can be hidden in national totals** — divisional or local data may reveal a pattern that a national total conceals; source §1.3, printed pp.16–17. Evidence: learner compares fictional division-level counts with a national total and explains why disaggregation matters.
11. **Evidence, hypothesis and uncertainty** — hypotheses about source, transmission and exposure must be assessed against evidence; source §1.5, printed pp.22–24. Evidence: learner separates observation, possible explanation and confirmed fact in a case study.
12. **Environmental pathways and disease risk** — environmental conditions can influence transmission pathways; source §1.5 and Figure 3, printed pp.22–23. Evidence: learner traces a fictional environmental pathway on a diagram without visiting hazardous sites.
13. **Prevention can interrupt exposure pathways** — public-health controls can target sources, transmission routes or exposure; source §1.5, printed p.24. Evidence: learner matches safe, general prevention examples to a simplified pathway diagram.
14. **Water, sanitation and disease prevention** — the guideline includes sanitation and water-purification measures among possible public-health controls; source §1.5, printed p.24. Evidence: learner explains how safe water and sanitation can reduce some exposure risks without attempting water treatment.
15. **Mosquito vectors and disease transmission** — the dengue section describes Aedes mosquitoes as vectors; source §4.5, printed pp.101–104. Evidence: learner explains the meaning of vector and labels a simple mosquito-to-human transmission diagram.
16. **Mosquito breeding environments** — vector control is part of prevention and environmental health; source §1.5, printed p.19, and §4.5, printed pp.101–104. Evidence: learner identifies, in safe photographs or fictional illustrations, containers that can collect standing water; no learner handles waste or enters unsafe sites.
17. **Animal reservoirs and environmental contamination** — the leptospirosis section describes animal reservoirs and environmental exposure through contaminated freshwater, floodwater, soil or mud; source §4.7, printed pp.107–110. Evidence: learner traces a fictional animal-to-environment exposure pathway and identifies why contaminated floodwater must be avoided.
18. **Rainfall, flooding and changing exposure risks** — the guideline links environmental conditions and post-disaster settings with disease patterns; source §1.1 and Figure 3, printed pp.16, 23. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional rainfall and risk timeline without forecasting disease or entering floodwater.
19. **Food and water contamination pathways** — selected disease sections describe food- and water-borne transmission; source §§4.3, 4.6 and 4.12, printed pp.96–100, 105–107, 125–128. Evidence: learner identifies safe, general contamination pathways in a fictional food/water flow diagram.
20. **Laboratory testing and confirmation** — the guideline distinguishes surveillance information from laboratory investigation and confirmation; source §2.6, printed pp.42–44, and disease sections. Evidence: learner explains why a laboratory result is different from a guess or symptom description.
21. **Public-health communication** — messages should be accurate, timely, consistent and understandable to the public; source §2.12, printed pp.53–54. Evidence: learner edits a fictional public-information notice for clarity, source attribution and non-alarming language.
22. **Communication and early care-seeking** — public messages can encourage people who are unwell to seek appropriate health services; source §2.12, printed p.54. Evidence: learner identifies a safe referral statement in a fictional health message; no diagnosis or treatment advice is created by learners.
23. **Preparedness, response, recovery and review** — outbreak communication and response are organised across phases; source §2.12, printed pp.53–54, and §2.13, printed p.58. Evidence: learner orders a fictional public-information timeline into preparation, response, recovery and review.
24. **Community partnership and coordination** — public-health communication involves relevant authorities, community leaders, schools and other stakeholders; source §2.12, printed pp.53–54. Evidence: learner identifies the appropriate responsible adult or public agency in a fictional coordination scenario.
25. **Post-event evaluation and learning** — review after an outbreak can identify lessons and improve future preparedness; source §2.13, printed p.58. Evidence: learner writes a short reflection identifying what worked, what evidence is missing and one improvement.

### Source B — Ministry of Health and Medical Services: Environmental Health and Communicable Diseases programme pages

- **Issuer:** Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Government of Fiji.
- **Current Ministry pages:** https://www.health.gov.fj/communicable-diseases-cd/ and https://www.health.gov.fj/our-work/
- **Inspected locations:** Communicable Diseases page, paragraphs describing surveillance, laboratory confirmation, public-health communication and research; Environmental Health section describing pollution, unsanitary conditions, poor water quality, improper waste management, vector breeding and poor food quality; listed environmental-health programme areas.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_PROGRAMME_INFORMATION; CURRENT_WEB_REFERENCE; NOT A STUDENT SYLLABUS.

26. **Environmental health risk factors** — pollution, unsanitary conditions, poor water quality, improper waste management, vector breeding and poor food quality are identified as environmental-health concerns. Evidence: learner categorises fictional environmental-health examples and explains one possible exposure pathway.
27. **Environmental health and public wellbeing** — environmental-health services promote and protect health-supportive environments. Evidence: learner explains how a clean and safe shared environment can support wellbeing without blaming individuals or communities.
28. **Laboratory services and public-health evidence** — laboratory services support diagnosis, confirmation and surveillance. Evidence: learner distinguishes a public report, a laboratory test and a confirmed result using fictional examples.
29. **Research and quality assurance** — public-health programmes use research, quality assurance and collaboration. Evidence: learner identifies why methods and data quality matter when comparing results.
30. **Interagency communication** — communicable-disease work uses communication networks between departments and stakeholders. Evidence: learner maps responsible organisations in a fictional response diagram without assuming students have official reporting roles.

### Source C — Fiji Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Public Advisory No.17 (22 February 2026): Leptospirosis precaution advisory

- **Issuer:** Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Government of Fiji.
- **Publication date:** 22 February 2026.
- **Official advisory:** https://www.health.gov.fj/ministry-urges-general-public-to-take-precaution-against-leptospirosis/
- **Inspected locations:** advisory paragraphs 1–6.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_PUBLIC_HEALTH_ADVISORY; DATED_CURRENT_AFFAIRS_CASE_STUDY; EVENT-SPECIFIC.
- **PacEdu-derived concepts from Source C:**
31. **Risk communication after a serious event** — a public advisory communicates a risk and precaution message after suspected cases and a public-health investigation. Evidence: learner identifies issuer, date, event, evidence status and intended audience in a source-analysis task.
32. **Rainfall and environmental exposure** — the advisory notes increased concern after heavy rain and describes an investigation linked to freshwater swimming. Evidence: learner analyses a fictional rainfall/exposure timeline and distinguishes association from proof of cause.
33. **Suspected versus confirmed information** — the advisory uses the wording “suspected” and reports that investigations are underway. Evidence: learner distinguishes suspected, investigated and confirmed claims in a short media-literacy exercise.
34. **Health information source checking** — public-health information should be attributed to the issuing Ministry and dated. Evidence: learner checks the authoring agency, date and link before using a public advisory in a report.
35. **Respectful reporting and privacy** — a serious public-health event should be discussed without identifying affected children or repeating distressing details. Evidence: learner rewrites a fictional report to remove identifying and sensational information.

### Source D — Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Fiji Leptospirosis, Typhoid and Dengue public information page

- **Issuer:** Ministry of Health and Medical Services, Government of Fiji.
- **Official page:** https://www.health.gov.fj/ltds/
- **Inspected information:** disease overview panels for leptospirosis, typhoid fever and dengue fever.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_PUBLIC_INFORMATION; CURRENT_WEB_PAGE; CONTENT/UPDATE DATE NOT CLEARLY DISPLAYED.
- **PacEdu-derived concept:**
36. **Disease-information comparison and source currency** — Ministry disease information pages can be compared for cause, prevention theme and publication/update date. Evidence: learner makes a source-comparison table and flags when a date is not shown. Do not copy undated clinical details as current treatment or diagnosis guidance.

### Source limitations and safeguards

- The 2016 guideline is an operational document for health workers and outbreak-response teams. It is not a school textbook, a student diagnostic manual, or a current clinical guideline.
- Disease-specific case definitions, outbreak thresholds, incubation periods, laboratory methods, treatment, medicines, isolation, quarantine, and official notification procedures must not be taught as learner instructions or reused as current clinical facts without Ministry confirmation.
- Learners must not diagnose classmates, collect illness histories, identify suspected cases, keep health registers, notify authorities on behalf of the Ministry, sample blood/stool/water, visit outbreak sites, handle mosquitoes or animals, or conduct field investigations.
- Use fictional, anonymised datasets; no names, addresses, phone numbers, GPS coordinates, household details, or real school illness records. Never map real patient locations or identify affected children.
- Disease case studies must be age-appropriate, non-graphic, non-stigmatising and trauma-aware. Do not imply that a person or community is responsible for disease.
- Use current Ministry advisories only with their date and context; an old advisory is not evidence of today's outbreak status. Any numerical disease counts or thresholds must be time-stamped and sourced.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Verify the current Ministry communicable-disease guideline and clinical/public-health advice; confirm the current Ministry education curriculum mapping and age suitability; obtain current prevention materials; set levels and prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

### Source A — Food and Health Guidelines for Fiji

**PacEdu-derived concepts grounded in the FAO profile of Fiji's 2018 guidelines**
1. **Variety across food groups** — the national food guide encourages a variety of foods from the three food groups in meals; source: FAO Fiji FBDG profile, messages section, lines 42–47. Evidence: learner classifies familiar local foods into the three groups as represented in the verified guide and builds a fictional balanced-meal example.
2. **Local foods and food diversity** — “go local” and variety of local foods are central messages; source: FAO profile, lines 39–44. Evidence: learner identifies local food examples from a teacher-approved list and compares seasonal availability without ranking families' diets.
3. **Salt, sugar, fat and oil awareness** — guideline message encourages choosing and preparing food and drinks with less salt, sugar, fat and oil; source: FAO profile, line 44. Evidence: learner compares mock product labels or recipe cards and identifies where these ingredients appear.
4. **Fruit and vegetable variety** — the guide promotes more local fruits and vegetables; source: FAO profile, lines 45–47. Evidence: learner groups fruits and vegetables by visible features, season or local availability using safe pictures.
5. **Healthy snacks** — the national messages include choosing healthy snacks; source: FAO profile, line 47. Evidence: learner compares fictional snack options using a balanced-choice explanation rather than moral labels.
6. **Healthy meals and snacks for children** — the guidelines include a message to give children healthy meals and snacks; source: FAO profile, line 49. Evidence: learner designs a fictional school snack using accessible, culturally familiar options.
7. **Clean and safe drinking water** — drinking clean and safe water is a dietary-guideline message; source: FAO profile, line 51. Evidence: learner distinguishes drinking-water safety from appearance and explains that only approved water sources should be used.
8. **Growing food** — growing one's own food is included in the national message set and food-guide design; source: FAO profile, lines 39–40 and 52. Evidence: learner sequences the basic needs of a plant and plans a small hypothetical food garden.
9. **Physical activity and wellbeing** — physical activity is part of the food guide and healthy-weight message; source: FAO profile, lines 39–45. Evidence: learner identifies examples of safe, inclusive movement and explains how activity complements healthy eating.
10. **Breastfeeding as an infant-feeding public-health message** — the guideline includes exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months; source: FAO profile, line 48. Evidence: age-appropriate learner task identifies that infant-feeding decisions belong with caregivers and qualified health workers; no learner is asked to advise or assess a parent.
11. **Food guide as a visual communication tool** — Fiji uses a pineapple-shaped food guide to communicate multiple food and lifestyle messages; source: FAO profile, lines 39–40 and 57–59. Evidence: learner interprets symbols, key messages and layout in an infographic.
12. **Guideline audience and limits** — the 2018 guidelines are directed to the healthy general public; source: FAO profile, lines 32–37. Evidence: learner distinguishes general public guidance from individualised clinical diet advice.

### Source D — Food Safety Regulations 2009 (supplementary legal-source cross-reference)

- **Title:** Food Safety Regulations 2009.
- **Official legal portal listing:** https://fijitradeportal.gov.fj/en-gb/site/display/166
- **Related principal Act:** Food Safety Act 2003, previously catalogued in Record 144.
- **Status caution:** Verify current consolidated regulations, amendments and applicable requirements before any compliance-focused learning. This record does not extract new legal duties or reproduce numerical food-temperature requirements.
- **Use in this record:** Legal source cross-reference only. Food hygiene concepts above are drawn from public health and school-food guidance, not represented as legal requirements from the Regulations.

### Version, rights and educational safeguards

- FAO's profile identifies the 2018 Fiji Food and Health Guidelines as a national public-health guideline and reports that a review process was underway in 2021. The Ministry page currently links a PDF from a 2014 upload directory. The exact edition of that linked file must be checked before it is treated as the 2018 edition.
- FAO reports the 2013 School Canteen Guidelines and 2017 School Food and Canteen Policy were under review, with the 2023 toolkit still in draft/finalisation at the time of its profile. Do not treat those historic materials as confirmed current operational rules.
- Do not use historic nutrition prevalence statistics, adult calorie examples, or serving targets as current individual dietary prescriptions. Avoid weight stigma, body comparisons, restrictive dieting, calorie counting for children, or public weighing and measuring.
- Infant feeding and breastfeeding content must be age-appropriate and respectful; learners must not be asked to counsel caregivers.
- Food allergies, medical diets and clinical nutrition require individual advice from qualified health professionals. Do not ask learners to disclose diagnoses, weight, food insecurity or household income.
- Food preparation activities require school risk assessment, food-safety controls, allergy checks and competent supervision. Do not use spoiled food, raw animal products or unsafe equipment.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Obtain and inspect the Ministry primary PDFs; confirm the current 2024/2018 Food and Health Guidelines edition; verify the latest School Food and Canteen Policy and toolkit status with the Ministry; cross-check current Food Safety Regulations; map concepts to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry indicators; set levels/prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 155 — Fiji crop production, farm management, soil capability and sustainable agriculture

**Record status:** SOURCE-EXTRACTED; PACEDU-DERIVED CONCEPTS; NOT OFFICIAL STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT INDICATORS

### Source A — Ministry of Agriculture, Crop Farmer's Guide: A Farmer's Guide to a Better Harvest (2020 edition)

- **Issuer:** Ministry of Agriculture, Government of Fiji.
- **Edition:** Updated edition 2020; preface identifies it as an update of the 2009 edition and says it includes disaster-risk/climate-change tips and common Fiji weeds.
- **Official PDF:** https://www.agriculture.gov.fj/documents/booklets/CFG_Contents%20Final%202020.pdf
- **Inspected locations:** preface, printed p.2; crop contents, printed p.1; Amaranthus, printed pp.1–2; Avocado, printed pp.3–4; selected crop profiles and guide structure.
- **Classification:** FIJI_PRIMARY_GOVERNMENT_AGRICULTURAL_TECHNICAL_GUIDE; 2020 EDITION; CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED.
- **Rights note:** Ministry publication; access to the PDF does not itself grant permission for wholesale copying, adaptation or commercial redistribution. Extract concepts and cite source; do not reproduce its tables, crop text or pesticide schedules.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source A**
1. **Crop diversity in Fiji** — the guide profiles root crops, vegetables, cereals, pulses, fruit trees, spices and other crops; source contents, printed p.1 and preface p.2. Evidence: learner classifies familiar Fiji crops by broad crop group using teacher-approved picture cards.
2. **Crop identification and scientific naming** — crop profiles pair common names with botanical names; source Amaranthus and Avocado profiles, printed pp.1 and 3. Evidence: learner matches selected common crop names to supplied botanical names, with spelling support.
3. **Crop variety and selection** — profiles identify recommended varieties or local selections; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner compares two fictional variety cards and identifies that variety selection depends on crop purpose and conditions.
4. **Planting season and crop calendar** — crop profiles provide planting or fruiting seasons; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner reads a fictional crop calendar and orders seasonal activities.
5. **Seed and planting material** — crop guides describe seed rates, seedlings, nursery raising and transplanting; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado pp.3–4. Evidence: learner sequences a diagram of seed, seedling, nursery and transplant stages.
6. **Germination and plant establishment** — the guide records germination timing and early crop establishment; source Amaranthus p.1. Evidence: learner records fictional daily germination observations in a table and identifies a pattern.
7. **Plant spacing and area** — crop profiles specify row and within-row spacing; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner calculates plant positions on a paper grid using fictional spacing values, not a real planting prescription.
8. **Soil analysis before nutrient application** — the guide repeatedly recommends soil analysis before planting or fertiliser application; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner explains why a soil test can inform a decision and distinguishes a test result from a guess.
9. **Organic matter, manure and mulch** — the guide discusses poultry manure and mulch as soil-management inputs; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner compares illustrated organic-material examples and explains the general role of mulch in protecting soil moisture.
10. **Weed competition and crop management** — crop profiles include weed-management considerations; source crop profile format and Amaranthus p.1. Evidence: learner identifies weeds as plants growing where they are not wanted in a fictional crop bed and describes non-chemical prevention concepts.
11. **Plant disease recognition as observation** — the guide identifies crop disease examples and discusses drainage and removal of affected plants; source Avocado p.3 and contents p.1. Evidence: learner distinguishes an observed plant symptom from a confirmed diagnosis; no disease diagnosis or treatment by learners.
12. **Insect pests and crop damage** — the guide includes pest profiles and crop-protection sections; source crop profile format and contents p.1. Evidence: learner interprets a safe photograph showing plant damage and records observations without handling insects or applying controls.
13. **Drainage and waterlogging** — crop profiles note the effect of drainage and prolonged waterlogging; source Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional field diagram and identifies why drainage conditions matter to plant growth.
14. **Harvest maturity and timing** — profiles include harvest timing and maturity descriptions; source Amaranthus p.1 and contents. Evidence: learner orders crop-growth stages and selects a stated harvest stage from a fictional profile.
15. **Yield and production measurement** — crop profiles present yields and units such as tonnes per hectare; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner reads a supplied yield table, identifies units and compares fictional values without assuming they are guaranteed.
16. **Food value of crops** — profiles include dietary fibre, minerals and vitamins; source Amaranthus p.1 and Avocado p.3. Evidence: learner links a crop with a food-value statement from an approved nutrition source.
17. **Staggered planting and continuous supply** — the Amaranthus profile describes staged planting and new planting after harvests; source p.1. Evidence: learner sequences a fictional staggered planting calendar and explains how timing can spread harvest periods.
18. **Crop responses to flood and drought conditions** — the guide includes disaster-risk and climate tips for crop profiles; source preface p.2 and Amaranthus/Avocado profiles. Evidence: learner compares fictional crop-planning choices for wet and dry conditions without treating them as universal advice.
19. **Mulch and soil-moisture conservation** — the guide links mulch or crop cover with reduced moisture loss; source Amaranthus p.1. Evidence: learner explains a diagram comparing bare and covered soil.
20. **Crop production and food security** — the preface identifies staple crops such as dalo, cassava, yam, kumala, dalo-ni-tana, breadfruit and rice as important to household diets; source p.2. Evidence: learner explains how crop diversity can support household and community food availability using a fictional example.
21. **Agricultural information requires extension advice** — the guide says it should be complemented by advice from Agricultural Field Officers and food specialists; source preface p.2. Evidence: learner identifies an appropriate expert source for a fictional crop-production question.

- **Host and contributors:** Fiji Soil Information System / Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research and Fiji partners; catalogue includes Ministry of Agriculture publications and research.
- **Scientific publications page:** https://fiji-psp.landcareresearch.co.nz/en/resources/scientific-publications
- **Crop suitability tool:** https://fiji-psp.landcareresearch.co.nz/crop-suitability

- **PacEdu-derived concepts grounded in the crop-suitability tool:** crop suitability is evaluated by comparing soil attributes and land qualities with crop requirements; the tool reports suitability classes from highly suitable to not suitable for selected Fiji crops. Evidence: learner interprets a teacher-supplied fictional suitability matrix and explains why site conditions matter.
- **Additional concept:** soil maps and land capability classifications provide evidence for land-use planning. Evidence: learner interprets a map legend and compares two fictional sites. Do not make real land allocation or customary land recommendations.

### Safety, rights, version and curriculum safeguards

- The 2020 Crop Farmer's Guide and 2014 Farm Management Manual contain pesticide and herbicide products, application rates, mixing instructions and chemical schedules. These are deliberately **not** extracted as learner competencies or instructions. Learners must not handle, mix, apply, transport or recommend agricultural chemicals.
- No learner should operate tractors, powered machinery, pumps, cutting tools, harvesting forks, sprayers or farm equipment. Avoid field activities involving steep slopes, rivers, drains, livestock, bees, unknown plants, mould, pesticides or contaminated soil.
- Crop calendars, planting rates, spacing, fertiliser amounts, yields, pest controls and prices are crop-, site-, season- and edition-specific. Treat all numeric values from the 2014 manual and 2020 guide as historical reference values until current Ministry technical advice confirms them.
- Do not use the 2014 manual's gross margins, prices or input costs as current market data. Any economics task must use dated, clearly labelled practice data or a current, attributable dataset.
- Respect customary land rights, land tenure, community consent and local knowledge. Do not ask learners to disclose family land ownership, lease terms or sensitive village land information.
- Ministry policy outcome indicators are sector performance measures, not automatically student learning indicators. All entries in this record are PacEdu-derived concepts.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Obtain current Ministry crop and farm technical guides; confirm current status of the 2025–2035 Non-Sugar Agriculture Sector Policy and its detailed indicator pages; retrieve and inspect the Fiji Land Use Capability Classification 2012 source; map concepts to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry indicators; set year levels/prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 156 — Fiji livestock production, animal welfare, animal health and biosecurity concepts

**Record status:** SOURCE-EXTRACTED; PACEDU-DERIVED CONCEPTS; NOT OFFICIAL STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT INDICATORS  
**Subject coverage:** Agriculture; Elementary Science; Basic Science; Healthy Living; Mathematics; Commercial Studies; Technology; English  
**Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending approved Fiji NCF and Ministry year-level mapping  
**CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT

### Source A — Fiji Livestock Sector Strategy, Final Report (11 March 2016)

- **Issuers/authors:** Fiji Livestock Sector Strategy Working Group and Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji.
- **Date:** 11 March 2016.
- **Document:** *Fiji Livestock Sector Strategy — Final Report*.
- **PDF:** https://pafpnet.spc.int/attachments/article/535/Fiji%20Livestock%20Sector%20Strategy.pdf
- **Inspected locations:** summary and logical framework, printed pp.1–2; policy and commodity scope, pp.4–5; productivity and feed resources, pp.12–13; animal welfare and quality/safety, pp.23–25 and 29–30; animal health and resilience, pp.41–45; good practices, pp.44–45; skills, pp.46–48.
- **Classification:** FIJI_GOVERNMENT_SECTOR_STRATEGY; HISTORICAL_POLICY_AND_SECTOR_ANALYSIS; CURRENT_POLICY_AND_PROGRAMME_CHECK_REQUIRED.
- **Version caution:** This is a 2016 strategy with historical statistics, prices, targets, institutional names and proposed activities. It is not evidence that every proposal was enacted or remains current. Do not reuse its old numerical productivity benchmarks as present-day standards.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source A**
1. **Livestock diversity in Fiji** — the strategy discusses cattle, dairy, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry and honey/beekeeping; printed pp.4–5 and sector chapters. Evidence: learner sorts supplied animal and product cards into livestock groups.
2. **Livestock products and uses** — the strategy identifies milk, beef, mutton, pork, poultry meat, eggs and honey as priority commodities; p.5. Evidence: learner matches a product to its animal source using picture cards.
3. **Animal life cycles and reproduction vocabulary** — the strategy uses production measures such as calving, lambing and piglets; p.12. Evidence: learner sequences an age-appropriate, teacher-provided animal life-cycle diagram without handling animals.
4. **Livestock productivity as measurable output** — the strategy discusses milk production, stock off-take and growth rates; pp.12–13. Evidence: learner reads a fictional production table and identifies the unit and period.
5. **Understanding indicators and benchmarks** — the strategy's productivity table compares average and potential values based on 2009 census and industry estimates; p.12. Evidence: learner distinguishes an observed value, an estimate and a target; historical values are explicitly dated.
6. **Livestock feed ingredients and sources** — the strategy describes local crop by-products and imported feed ingredients; p.13. Evidence: learner classifies teacher-provided examples as locally sourced or imported feed materials without formulating a ration.
7. **Feed quality and truthful labelling** — the strategy discusses feed composition, protein claims, testing and quality assurance; p.13 and pp.29–30. Evidence: learner identifies the purpose of a label and why a claim needs evidence.
8. **Feed safety and contamination** — the strategy identifies contaminants and the need for competent analysis and quality controls; p.13. Evidence: learner explains why feed should come from an appropriate, quality-assured source; no sampling or testing by learners.
9. **Animal nutrition as a specialist topic** — the strategy links appropriate rations and quality feed with livestock production; pp.13 and 24. Evidence: learner recognises that animal diets differ by species and life stage and that ration design requires competent advice.
10. **Animal health and disease risk** — the strategy identifies animal health and disease as factors affecting livestock performance; sector situation discussion and pp.41–43. Evidence: learner distinguishes an observation (for example, an animal behaving unusually) from a veterinary diagnosis.
11. **Veterinary and para-veterinary roles** — the strategy calls for stronger veterinary and para-veterinary services to reduce disease risks; p.42. Evidence: learner identifies a veterinarian or authorised animal-health professional as the appropriate person for assessment.
12. **Disease prevention, monitoring and reporting** — the strategy describes reducing the introduction and spread of infectious agents through capacity to monitor, report and act; p.42. Evidence: learner explains a fictional reporting pathway to a responsible adult or authorised officer; learners do not investigate outbreaks.
13. **Biosecurity and movement risk** — the strategy treats biosecurity as protection against animal disease threats and invasive agents; pp.23, 29 and 42. Evidence: learner explains why animal and animal-product movement may be controlled to protect animal and community health.
14. **Animal welfare** — the strategy identifies animal welfare as a quality and safety concern and includes it in good-practice training; pp.23, 29 and 44–45. Evidence: learner identifies basic welfare needs from teacher-approved illustrations and explains that animals must be treated humanely.
15. **Husbandry as a connected set of practices** — the strategy lists production, nutrition, husbandry, hygiene, biosecurity, health and welfare together; p.44. Evidence: learner groups husbandry examples under care, housing, feeding, hygiene and health, using safe scenario cards.
16. **Hygiene and livestock-product safety** — the strategy connects food safety, quality standards and animal production; pp.23–25 and 37–38. Evidence: learner traces a fictional safe-product pathway and identifies points where hygiene matters.
17. **Quality assurance and laboratory roles** — the strategy proposes analytical and laboratory capacity for animal health products, livestock products and feeds; pp.29–30. Evidence: learner describes why specialist testing supports reliable quality claims.

### Safeguards, legal currency and curriculum mapping

- The 2016 Livestock Strategy is historical policy analysis. Its production statistics, productivity comparisons, prices, targets, institutional arrangements and proposals must not be represented as current.
- The Biosecurity Act 2008 legal text must be checked against the latest official consolidated version, amendments and subsidiary legislation before any legal rule is taught. This record does not establish current permit rules, offences or penalties.
- Do not teach disease diagnosis, treatment, vaccination schedules, medicine use, drug dosages, feed-ration formulation, slaughter, animal handling, specimen collection or outbreak investigation as learner tasks. These require qualified professionals and appropriate safeguards.
- No learner should touch sick, injured, dead, stray or unfamiliar animals; handle animal waste, blood, carcasses, raw animal products or veterinary medicines; enter animal housing or farms without approved supervision and risk assessment; or transport animals or animal products for a school activity.
- Use photographs, diagrams, fictional datasets and teacher-created scenarios. Respect animal welfare and avoid activities that frighten, restrain, injure or exploit animals.
- Food safety activities must use age-appropriate classroom examples only. Do not prepare or consume animal products as part of an activity without a separate approved food-safety assessment.
- Do not collect identifiable farmer, household, farm-location, animal-health or veterinary records from learners or their families.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Retrieve current Ministry livestock production and animal-health education materials; verify current livestock policy and Biosecurity Act consolidated text/subsidiary rules; page-check the 2024–2028 Strategic Development Plan; map concepts to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry achievement indicators; set year levels/prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

### Safeguards, rights and curriculum mapping

- The National Fisheries Policy 2024–2028 and Aquaculture Development Plan 2024–2028 contain policy objectives, targets and proposed actions. Do not represent them as official student achievement indicators or claim that planned targets have been achieved.
- The Aquaculture Act 2024 commencement notice and current subsidiary regulations must be verified before teaching any operative legal requirements. The Fisheries (Amendment) Act 2025 commencement date is recorded as 18 February 2026, but the consolidated Fisheries Act 1941 as amended and all applicable regulations must be checked before any legal-rule teaching.
- Do not teach fishing, diving, spear use, net setting, boat operation, aquaculture equipment operation, specimen collection, fish disease diagnosis, veterinary treatment, chemical use, or handling of live, injured or dead aquatic animals as learner tasks.
- No school activity should take learners onto reefs, mangroves, shorelines, rivers, boats, fish farms, hatcheries, landing sites or processing facilities without separate risk assessment, permissions, trained supervision and environmental safeguards. Use classroom diagrams, photographs and fictional datasets by default.
- Do not encourage learners to collect coral, shells, live organisms, eggs, juveniles, marine plants or protected species. Do not disturb habitats or remove organisms.
- Food safety and post-harvest activities must remain diagrammatic unless a separate approved food-safety assessment authorises supervised practice.
- Respect customary fishing rights, customary marine tenure, community protocols, local knowledge, consent and privacy. Do not ask learners to disclose household fishing locations, catches, licences, income or customary access details.
- Fisheries surveillance and enforcement data can be sensitive. Use fictional datasets only; do not reproduce vessel identities, personal data or operational enforcement details in learner activities.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Obtain and page-check the full Aquaculture Development Plan 2024–2028; verify Aquaculture Act commencement notice and regulations; retrieve the current consolidated Fisheries Act and relevant regulations; check current National Fisheries Policy implementation/successor status; map concepts to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry achievement indicators; assign levels/prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

### Safeguards, rights and curriculum mapping

- These are PacEdu-derived concepts, not official Fiji student achievement indicators. The NBSAP targets and coral action-plan priorities are national policy outcomes, not classroom standards.
- The full Fiji National Action Plan for Coral Reef Conservation must be retrieved and checked before extracting detailed targets, indicators or implementation commitments. The WCS launch report is only a summary.
- The Mangrove Guideline is a technical and community-management reference. Its recommendations do not replace current laws, agency approvals, landowner permissions or local customary protocols.
- Mangrove planting is not automatically appropriate at every site. The guideline emphasises normal hydrology, site ecology, informed consent and natural regeneration where suitable. Do not turn its planting schedules, species selection or survival benchmarks into universal instructions.
- Do not take learners onto reefs, mangrove mudflats, tidal channels, shorelines, boats, estuaries, rivers or restoration sites without separate risk assessment, permissions, trained supervision and accessibility arrangements. Use diagrams, photographs and fictional datasets by default.
- Learners must not collect coral, mangrove propagules, seedlings, shells, marine organisms or samples; climb or walk on coral; disturb roots or mudflats; handle wildlife; or plant/replant mangroves as an unsupervised class activity.
- Respect customary tenure, traditional authorities, community protocols, informed consent and equitable participation. Do not disclose or collect household fishing, land, qoliqoli, resource-use or location information.
- Do not reproduce copyrighted photographs, maps, diagrams or tables from the 2022 Mangrove Guideline or WCS action-plan materials without permission. Use original PacEdu diagrams and properly licensed sources.
- Treat climate statistics as dated observations requiring their underlying source, period, location and method. Never present a target or modelled prioritisation result as a completed conservation outcome.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Retrieve the full Coral Reef Conservation Action Plan; verify current legal and policy instruments for mangrove/coastal management; map concepts to approved Fiji NCF and official Ministry achievement indicators; assign year levels/prerequisites; complete rights review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 159 — Fiji native biodiversity, invasive alien species, species protection and biosecurity concepts

- **Record status:** SOURCE-REVIEWED SUPPLEMENTARY CONCEPTS; not an official student achievement-indicator set.
- **Concept count:** 40 PacEdu-derived concepts.
- **Subjects:** Elementary Science; Basic Science; Social Science; Agriculture; Technology; Mathematics; English.
- **Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED. Map only after approved Fiji curriculum and official year-level indicators are checked.
- **Prerequisites:** Basic living/non-living classification, habitat, organism, simple observation and comparison; adjust only after curriculum mapping.
- **Evidence approach:** Use teacher-provided photographs, original diagrams, fictional case studies and de-identified datasets. No field collection, handling, release, transport or eradication activity.

### Source A — Fiji Agricultural Journal, Volume 60, Issue 1 (July 2023)

- **Issuer:** Ministry of Agriculture & Waterways, Government of Fiji; journal editorial board and contributing researchers.
- **Journal PDF:** https://www.agriculture.gov.fj/documents/booklets/FAJ%202023%20Website.pdf
- **Copyright:** © Ministry of Agriculture, Republic of Fiji, 2023. The journal contains authored research and species-list material; do not assume all figures, photographs or article text are freely reusable. Extract concepts in PacEdu's own wording and complete rights review before reproducing source material.
- **Inspected sections:** pp. 3–9, “White and Black list of Fiji’s Invasive Alien Species”; journal contents pp. 1–2. Additional article titles are listed in the contents but not fully extracted here.
- **Lead article authors:** Senilolia H. Tuiwawa, Alivereti N. Naikatini, Marika V. Tuiwawa, Hilda Waqa-Sakiti and Lekima Copeland.
- **Important version limitation:** Article reports the technical committee's reviewed 74-taxon list, derived from a 2020 consultation and published in 2023. Its authors explicitly say the list is not exhaustive and should be updated, preferably every five years. Do not present it as the current 2026 authoritative list without checking the newer national framework and BAF data.
- **Classification:** FIJI_RESEARCH_PUBLICATION_CONCEPT; HISTORICAL_LIST_REQUIRES_CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK.

**PacEdu-derived concepts from Source A**

1. **Native range and introduced range** — compare an organism's natural geographical range with a place where people or natural pathways have introduced it. Evidence: learner distinguishes native-range and introduced-range examples on a fictional map.
2. **Introduced organism versus invasive organism** — presence outside a native range alone is not enough; the article's Fiji definition includes establishment, spread and harmful effects. Evidence: learner sorts case cards and explains why introduction and invasion are not synonyms.
3. **Naturalisation and establishment** — explain how an introduced organism may survive and reproduce in a new environment. Evidence: learner orders a fictional establishment sequence.
4. **Spread and abundance** — describe how distribution and population abundance can change over time. Evidence: learner interprets a teacher-provided time-series graph.
5. **Harm to native biodiversity** — connect invasive organisms with pressures on native species and ecological relationships. Evidence: learner completes a simple food-web impact diagram.
6. **Ecosystem services and human well-being** — consider ecological, social, economic and health dimensions of biological invasions. Evidence: learner sorts fictional impacts into environmental, livelihood and wellbeing categories.
7. **Habitat vulnerability** — compare how abiotic conditions, disturbance and interactions among organisms can affect susceptibility to invasion. Evidence: learner compares two fictional habitat profiles.
8. **Species-specific and habitat-specific effects** — recognise that a species may not have the same impact in every habitat. Evidence: learner avoids making a universal claim from one case study.
9. **Taxonomic groups and biodiversity recording** — classify recorded organisms into broad groups such as plants, fish, mammals, birds, land invertebrates and herpetofauna. Evidence: learner organises a supplied dataset into categories.
10. **Scientific names and common names** — understand that scientific names help distinguish organisms when local/common names vary. Evidence: learner matches a small teacher-checked name set without independently identifying wild organisms.
11. **Evidence-based species classification** — explain why expert review, taxonomic knowledge and field evidence are used to assess invasive status. Evidence: learner identifies evidence needed before making a classification.
12. **White-list and black-list categories as source-specific terms** — interpret the journal's 2023 categories accurately: black-listed taxa were described as widespread/problematic, while white-listed taxa were potential or habitat-limited risks in that paper. Evidence: learner explains the paper's definitions and notes that categories are not permission to import or move species.
13. **Uncertainty and missing biodiversity data** — identify how limited field observations or incomplete data affect confidence in a species assessment. Evidence: learner marks missing data and avoids treating unknown status as proof of safety.
14. **Monitoring and repeat assessment** — explain why species lists and conservation observations need periodic review. Evidence: learner compares two dated fictional monitoring records.
15. **Protected areas as biodiversity monitoring locations** — understand the role of protected-area networks in observing ecological change. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional monitoring-site map; no site visit implied.
16. **Awareness and public communication** — communicate why invasive-species awareness is relevant to biodiversity protection. Evidence: learner prepares an original, evidence-based short message using teacher-verified facts.
17. **Population distribution tables** — read counts by organism group and status category from a supplied table. Evidence: learner accurately describes a chart without assuming counts equal total national abundance.
18. **Data limitations in published checklists** — distinguish a checklist's recorded taxa from a complete inventory of all organisms present. Evidence: learner writes a limitation statement for a supplied dataset.

### Curriculum, rights, currency and safety controls

- All 40 entries are **PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT**, not official achievement indicators, CLOs or achievement standards. No source above supplies verified year-level outcomes for this record.
- The 2023 journal's white/black list is not exhaustive and was recommended for periodic update. Do not use its list to label a species' present-day legal status, safety, import eligibility or current invasive status without BAF/MECC confirmation.
- The 2026 NBSAP and NISFSAP are national strategies, not classroom syllabi. Retrieve and inspect the full NISFSAP and full NBSAP targets before extracting specific national targets, indicator wording or performance claims.
- Cabinet's reported totals (650+ non-native, 400+ invasive) require the underlying current inventory, definition, reference date and methodology before use in student calculations or public-facing claims.
- The Biosecurity Act portal summary is not a substitute for the current consolidated Act, regulations, amendments, commencement notices or BAF directions. Do not teach legal compliance as a definitive rule from this summary alone.
- Do not direct learners to collect, identify by handling, transport, release, feed, trap, poison, dissect, eradicate or biologically control plants, animals, insects, reptiles, fish, pathogens or other organisms. No student-led species control or import/export decisions.
- Do not encourage learners to approach suspected invasive iguanas, mongoose, cane toads, ants, snakes, feral animals or unknown plants. Use teacher-verified photographs and safe fictional data.
- Do not enter forests, protected areas, farms, waterways, islands or private/customary lands for survey work without permissions, risk assessment, trained supervision, accessibility planning and community protocols.
- Respect customary ownership, traditional knowledge, community consent and benefit-sharing. Do not solicit or publish sensitive species locations, rare-species nests, sacred sites or customary resource information.
- Use original PacEdu diagrams and data tables; do not copy journal photographs, tables, maps or substantial text without rights clearance. SPREP Public Licence applies only as stated by the portal and should be checked before reuse.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Required first: retrieve full NISFSAP; inspect full NBSAP targets; verify current BAF/MECC species inventory and legal controls; check rights; map each concept to approved Fiji NCF and official achievement indicators; assign level/prerequisite; complete teacher review.
