## Record 170 — Fiji Primary Ear Disease and Hearing Care Guideline (2019): hearing science, communication access and inclusive learning concepts

**Record status:** APPENDED — source-inspected supplementary concept extraction  
**Concept count:** 30  
**Classification:** All concepts are `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; this is a clinical practice guideline, not a Fiji curriculum syllabus or achievement-indicator document.  
**Source edition:** 2019, Fiji Ministry of Health and Medical Services; lead author Dr Chunghyeon Oh.  
**Currentness:** `CURRENT_VERSION_CHECK_REQUIRED`. The guideline says it should be reviewed every five years (p.4), so its scheduled review point was 2024. The Ministry's current Guidelines page still lists it, but listing does not confirm that its clinical content remains current.  
**Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED.  
**CAS contact:** `DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT`.

### Source inspected

1. **Clinical Guidelines: Primary Ear Disease and Hearing Care in Fiji.** Fiji Ministry of Health and Medical Services, 2019, 39 pages. Official Ministry PDF: https://www.health.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Clinical-Guidelines-Primary-Ear-Disease-and-Hearing-Care-in-Fiji.pdf. Inspected pp.3–4 (purpose, scope, authorship and five-year review statement); pp.16–23 (hearing assessment, communication, prevention, language development and noise); Annexes and service information only where relevant to the concept boundaries.
2. **Ministry of Health and Medical Services — Guidelines catalogue.** https://www.health.gov.fj/moh-standard-treatment-guidelines/. The catalogue currently lists “Clinical Guidelines Primary Ear Disease and Hearing Care in Fiji”; this confirms catalogue presence only, not a new edition or clinical validation.
3. **WHO — World Report on Hearing (2021).** https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020481. General international context for hearing care and communication access; not a Fiji curriculum outcome and not used to replace Fiji-specific clinical advice.

### Extracted concepts for later curriculum mapping

1. **Sound as vibration:** describe sound as a physical phenomenon involving vibrations travelling through a medium and reaching the ear. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Elementary Science, Basic Science. Source context: guideline pp.16–17.
2. **Sound frequency:** distinguish higher- and lower-frequency sounds as different properties of sound; use neutral audio examples, not assumptions about an individual's hearing. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Mathematics. p.21.
3. **Sound level and loudness:** explain that sound level can be measured and compared, while recognising that perceived loudness and hearing ability vary. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Mathematics. pp.16, 23.
4. **Decibel as a unit:** recognise decibels as a logarithmic unit used in sound measurement; any detailed calculations require a suitable approved science resource. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Mathematics, Basic Science. pp.16, 23.
5. **Audiometer:** identify an audiometer as specialist equipment used to measure hearing thresholds. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Technology. p.16.
6. **Hearing threshold:** explain at a basic level that a hearing threshold is the quietest sound level detected under specified test conditions. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Mathematics. p.16.
7. **Audiogram and data display:** interpret a teacher-provided fictional graph of sound frequency and hearing threshold, with no real learner health data. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Mathematics, Computer Studies, Science. pp.16–17.
8. **Screening versus diagnosis:** distinguish a screening check that identifies a reason for further assessment from a professional diagnostic assessment. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Healthy Living, Social Science. pp.16–19.
9. **Limits of informal tests:** explain that informal listening activities cannot diagnose hearing loss and must never be used to label classmates. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Healthy Living. pp.18–20.
10. **Ear structures and function:** recognise the outer ear, ear canal, eardrum and middle-ear structures as parts involved in hearing; detailed anatomy must be mapped to approved level-specific materials. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science. Contents and pp.6–15.
11. **Outer-ear and middle-ear distinction:** identify that the guideline separately discusses outer-ear and middle-ear conditions; use this only as broad health-literacy vocabulary, not diagnosis. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Healthy Living. Contents pp.2–15.
12. **Hearing and communication:** explain that access to spoken information may differ between people and that communication can use more than one mode. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Social Science, Healthy Living. pp.21–22.
13. **Sign language:** recognise sign language as a valid language and communication mode, not merely a substitute gesture system. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Social Science, Arts. pp.16, 19, 21.
14. **Lip-reading and visual communication:** identify face visibility, adequate lighting and clear visual access as factors that may support some people's communication preferences. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Arts, Technology. p.21.
15. **Gestures, pictures and objects:** describe how pointing, drawings, pictures and objects can supplement communication where useful and chosen by the person. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Arts, Technology. p.21.
16. **Multiple communication modes:** compare spoken language, sign language, written text, captions, pictures and tactile communication as different possible access modes; select according to individual preference, not assumptions. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Technology, Social Science. pp.19–22.
17. **Language development:** explain that rich access to language, stories, reading, conversation and early writing supports language learning; do not equate speech production with intelligence. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, ECE, Social Science. pp.21–23.
18. **Quiet learning environment:** identify how background noise and competing sound can make communication and listening more difficult for some learners. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Technology, Healthy Living. p.21.
19. **Classroom acoustics:** investigate sound reflections, background noise and room arrangement using safe, non-clinical classroom observations. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Technology, Mathematics. pp.21, 23.
20. **Accessible teacher communication:** explain why a teacher may gain attention before speaking, face the class, keep the face visible, speak clearly and provide written/visual instructions. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Social Science, Technology. p.21.
21. **Captions and written instructions:** identify captions, transcripts and written instructions as practical ways to make audio/video learning content accessible; this is a PacEdu-derived accessibility application, not a direct clinical prescription in the guideline. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Computer Studies, Technology.
22. **Assistive technology:** recognise hearing aids and specialist hearing equipment as technologies that may support some users, while recognising that users choose their own communication preferences. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Technology, Social Science. pp.16, 19, 21.
23. **Environmental noise protection:** explain that prolonged or excessive noise exposure can pose a risk to hearing and that reducing exposure is a prevention concept. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Science, Healthy Living, Technology. p.23.
24. **Noise measurement and workplace safety:** interpret a fictional noise-level chart and explain why workplace noise controls matter; do not treat the guideline's 2003 regulation quotation as confirmation of current legal limits. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Mathematics, Science, Social Science. p.23.
25. **Health information and stigma:** identify and challenge unfair assumptions that a person who does not respond to speech is inattentive, rude, uninterested or less capable. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Social Science, Healthy Living. p.23.
26. **Inclusive participation:** explain why people with hearing differences must have equal access to classroom discussion, group work, announcements, assessment instructions and school activities. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Social Science, English, Technology. pp.21–23.
27. **Individual communication choice:** recognise that communication strategies should be developed with the person and family/support network rather than imposed based on a hearing label. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Social Science, English, Healthy Living. pp.21–22.
28. **Referral pathways:** understand at a general health-literacy level that concerns about hearing should be discussed with a qualified health professional; school staff and learners do not diagnose or prescribe. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Healthy Living, Social Science. pp.18–20, 23.
29. **Prevention and public-health education:** identify safe, general prevention messages such as avoiding insertion of objects into the ear and seeking qualified help for ear concerns; do not turn clinical procedures into student practicals. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; Healthy Living, Science. pp.22–23.
30. **Evidence currency and review cycles:** explain why health guidance needs periodic review and why a document's continued presence on a website does not prove it is the latest edition. `PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT`; English, Mathematics, Computer Studies, Social Science. p.4 and current Ministry catalogue.

### Evidence, safety and accessibility controls

- The guideline is intended for medical officers, nursing practitioners, maternal/child health nurses and ear-screening officers (p.3). Its diagnostic pathways, clinical thresholds, treatment instructions, medicine doses, ear examination methods, ear cleaning, ear drops, ear flushing, ear mops/wicks and infant screening procedures are **not student activities** and must not be copied into learner worksheets.
- The guideline explicitly states that it should be reviewed every five years or earlier when audiology services change (p.4). Its 2019 edition reached its review point in 2024. The Ministry's present online catalogue lists it, but no replacement edition or review outcome was located during this search. Treat all clinical advice, statistics, referral-centre lists, thresholds and legal references as historical until verified against current official guidance.
- Historical prevalence figures in the 2019 guideline must not be represented as current Fiji prevalence. No learner or family member should be screened, tested, diagnosed, ranked or asked to disclose hearing status for a PacEdu activity.
- The educational concepts are suitable only for later age/level mapping. They are not official Fiji achievement indicators. Map against current approved NCF/CAS outcomes before use; retain `LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED` until then.
- Accessibility applications such as captions, transcripts, visual directions, sign-language access, tactile alternatives and learner-selected communication modes are PacEdu-derived applications. They must not be presented as verbatim Ministry policy requirements unless supported by a separate current authoritative source.
- Use fictional audio graphs, invented sound-level datasets and classroom acoustics examples. Never use a learner's audiogram, hearing aid settings, health record or identifiable disability information.
- Do not ask learners to insert objects into ears, use ear drops, inspect ears, perform hearing tests, use noisemakers to test babies, or conduct any clinical demonstration.
- **Rights review:** `RIGHTS_REVIEW_REQUIRED`. The Ministry PDF was inspected for concepts; no permission for reproduction, adaptation, translation or commercial worksheet use has been established. Use original paraphrases only pending written rights clearance.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Required: approved Fiji curriculum mapping; level/prerequisite assignment; current clinical source check; rights review; disability/accessibility review; teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** `DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT`.

## Record 171 — Fiji National Vital Statistics Report 2020–2022: civil registration, population data, statistical rates and evidence quality

**Record status:** PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT only. This is a national statistical report, not a Fiji curriculum syllabus, achievement indicator, health instruction or learner assessment standard. All 30 concepts below are original educational paraphrases derived from the cited report. **Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending mapping to approved Fiji NCF/CAS curriculum outcomes.

### Source register

1. **Primary source:** Fiji Bureau of Statistics (FBoS), *Republic of Fiji Vital Statistics Report 2020–2022*, published April 2026; compiled with support from the Ministry of Health and Medical Services Data Analysis Management Unit. Official PDF: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/download/246/report/6163/fiji-national-vital-statistics-report-2020-2022.pdf . Official report landing page: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/fiji-national-vital-statistics-report-2020-2022/ . Relevant sections: foreword and data provenance (printed pp. 2–3); summary indicators (p. 6); methodology and administrative data sources (pp. 7–13); births and fertility (pp. 14–22); mortality and life expectancy (pp. 23–31); appendices (pp. 32 onward).
2. **Issuing authority and date:** Fiji Bureau of Statistics; published April 2026. The report describes data primarily for 2020–2022; selected mortality series extend through 2023. Publication date must not be mistaken for observation period.
3. **Related official source:** FBoS report landing page confirms the report covers registered births, deaths and other vital events over the three-year period and draws on Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, Registrar-General and MHMS data: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/fiji-national-vital-statistics-report-2020-2022/ .

### Extracted teachable concepts — 30 entries

1. **Vital events as population data:** explain that births and deaths are examples of vital events recorded to describe population change. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science, Basic Science. Source: pp. 7–8. Observable evidence: learner classifies fictional events as vital or non-vital and explains the distinction.
2. **Civil registration purpose:** describe, at a general civic-literacy level, why governments maintain official records of births and deaths. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Source: pp. 7–12. Evidence: learner explains two public-planning uses without handling real personal records.
3. **Administrative data versus survey data:** distinguish records generated during service/registration processes from information collected through a sample survey or census. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 7–8, 10–13. Evidence: learner sorts fictional examples by data-collection method.
4. **Multiple data sources:** identify that one national indicator may be assembled from several administrative systems, each with a different role. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 8–12. Evidence: learner labels a simplified, fictional data-flow diagram.
5. **Data provenance:** identify who collected, maintained, compiled and published a dataset, and why those roles should be documented. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Computer Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 2–3, 8–12. Evidence: learner completes a source-and-custodian record for a fictional dataset.
6. **Record versus aggregate:** distinguish an individual record from a total count grouped by month, facility, year or region. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies. Source: pp. 8–11. Evidence: learner converts a fictional set of records into a tally table.
7. **Data reconciliation:** explain why totals from two systems may differ and why reconciliation is required before publication. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies. Source: pp. 10–11. Evidence: learner compares two invented totals and lists possible non-causal administrative explanations such as timing or duplicate/missing entries.
8. **Completeness of records:** interpret completeness as the proportion of expected records captured, and recognise that completeness can vary by year and source. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 10–11. Evidence: learner calculates a simple completeness percentage from fictional counts.
9. **Completeness above 100 percent:** explain that an estimated completeness value above 100% signals that the numerator and comparison estimate may not align perfectly; it is not proof that more than all real events occurred. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English. Source: p. 11. Evidence: learner writes a cautious interpretation of a fictional 102% administrative completeness estimate.
10. **Timeliness and delayed registration:** distinguish when an event occurs from when its record is entered, received or updated. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 10–11. Evidence: learner places fictional event and registration dates on a timeline.
11. **Data quality dimensions:** identify completeness, consistency, accuracy, timeliness and comparability as separate questions when evaluating a dataset. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies, English. Source: pp. 10–13. Evidence: learner applies a checklist to a synthetic table.
12. **Metadata and definitions:** explain why a statistical table needs a title, unit, population, time period, source and definition. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English, Computer Studies. Source: pp. 6–8, 12–13. Evidence: learner adds missing metadata to a fictional chart.
13. **Population denominator:** distinguish a count (numerator) from the population or event base (denominator) used to calculate a rate. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 12–13, 15–16. Evidence: learner identifies numerator and denominator in a fictional rate statement.
14. **Rate per 1,000:** calculate and interpret a rate expressed per 1,000, keeping the unit attached to the result. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 12–13, 15–16. Evidence: learner solves a fictional, non-health context problem and writes the unit correctly.
15. **Percentage versus rate:** distinguish a percentage from a rate per 1,000 or per 100,000 and convert only when the base is stated. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 12–13. Evidence: learner explains why 20 per 1,000 is not 20 percent.
16. **Crude rate:** describe a crude population rate as an overall measure that does not adjust for differences in population age structure. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 12–13, 15. Evidence: learner identifies the limitation in a fictional comparison.
17. **Age-specific rates:** explain why a rate can be calculated for a defined age group using the relevant group population as its denominator. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 12–13, 17–20. Evidence: learner matches fictional subgroup numerators and denominators.
18. **Age standardisation:** explain conceptually that standardisation helps compare populations with different age structures by applying a common reference population. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 12–13, 29–30. Evidence: learner describes the purpose using a non-health analogy; no advanced clinical interpretation.
19. **Confidence intervals:** interpret a confidence interval as a way of communicating statistical uncertainty around an estimate, not as a guarantee that a particular value is true. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 13, 15–20, 25–31. Evidence: learner compares fictional estimates and intervals in plain language.
20. **Comparing estimates cautiously:** identify that differences in data completeness, definitions, time coverage and denominators can affect comparisons between years or groups. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English, Social Science. Source: pp. 10–13, 17–20. Evidence: learner lists limitations before making a comparison.
21. **Time-series reading:** read a table or line graph across successive years, identify direction of change and avoid assuming that a trend will continue. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English. Source: pp. 14–18, 23–31. Evidence: learner describes a synthetic three-year trend and states one limitation.
22. **Graph construction and critique:** choose an appropriate chart for categorical counts or time-based rates and label axes, scale, units, years and source. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies. Source: pp. 14–18, 23–31. Evidence: learner constructs and critiques a chart from invented data.
23. **Disaggregation:** explain that aggregate totals can conceal variation across clearly defined groups or locations, and that disaggregation needs reliable data and careful interpretation. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 14–22, 24–30. Evidence: learner compares fictional regional totals without stereotyping groups.
24. **Classification systems:** recognise that standard classification systems help organise records consistently across institutions and time. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Computer Studies, Mathematics, Basic Science. Source: pp. 11–12. Evidence: learner sorts fictional non-sensitive events using a supplied codebook.
25. **Data-processing workflow:** describe a simplified workflow from collection and checking through coding, analysis, tabulation and publication. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Computer Studies, Mathematics, English. Source: pp. 8–13. Evidence: learner orders process cards and identifies a quality check at each stage.
26. **Digital and paper systems:** compare possible strengths and limitations of paper forms, electronic entry and data exchange, including the need for reliable power, equipment and connectivity. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Computer Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 8–12. Evidence: learner evaluates a fictional service's paper/electronic workflow without assuming that digitisation alone ensures accuracy.
27. **Population projections:** explain that a projection is an estimate built from assumptions and available demographic information, not a direct count of every person. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 12–13, Appendix 4. Evidence: learner distinguishes census count, administrative count and projection in a matching exercise.
28. **Statistics for public planning:** explain how population information can support planning for schools, infrastructure, services and resource allocation. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 7–8. Evidence: learner uses fictional population figures to justify a hypothetical planning choice.
29. **Responsible interpretation and uncertainty:** write a short evidence-based statement that separates what a table shows from what it cannot establish, including possible data gaps or changes in recording practice. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 7–13, 17–20. Evidence: learner produces a claim, supporting figure and limitation statement.
30. **Privacy, confidentiality and ethical data use:** explain why individual birth/death records and family details are sensitive, why public learning tasks should use synthetic or properly aggregated data, and why learners must not collect or disclose personal family/health information. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Computer Studies, English. Source: pp. 8–12 and the report's description of unit records. Evidence: learner identifies personal information in a fictional example and selects a privacy-preserving alternative.

### Curriculum mapping and classroom-use controls

- These are **30 PacEdu-derived concepts**, not official Ministry/CAS achievement indicators or official CLOs. They must not be entered into the official-indicator register as if copied from a Fiji syllabus.
- Potential subject mapping is Mathematics, English, Social Science, Computer Studies and Technology. Keep LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED until each concept is mapped to an approved Fiji NCF 2013/CAS outcome and age-appropriate prerequisite sequence.
- Use synthetic datasets only. Do not reproduce or ask learners to collect birth, death, fertility, ethnicity, family, medical-certificate or other identifiable personal records. Avoid tasks that invite students to disclose family histories or sensitive experiences.
- For numerical practice, create original fictional examples with neutral contexts (e.g., library books, school equipment or fictional island transport counts). If the report itself is used as a source for statistical literacy, use only carefully selected aggregated figures with the 2020–2022 observation period clearly stated and appropriate safeguarding/age review. Do not turn sensitive reproductive or mortality statistics into classroom discussion prompts for young learners.
- Do not treat the report's 2020–2022 values as current 2026 population indicators. The report's publication date is April 2026, but the principal observation period is historical; selected mortality series extend to 2023. For current population claims, locate the newest official FBoS release and verify its definitions and revision status.
- The report itself notes differences between administrative sources, varying completeness, use of population projections and uncertainty intervals. Preserve those limitations when deriving any example; do not present a single table as perfectly complete or exact.
- **Rights review:** RIGHTS_REVIEW_REQUIRED. FBoS website and report are official sources, but no permission for copying report tables, charts, substantial text, adapting figures or commercial worksheet reproduction has been established. Use original paraphrases and synthetic data unless a suitable licence or written permission is confirmed. Do not reproduce the report's tables or figures verbatim.
- **Clinical and safeguarding boundary:** this is a statistical and administrative report, not a clinical guide. Do not teach diagnosis, treatment, fertility counselling, mortality investigation or death certification. No student handling of real certificates, registers, datasets or identifiable records.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Required before activity creation: approved Fiji curriculum mapping, level/prerequisite assignment, rights review, age/safeguarding review, accessibility review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 172 — Fiji Employment and Unemployment Survey 2023–2024: work, enterprise, labour-market literacy and statistical interpretation

**Record status:** PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT only. The source is a national household labour-force survey, not a Fiji curriculum syllabus or official student achievement-indicator document. The 30 concepts below are original educational paraphrases. **Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending mapping to approved Fiji NCF/CAS outcomes.

### Source register

1. **Primary source:** Fiji Bureau of Statistics (FBoS), *Fiji Employment and Unemployment Survey 2023–2024: Main Report*, published February 2026, 120 pages. Official PDF: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/download/430/employment-2023-24/6078/2023-24-fiji-employment-and-unemployment-survey-main-report.pdf . Official landing page: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/2023-24-fiji-employment-and-unemployment-survey-main-report/ .
2. **Issuing authority:** Fiji Bureau of Statistics; report acknowledges technical support from the International Labour Organization (ILO). The report's main statistical reference year is 2024; the survey fieldwork spans 12 months. Do not confuse the February 2026 publication date with the observation period.
3. **Source sections:** methodology and sample design, printed pp. 12–13; executive summary and labour-force indicators, pp. 14–24; demographic and labour-force structure, pp. 25–38; employment and occupations, pp. 39–59; unemployment and labour underutilisation, pp. 60–70; informal employment, pp. 71–78; hours and earnings, pp. 79–97; subsistence work, pp. 98–102; functioning challenges and employment barriers, pp. 103–108; definitions and classifications, pp. 114–119.
4. **Rights:** the report explicitly permits reproduction and publication of any table or material without prior FBoS approval provided the source is identified and acknowledged (printed p. 2). This permission is recorded for source material; PacEdu should still cite FBoS and avoid exposing respondent-level or sensitive personal data.

### Extracted teachable concepts — 30 entries

1. **Work and economic activity:** explain that people contribute to economic and community life through different forms of work, including paid jobs and own-use production. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science, English. Source: pp. 39–42, 98–102, 114. Evidence: learner sorts fictional examples of work into supplied categories and explains the choice.
2. **Working-age population as a statistical definition:** recognise that labour statistics use a defined working-age population and that the survey's main working-age group is 15 years and above. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 14–15, 114. Evidence: learner identifies the population covered by a fictional indicator; do not apply adult labour definitions to children.
3. **Labour force:** explain that the labour force combines people in employment and people who are unemployed under the survey's stated criteria. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 30–31, 114–115. Evidence: learner completes a simple fictional classification diagram.
4. **Employment status:** distinguish employed, unemployed and outside-the-labour-force categories using the report's definitions and reference period. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Source: pp. 30–31, 114–115. Evidence: learner classifies neutral fictional scenarios and explains why a definition matters.
5. **Unemployment is not simply “not working”:** explain that the survey's unemployment definition includes criteria concerning seeking work and availability, so not every person without a job is counted as unemployed. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Source: pp. 114–115. Evidence: learner distinguishes three invented scenarios using a supplied definition card.
6. **Labour-force participation rate:** calculate a participation rate from a supplied numerator and working-age denominator, and explain what the percentage represents. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 30–38, 114–115. Evidence: learner calculates a rate from synthetic data and labels the denominator.
7. **Employment-to-population ratio:** distinguish the share of the working-age population in employment from the labour-force participation rate. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 44–49, 114–115. Evidence: learner compares two fictional indicators and explains why their denominators/meanings differ.
8. **Time-related underemployment:** describe a situation where an employed person wants and is available to work additional hours but works below the survey's specified hours threshold. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 63–65, 114–115. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional hours-worked scenario without assuming all part-time work is underemployment.
9. **Potential labour force:** explain that some people outside the labour force may have a marginal attachment to the labour market, for example being available but not actively seeking, or seeking but not currently available. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Source: pp. 63–65, 114–115. Evidence: learner distinguishes the supplied categories in a fictional example.
10. **Labour underutilisation measures:** recognise that unemployment alone does not describe every form of unused labour capacity; the report presents broader LU1–LU4 measures. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 63–65, 114–115. Evidence: learner matches a plain-language description to a supplied measure without memorising policy claims.
11. **Occupation versus industry:** distinguish the kind of work a person performs (occupation) from the economic activity of the establishment or industry in which the work occurs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 41–44, 118–119. Evidence: learner classifies fictional jobs by occupation and industry separately.
12. **Economic sectors and activities:** identify broad activity groupings such as agriculture, forestry and fishing, industry and services, and explain how these categories organise economic statistics. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Agriculture, Social Science. Source: pp. 41–42, 74–76, 118–119. Evidence: learner sorts fictional enterprises by activity.
13. **Employment status and work relationships:** distinguish employee, employer, own-account worker and contributing family worker as different work relationships. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 51–58, 118–119. Evidence: learner identifies the relationship in invented business scenarios.
14. **Independent and dependent work:** explain the difference between working independently on one's own account and working in a dependent relationship, using the report's classification framework. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 51–58, 118–119. Evidence: learner compares fictional work arrangements without making legal determinations.
15. **Formal and informal employment:** distinguish informal employment from informal-sector employment; a person may have informal employment even when the production unit belongs to the formal sector. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 71–78, 118–119. Evidence: learner uses a two-axis fictional example to avoid treating the terms as synonyms.
16. **Own-account work and microenterprise:** explain that own-account workers operate on their own behalf and that self-employment can involve household market enterprises. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Home Economics. Source: pp. 52–53, 76–77, 118–119. Evidence: learner develops a simple fictional microenterprise profile with roles and resources.
17. **Contributing family work:** recognise that people may contribute labour to a family enterprise without being classified as an employee or employer. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 52–53, 76–77, 118–119. Evidence: learner identifies tasks and roles in a fictional family business; do not normalise exploitative or unsafe child labour.
18. **Subsistence and own-use production:** distinguish producing goods primarily for household use from producing goods or services for sale, while recognising that households may combine both. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Agriculture, Home Economics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 98–102, 114. Evidence: learner classifies fictional garden, fishing and craft examples by intended use.
19. **Multiple economic activities:** explain that a person may have a main job and secondary economic activities, so one job title may not describe all work performed. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 14–15, 39–42. Evidence: learner represents a fictional work portfolio in a table.
20. **Working hours and reference periods:** read weekly hours and distinguish hours actually worked from usual hours or contracted arrangements. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 79–82, 114–115. Evidence: learner calculates weekly totals from fictional shift records and labels the measure used.
21. **Earnings versus wages:** distinguish wages received by employees from earnings generated through self-employment, and identify the measure and time period shown in a table. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 83–97. Evidence: learner reads a fictional income table without assuming that average earnings equal every worker's pay.
22. **Average and distribution:** explain that an average summarises a group and does not mean every individual receives that amount. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 83–97. Evidence: learner compares a mean with several fictional individual values and explains variation.
23. **Low pay as a defined statistical measure:** recognise that a low-pay indicator depends on a stated threshold and reference measure; it is not a complete judgement about an individual's living conditions. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 96–97, 118–119. Evidence: learner identifies the threshold in a supplied fictional example and states one limitation.
24. **Sampling and representativeness:** explain why a household survey samples selected households and uses its design to make estimates about a wider population. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: pp. 12–13. Evidence: learner distinguishes a sample from the population it represents.
25. **Stratified and two-stage sampling:** identify division/urban-rural strata, selection of enumeration areas, and subsequent selection of households as stages in the report's sample design. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies. Source: pp. 12–13. Evidence: learner orders a simplified fictional sampling flow diagram.
26. **Probability proportional to size and systematic random sampling:** explain at a basic level why larger enumeration areas may have a higher selection probability and how a fixed interval or systematic procedure can select households. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: pp. 12–13. Evidence: learner demonstrates a simple classroom selection using invented numbered cards, not real household data.
27. **Seasonality in work:** explain why a 12-month survey period can help capture seasonal differences in labour-market activity and why a single short snapshot may miss them. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Agriculture, Social Science. Source: pp. 12–13. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional seasonal work calendar.
28. **Classification standards and comparability:** recognise that common international classifications for occupations, industries and work relationships help make statistics more comparable across places and time. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Computer Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 4, 11, 118–119. Evidence: learner applies a supplied code list to fictional job descriptions.
29. **Disability inclusion and workplace barriers:** identify that access to work can be affected by environmental, communication, transport, equipment and workplace-support barriers; focus on removing barriers rather than assuming incapacity. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Technology, English. Source: pp. 103–108. Evidence: learner audits a fictional workplace for accessibility and proposes practical inclusive adjustments.
30. **Evidence-based career and skills planning:** explain how aggregate labour-market information can inform discussion of skills, training and changing economic activities, while recognising that national statistics do not predict an individual learner's future or prescribe a career. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, English, Social Science. Source: pp. 4, 14–15, 39–44. Evidence: learner compares fictional career pathways using interests, skills and public information without ranking learners by demographic group.

### Curriculum mapping and classroom-use controls

- All 30 entries are **PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT**, not official Ministry/CAS achievement indicators or CLOs. Keep them separate from the official-indicator register.
- Likely subject links: Commercial Studies, Mathematics, Social Science, English, Agriculture, Home Economics and Computer Studies. Keep LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED until mapped to approved Fiji NCF 2013/CAS outcomes and prerequisites.
- The report concerns people aged 15 years and above and adult labour-market definitions. Do not classify schoolchildren as unemployed, outside the labour force or NEET. Use neutral fictional adults or anonymised, aggregated public figures.
- Avoid classroom prompts asking learners to disclose household income, parents' employment, family debts, disability, ethnicity, migration status or employment insecurity. Do not ask learners to identify or rank classmates/families by income or work status.
- Use the report's figures only with the reference year (2024), denominator, unit and source clearly stated. Do not present 2024 survey estimates as current 2026 values. Preserve rounding notes and methodological limitations.
- The report itself states that totals may differ from component sums due to rounding. Keep this caveat in any derived numerical exercise.
- Do not treat correlations between education and labour-force indicators as proof that one causes the other. Avoid stereotypes about sex, age, ethnicity, rural/urban residence or disability; use the source for critical data literacy and equitable-access analysis, not deterministic claims.
- **Rights review:** the report states on printed p. 2 that tables and material may be reproduced without prior FBoS approval provided the source is identified and acknowledged. Record this permission and require clear FBoS attribution for any later permitted use. Do not disclose respondent-level or identifiable records.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Required: approved Fiji curriculum mapping, level/prerequisite assignment, age/safeguarding review, accessibility review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.

## Record 173 — Fiji Education 2024 Economic Survey: education establishments, financial literacy, resources and statistical interpretation

**Record status:** PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT only. This is an FBoS establishment survey about education as an economic activity, not a school curriculum or Ministry/CAS achievement-indicator document. The 30 concepts below are original educational paraphrases. **Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending mapping to approved Fiji NCF/CAS outcomes.

### Source register

1. **Primary source:** Fiji Bureau of Statistics (FBoS), *Economic Surveys: Education 2024*, published August 2026, 40 pages, ISBN 978-982-510-023-2. Official PDF: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/download/283/education/6586/2024-education.pdf . Official landing page: https://www.statsfiji.gov.fj/education-2024/ .
2. **Issuing authority and observation period:** Fiji Bureau of Statistics, Economic Statistics Division. The report was published August 2026 and reports establishment activity for calendar year 2024; persons engaged are counted as at 30 June 2024. Do not describe 2024 observations as current 2026 school conditions.
3. **Relevant source locations:** reproduction statement and scope (printed pp. iii–iv); survey methodology (pp. 2–4); response, establishment classifications and persons engaged (pp. 5–7); economic aggregates, capital formation, loans and comparison (pp. 8–10); concepts and definitions (pp. 11–12); composition of aggregates (pp. 13 onward); school and teacher series (Appendix IV, printed p. 30); school enrolment by sex (Appendix V, printed p. 31); macroeconomic series (Appendices VI–VII, printed p. 32).
4. **Rights statement:** printed p. iii states that any table or material in the report may be reproduced and published without prior FBoS approval, provided the source is identified and acknowledged in all modes of presentation. Retain clear FBoS attribution if any table or material is later reused. This permission does not remove privacy obligations or authorise disclosure of respondent-level information.

### Extracted teachable concepts — 30 entries

1. **Education as an economic activity:** explain that education establishments provide services and contribute to employment, production and the wider economy. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science, English. Source: pp. iv, 2. Evidence: learner describes two ways a fictional education provider contributes to its community and economy.
2. **Types of education services:** identify pre-primary, primary, secondary, technical/vocational, higher, sports/recreation, cultural and educational-support activities as distinct statistical categories. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 5–7. Evidence: learner sorts fictional provider descriptions using a supplied category list; do not confuse statistical categories with Fiji curriculum stages.
3. **Formal statistical classification:** explain why establishments are grouped using a standard industry classification such as FSIC 2010. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Computer Studies, Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 2, 5–7. Evidence: learner assigns fictional providers to a supplied classification and explains consistent coding.
4. **Statistical unit:** distinguish an establishment (the reporting unit in this survey) from an individual student, teacher, classroom or entire ministry. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies. Source: p. 3. Evidence: learner identifies the unit represented by each row in a fictional data table.
5. **Survey frame and business register:** explain that a survey frame is the list used to identify establishments for a survey and that registers require updating. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies, Commercial Studies. Source: p. 3. Evidence: learner identifies a coverage problem in a fictional outdated register.
6. **Questionnaire design:** recognise that a common questionnaire can collect comparable information about organisation type, income, expenditure, assets, liabilities and employment across different establishments. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: p. 3 and Appendix III. Evidence: learner matches sample questions to the data field they collect.
7. **Survey response rate:** calculate a response rate as returns received divided by the survey frame, multiplied by 100, and explain that response rate is not the same as data accuracy. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics. Source: p. 5. Evidence: learner calculates a fictional response rate and states one limitation.
8. **Non-response and follow-up:** explain why survey teams follow up missing returns and check omissions or inconsistencies before analysis. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 3–4. Evidence: learner sequences a fictional data-quality workflow.
9. **Estimation for non-respondents:** describe at a basic level why statistical agencies may estimate values for non-responding establishments and why estimates must be distinguished from directly reported observations. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: p. 4. Evidence: learner marks fictional table entries as observed or estimated.
10. **Size groups and rate-up factors:** recognise that the report groups establishments by number of persons engaged and uses group-based factors to estimate non-response. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: p. 4. Evidence: learner groups fictional businesses by staff-size bands and explains why like groups may be compared.
11. **Actual versus estimated tables:** identify that the report explicitly marks which tables contain actual survey data and which include non-response estimates. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English. Source: p. 5. Evidence: learner reads a table note before making a claim.
12. **Confidentiality and grouped reporting:** explain why some establishment categories are combined in published tables to protect the confidentiality of information supplied by businesses. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Computer Studies, English. Source: p. 5. Evidence: learner explains why small groups may be aggregated and why individual returns should not be exposed.
13. **Persons engaged:** distinguish the report's measure of persons engaged—which includes regular paid workers, working proprietors, active partners and unpaid family workers—from a count of employees only. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 6–7, 12. Evidence: learner identifies who is included in a fictional establishment headcount.
14. **Paid and unpaid work categories:** interpret separate counts for paid workers, proprietors and unpaid family workers without assuming they are interchangeable categories. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. 6–7, 12. Evidence: learner classifies invented roles in a fictional provider.
15. **Gender-disaggregated workforce data:** read a table showing male and female persons engaged and calculate totals or proportions accurately. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science. Source: p. 7. Evidence: learner interprets a synthetic two-category table without stereotyping occupations or individuals.
16. **Gross output:** explain that gross output represents the gross value of goods and services produced and other specified income during the accounting period. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 8, 11, 13. Evidence: learner identifies output items in a fictional service business.
17. **Intermediate consumption:** distinguish goods and services used up in production within the accounting period from employee compensation and long-lived fixed assets. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 8, 11, 13–15. Evidence: learner sorts fictional expenses into intermediate inputs or other categories using a supplied definition.
18. **Gross value added:** calculate value added as gross output minus intermediate consumption and explain why it helps measure an industry's contribution without double counting intermediate inputs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: pp. 8, 11, 13. Evidence: learner completes a worked example with fictional FJD amounts.
19. **Compensation of employees:** identify wages, salaries and specified employer contributions as components of employee compensation, distinguishing this from total establishment output. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 8, 11, 14–15. Evidence: learner interprets a fictional payroll summary.
20. **Consumption of fixed capital:** explain conceptually that equipment and buildings wear out over time and that accounting for this consumption differs from recording a new purchase. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Technology, Mathematics. Source: pp. 8, 11, 15. Evidence: learner distinguishes a repair expense, an asset purchase and depreciation-like consumption in a fictional scenario.
21. **Operating surplus:** recognise that operating surplus is a defined national-accounts measure derived after specified costs and adjustments, not simply cash left in a bank account. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 8, 11, 13. Evidence: learner explains why a simplified profit figure should not be confused with the report's defined measure.
22. **Gross fixed capital formation:** identify long-lived investment categories such as buildings, equipment, furniture, vehicles, ICT equipment, software and databases. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 9, 16. Evidence: learner classifies fictional purchases as current-use supplies or long-lived capital assets.
23. **Capital versus operating expenditure:** distinguish a long-lived asset investment from recurring expenses such as electricity, water, stationery, travel and cleaning services. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Mathematics. Source: pp. 9, 13–15. Evidence: learner sorts a fictional school's budget items and justifies the classification.
24. **Loans and advances:** interpret a table of closing loan balances and distinguish a loan balance from annual revenue, expenditure or grant income. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: p. 10. Evidence: learner labels fictional financial values by type and period.
25. **Year-on-year comparison:** calculate absolute and percentage changes between two reporting years, ensuring that the base year is identified. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: p. 10. Evidence: learner computes a change using invented values and states the comparison years.
26. **Current prices and inflation limitation:** recognise that values reported in current FJD prices are not automatically adjusted for price changes; comparisons over time may require an appropriate price index. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Source: p. 5. Evidence: learner explains why a nominal increase does not by itself prove a real increase in purchasing power.
27. **Rounding and symbols:** interpret the report's note that totals may differ because of rounding and that a displayed zero may mean nil or less than half the stated unit. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English. Source: p. v. Evidence: learner writes a cautious interpretation of a rounded table.
28. **Education supply and economic interdependence:** explain how education services connect with other industries through employment, purchases, investment and national accounts input-output relationships. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Commercial Studies, Social Science. Source: pp. iv, 2. Evidence: learner draws a simple fictional flow diagram linking an education provider with suppliers and households.
29. **School, teacher and enrolment statistical appendices:** read school/teacher counts and enrolment tables, identify the year and category, and distinguish establishment-level economic survey data from education-system administrative statistics. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Social Science, English. Source: Appendices IV–V, printed pp. 30–31. Evidence: learner extracts a value from a labelled table and notes its source and period.
30. **Evidence-informed resource planning:** use aggregated information about enrolment, staffing, buildings, ICT equipment and other capital items to explain how planners might assess education-sector capacity, while recognising that this establishment survey is not a direct measure of classroom quality, learner achievement or the full public-school system. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies, Technology, Social Science. Source: pp. 2–10 and Appendices IV–V. Evidence: learner writes a claim, supporting statistic and limitation using a fictional planning case.

### Curriculum mapping and classroom-use controls

- All 30 entries are **PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT**, not official Ministry/CAS achievement indicators or official CLOs. Do not transfer them into the official-indicator register as if extracted from a syllabus.
- Likely subject links: Mathematics, Commercial Studies, Social Science, English, Computer Studies and Technology. Keep LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED until mapped to approved Fiji NCF 2013/CAS outcomes and prerequisites.
- The survey is about establishments in the education industry. It explicitly excludes central government ministries and government-operated schools from this particular survey's coverage because those activities are covered under general-government statistics (printed p. 2). Do not treat the report's establishment totals as a complete census of every Fiji school or as a complete account of Ministry school expenditure.
- The report says some small units without regular paid workers may have been omitted; non-response was estimated; and some categories were combined to protect confidentiality. Preserve these limitations in any later numerical activity.
- Reported education-sector figures are for calendar year 2024 and current FJD prices. Do not describe them as 2026 conditions or inflation-adjusted values. The persons-engaged table is dated 30 June 2024.
- The appendices contain school and teacher numbers and enrolment by sex, but these are not achievement outcomes, attendance measures, learner progression records or evidence of individual school performance. Do not infer teaching quality, learner achievement or individual gender ability from these tables.
- Use original fictional school-enterprise budgets and synthetic data for student practice. Do not ask learners to disclose family income, school debt, staff salary or confidential financial records.
- **Rights review:** FBoS expressly permits reproduction of any table or material in this report without prior approval, provided the source is identified and acknowledged. If PacEdu later reproduces report material, retain FBoS attribution and the observation year. This permission does not extend to third-party material not owned by FBoS or override confidentiality.

## Record 174 — Fiji School Accessibility and Inclusion Assessment Form and Education in Emergencies and School Safety Policy: accessible environments, inclusive participation and preparedness

**Record status:** PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT only. The primary form is an administrative school self-assessment tool, and the policy is an operational safety framework. Neither is a Fiji student syllabus or official achievement-indicator document. The 30 concepts below are original educational paraphrases. **Level:** LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED pending approved Fiji NCF/CAS mapping.

### Source register

1. **Primary source:** Fiji Ministry of Education, *School Accessibility and Inclusion Assessment Form*, version 1.2, official PDF: https://www.education.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/SchoolAccessibilityInclusionForm_v1.2.pdf . The form asks school management committees and head teachers to assess accessibility, with participation from students with disabilities and parents where possible; a Disabled Persons Organisation may also assist. Relevant printed sections: general access and transport (pp. 1–2); WASH and buildings (pp. 2–3); specialist materials and equipment (p. 4); inclusion activities, specialist support, IEPs and policy (pp. 5–6); out-of-school inclusion section (p. 7).
2. **Supporting source:** Fiji Ministry of Education, *Education in Emergencies and School Safety Policy*, official PDF: https://www.education.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/EiE_Policy.pdf . The document states its objective, scope and three pillars at printed pp. 2–3; definitions at pp. 4–5; planning, multi-hazard assessment and preparedness at pp. 6–11; safe facilities, drills, continuity and risk-reduction education at pp. 12–18. The policy identifies its framework as aligned with Comprehensive School Safety and INEE minimum standards.
3. **Supplementary source:** Fiji Ministry of Education, *Revised Infrastructure Assessment Report — Suva-Nausori Urban Schools*, 2025, official PDF: https://www.education.gov.fj/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Revised-Infrastructure-Assessment-Report-Suva-Nausori-Urban-School-2-1.pdf . Search-indexed report text describes assessment stages, overcrowding, WASH adequacy, disability access, cyclone resilience and land availability; the PDF could not be fully opened during this extraction, so its detailed numerical criteria are not used as independently verified standards. The official launch statement reports assessments of 86 primary and secondary schools in the Suva–Nausori corridor: https://www.pmoffice.gov.fj/launch-of-the-infrastructure-assessment-report-for-suva-nausori-schools-25-02-2025/ .
4. **Currency and scope note:** Form version 1.2 and the policy are official Ministry documents, but their present operational status and any later replacement versions have not been confirmed. Treat them as source material for concepts, not as proof that every listed facility or procedure is currently compliant with law or latest technical standards.

### Extracted teachable concepts — 30 entries

1. **Accessible route to school:** identify how roads, paths, crossings and rainy-season conditions can affect whether learners can reach school safely and independently. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Technology, Healthy Living. Form: p. 1. Evidence: learner reviews a fictional route map and identifies access barriers without inspecting or identifying a real child.
2. **Entrance access:** explain why a school entrance needs a safe, usable route for people with different mobility needs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Mathematics, Social Science. Form: p. 1. Evidence: learner identifies design features on a fictional building plan.
3. **Ramps and steps:** recognise that steps can create barriers and that a properly designed, maintained ramp can provide an alternative route for some users. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Mathematics. Form: p. 1. Evidence: learner compares two fictional entrance diagrams; no construction or safety certification task.
4. **Handrails and safe movement:** identify handrails as one feature that may support safer movement on accessible routes and around facilities. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Healthy Living. Form: pp. 1–2. Evidence: learner labels a fictional accessible-facility diagram.
5. **Accessible shared spaces:** explain why assembly areas, libraries, first-aid rooms and recreation areas should be usable by all members of the school community. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Form: p. 1. Evidence: learner checks a fictional school plan for inclusion gaps.
6. **Accessible signage and wayfinding:** identify clear signs, tactile markers and other navigation cues as information-access features for people with different sensory access needs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Technology, Computer Studies. Form: p. 1. Evidence: learner proposes a simple accessible sign system for a fictional school.
7. **Emergency information accessibility:** explain why emergency procedures and information must be understandable and usable by people with different disabilities. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Social Science, Technology. Form: p. 1; Policy: pp. 2, 6–7. Evidence: learner adapts a fictional evacuation notice using plain language and visual/tactile alternatives.
8. **Accessible toilets:** identify ramp access, handrails, usable space and appropriate layout as features relevant to accessible sanitation. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Healthy Living, Social Science. Form: p. 2. Evidence: learner identifies access features on a fictional toilet-block plan; no learner physical inspection.
9. **Accessible handwashing:** explain why taps, soap and handwashing points need to be reachable and usable by learners with different mobility needs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Healthy Living, Technology. Form: p. 2. Evidence: learner proposes an accessible arrangement in a fictional WASH layout.
10. **Accessible drinking water:** identify access to drinking water as an inclusion and school-wellbeing issue, not only a supply-volume issue. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Healthy Living, Social Science, Technology. Form: p. 2. Evidence: learner compares two fictional water-point layouts.
11. **Building access data:** interpret counts of buildings, storeys and classrooms and distinguish the total number from the number accessible to users with mobility needs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Computer Studies. Form: pp. 2–3. Evidence: learner calculates an access proportion from synthetic building data.
12. **Transport accessibility:** identify adapted transport and other transport arrangements as factors affecting access to and from school. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Technology. Form: p. 3. Evidence: learner compares fictional transport options using safety, access and reliability criteria.
13. **Accessible learning materials:** recognise Braille books, audiobooks, hearing loops, modified furniture, grip aids, screen readers and large-print signage as examples of different access supports. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Technology, Computer Studies. Form: p. 4. Evidence: learner matches a fictional access barrier to a possible support without assuming every learner needs the same support.
14. **Assistive technology and choice:** explain that assistive tools can provide alternative ways to read, listen, communicate, write or navigate, and that selection should respond to the user's preferences and needs. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, English, Social Science. Form: p. 4. Evidence: learner describes two possible access routes to the same learning resource.
15. **Availability versus adequacy:** distinguish whether a school has a resource from whether it has enough of the resource, whether it works and whether the intended users can access it. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies, Technology. Form: p. 4. Evidence: learner evaluates a fictional inventory with quantity and condition columns.
16. **Specialist support roles:** identify examples of specialist support roles listed in the form, such as Braille specialists, sign-language interpreters, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and visiting special-education specialists. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Form: pp. 5–6. Evidence: learner matches fictional support needs to professional roles at a general awareness level; no diagnosis or referral decision.
17. **Support availability and scheduling:** interpret a schedule showing whether specialist support is available weekly, monthly or at longer intervals, and explain why availability frequency matters for planning. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Form: pp. 5–6. Evidence: learner reads a fictional service calendar.
18. **Individual Education Plans as coordinated support:** recognise an IEP as a school support-planning mechanism for an individual learner and understand that personal plans are confidential. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Social Science. Form: p. 6. Evidence: learner explains the purpose using a fictional, anonymised case; never request or expose a real IEP.
19. **Family and learner participation:** explain why learners and parents/guardians should have a meaningful voice in planning accessible school environments and supports. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Social Science. Form: pp. 1, 6. Evidence: learner identifies respectful consultation methods in a fictional school-planning scenario.
20. **School management responsibilities:** identify school management and head-teacher roles in reviewing accessibility, recording gaps and planning improvements. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, Commercial Studies. Form: pp. 1, 6. Evidence: learner orders a fictional school-improvement workflow.
21. **Disability inclusion policy:** explain why a school policy should state practical actions for inclusion and be reviewed periodically. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; English, Social Science. Form: p. 6. Evidence: learner identifies whether a fictional policy statement includes an action, responsibility and review date.
22. **Multi-hazard awareness:** identify that school safety planning considers multiple hazards and local conditions rather than focusing on only one type of emergency. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Basic Science, Social Science, Healthy Living. Policy: pp. 3–6. Evidence: learner sorts fictional hazards into a school safety planning chart.
23. **Hazard, vulnerability and capacity:** distinguish a hazard from the vulnerability of people or buildings and from the resources/capabilities available to respond. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Basic Science, Mathematics, Social Science. Policy: pp. 4–6. Evidence: learner analyses a fictional, non-graphic scenario using the three terms.
24. **Risk assessment process:** describe a basic sequence of identifying hazards, considering who may be affected, evaluating likelihood and possible severity, checking precautions and reviewing findings. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, Basic Science, Social Science. Policy: pp. 6–7. Evidence: learner completes a paper-based risk matrix for a fictional classroom scenario; no unsupervised inspection.
25. **Whole-school safety roles:** explain why students, teachers, school leaders, families, education authorities and technical specialists need clear roles in school safety planning. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Policy: pp. 2, 6–8. Evidence: learner matches fictional responsibilities to stakeholder roles.
26. **Preparedness and practice:** explain how rehearsed procedures and drills can help a school community understand its emergency roles and reveal weaknesses in plans. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Social Science, English. Policy: pp. 7–11. Evidence: learner identifies the purpose of a supervised school drill from a fictional case; PacEdu must not independently schedule or conduct drills.
27. **Continuity of education:** explain why schools plan how to continue or restore learning when electricity, water, buildings or normal operations are disrupted. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Computer Studies, Social Science. Policy: pp. 4, 6, 12–15. Evidence: learner designs a fictional continuity flowchart using printed/offline learning alternatives.
28. **Safe facilities and maintenance:** identify routine maintenance, safe building condition, accessible design and risk reduction as connected parts of a safe learning environment. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Technology, Mathematics, Commercial Studies. Policy: pp. 2, 12–15. Evidence: learner categorises fictional maintenance items by urgency using a supplied, non-technical checklist.
29. **Risk-reduction education:** explain how hazard awareness and practical problem-solving can help communities reduce vulnerability, while recognising that technical safety decisions belong to qualified authorities. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Basic Science, Social Science, English. Policy: pp. 2–3, 7–8, 15–17. Evidence: learner proposes a safe, age-appropriate prevention message for a fictional school.
30. **Accessibility audit and improvement tracking:** use a fictional checklist to identify a barrier, record a proposed improvement, assign a responsible role and set a review date. PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT; Mathematics, English, Technology, Commercial Studies. Form: pp. 1–6; Policy: pp. 6–7, 12–15. Evidence: learner completes an anonymised improvement log with no real disability or health data.

### Curriculum mapping and safeguarding controls

- All 30 concepts are PACEDU_DERIVED_CONCEPT, not official Ministry/CAS achievement indicators or CLOs. Keep them separate from the official-indicator register.
- Potential subjects: Social Science, English, Mathematics, Technology, Computer Studies, Basic Science and Healthy Living. Keep LEVEL_NOT_SPECIFIED until mapped to approved Fiji NCF 2013/CAS outcomes and prerequisites.
- The form includes a section requesting names, locations, ages, sex and functioning difficulties of primary-age children with disabilities who are not attending school (printed p. 7). **Do not reproduce this personal-data collection in PacEdu learner activities, student files or public dashboards.** Do not ask students to identify children with disabilities, disclose diagnoses, or report family circumstances. Any genuine administrative collection must remain under authorised school/MoE governance, consent, access controls and privacy law.
- The form also asks about vision/hearing screening programmes and specialist staff. PacEdu must not screen, diagnose, classify or score learners' disabilities. Use fictional scenarios and inclusive design examples only.
- Do not make learners test ramps, toilets, buildings, electrical systems, evacuation routes or structural safety. Do not conduct drills or simulate hazardous emergencies through PacEdu. Practical school safety assessment and evacuation drills are for authorised school leadership and qualified personnel.
- The 2025 Suva–Nausori infrastructure report PDF could not be fully inspected during this record. Its indexed text mentions alternative classroom-space assumptions (including 1.1 m², 1.5 m² and 2 m² per student in different references), demonstrating why no single classroom area ratio should be copied into PacEdu as a universal legal minimum without checking the full report, building code and current Ministry standards.
- The 2022 EiE policy refers to historic instruments and standards. Confirm current policy, legal requirements, technical building standards, WASH standards and emergency instructions before any compliance claim or operational use.
- **Rights review:** RIGHTS_REVIEW_REQUIRED for reproduction/adaptation of the form and policy. They are publicly accessible Ministry documents, but no explicit open licence or permission for commercial worksheet adaptation was established. Use original paraphrases and source citations pending rights review.
- **Worksheet gate:** NOT YET AUTHORISED. Required: approved Fiji curriculum mapping, level/prerequisite assignment, source-currentness review, rights review, privacy and disability-inclusion review, accessibility review and teacher review.
- **CAS contact:** DEFERRED_UNTIL_PILOT.
